en: The Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-five Thousand Lines, Part II.
Then, indeed, all those great kings who were in this triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system gathered together in that very assembly along with many thousands of sons of gods;
likewise Śakra, the lord of the gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, and the Brahma-pārṣadya gods.

As far as the Great Brahmās, and those gods of Limited Light within this triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, up to the gods belonging to the Pure Abodes— all these, together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gods belonging to the Pure Abodes,
had assembled in that very assembly. And there was the bodily radiance of those gods belonging to the Four Great Kings, born of the ripening of their karma.

And whatever bodily radiance produced by the ripening of karma belongs to the sons of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, the Nirmāṇarati heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven, and so on up to the Śuddhāvāsa host, it does not approach even a hundredth part of the natural radiance of the Tathāgata; it does not approach a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousand-billionth part; it does not approach any number, fraction, calculation, comparison, or resemblance whatsoever.

In the presence of the Tathāgata’s radiance, the radiance of those gods does not endure. Only the radiance of the Tathāgata is declared to be foremost, the eldest, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, the most refined, the unsurpassed, the peerless, and the ever-surpassing. It is just as, for example, when black iron does not gleam, does not glow, and does not shine in the presence of Jambūnada gold.

In the same way, in the presence of the natural radiance of the Tathāgata, that radiance of the gods produced by the ripening of karma does not shine, does not glow, and does not gleam. Only the radiance of the Tathāgata is declared among them to be the foremost,
the eldest, the best, the most excellent, and the most sublime.

"It is proclaimed as excellent, unsurpassed, peerless, and ever-surpassing. Thus was the obscuration of the gods' splendor effected; then indeed Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the venerable Subhūti:

"Venerable Subhūti, all those gods in this trichiliocosm— the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, up to the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm— all have assembled to hear the venerable Subhūti’s exposition of the perfection of wisdom."
They desired to hear the instruction on the perfection of wisdom. "And how, Venerable Subhūti, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva stand in the perfection of wisdom?
And what is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?"

When this suitability had been thus stated, the venerable Subhūti said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "In that case, Kauśika, through the power of the Buddha and through the empowerment of the Buddha, I shall teach the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, as it is [to be practiced] by a bodhisattva, the mahāsattva."
One should abide in the perfection of wisdom.

And those sons of the gods who have not yet generated the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment should generate that mind for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. However, those who have already entered the fixed course of realization are incapable of generating the mind for unexcelled [enlightenment].
To generate the mind set on perfect enlightenment. For what reason?
Because they have established a boundary against the stream of saṃsāra.
Thus is the restriction of the object.
Moreover, I indeed rejoice even in them if they should generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. This is the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
"I do not create an obstacle to their side of wholesome qualities"—this is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
One should take as one's objective support those dharmas that are most distinguished among distinguished dharmas.
Thus has the activity been described, beginning with the "darkening" [of the world] and so forth.
In this regard, Kauśika, what is the *prajñāpāramitā* of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
Here, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through mental states associated with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), [regards] form as impermanent...

He attends to it as suffering, as non-self, as peace, as a disease, as an abscess, as a thorn, as a calamity, as alien, as subject to disintegration, as unstable, as fragile, as fearful, as a portent, and as a disaster—and he does so by way of non-apprehension.
He attends likewise to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and similarly to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

In this way, one attends to the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element as impermanent; one attends to them as suffering, as non-self, as peaceful, as a disease, as a boil, as a thorn, as a calamity, as alien, as subject to destruction, as unstable, as fragile, as fearful, as a portent, and as a misfortune— doing so by means of non-apprehension and in connection with omniscience.

By means of the production of the thought [of awakening], he thus attends to the formative forces conditioned by ignorance as impermanent, as suffering, as non-self, as peaceful, as a disease, as an abscess, as a thorn, as a calamity, as alien, as subject to destruction,
as unstable, as fragile, as fearful, as a portent, and as a misfortune; and [he attends to] consciousness conditioned by the formative forces, and name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.

With name-and-form as condition, the six sense-bases arise; with the six sense-bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being. Thus occurs this entire great mass of suffering.

He attends to the origin of the mass of suffering as impermanent, as suffering, as non-self, as peaceful, as a disease, as an abscess, as a thorn, as a calamity, as alien, as subject to destruction, as unstable, as fragile, as fearful, as a portent, and as a misfortune; and he does so by means of non-apprehension, through the production of the thought of mind associated with omniscience.

He attends to the cessation of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) due to the cessation of ignorance, [viewing it] as selfless, peaceful, secluded, empty, signless, wishless, and unconditioned. Due to the cessation of formative forces, there is the cessation of consciousness;

due to the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form; due to the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases; and due to the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact.
From the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging;

from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; and from the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering, and that [cessation] is due to selflessness.
He attends to it as peaceful, as secluded, as empty, as signless, as wishless, and as without formative activity,
and he does so by way of non-apprehension through mental engagements associated with omniscience.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a mind associated with omniscience, [cultivates] the four...
He cultivates the foundations of mindfulness, and that by way of non-apprehension. Likewise, he cultivates the four right efforts,
the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path,
the four immeasurables, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the four [fearlessnesses].

He cultivates the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha through mental engagements associated with omniscience, and that by way of non-apprehension.
Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, with a thought of mind-generation associated with omniscience...
He practices the perfection of generosity, and that by way of non-apprehension. Likewise, with mental states associated with omniscience,

he practices the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, and that by way of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom joins phenomena with phenomena in this way; moistening, saturating, fulfilling, and pervading phenomena with this very nature of phenomena, he contemplates them, [seeing that] "all these phenomena are indeed selfless, devoid of self and what belongs to a self. For what reason?
For it is thus: that mind of roots of goodness belonging to a bodhisattva mahāsattva is not conjoined with the thought of awakening;

that mind of dedication is not conjoined with either the thought of awakening or the mind of roots of goodness; and that thought of awakening is not conjoined with the mind of dedication. Why is that?

Kauśika, that which is the thought of awakening does not exist and is not apprehended within the thought of dedication; that which is the thought of dedication does not exist and is not apprehended within the thought of awakening. This, Kauśika, is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, in that he thus examines all phenomena and yet does not adhere to or apprehend any phenomenon whatsoever.
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the elder Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti, how is it that the mind of dedication is not conjoined with the mind of awakening?
And how is it that the mind of awakening is not conjoined with the mind of dedication?"
"How is it that the thought of dedication is not found and is not apprehended within the thought of awakening?
And how is it that the thought of dedication is not found and is not apprehended within the thought of awakening?
Subhūti said:

Kauśika, that mind of dedication is no-mind; that mind of awakening is no-mind. For one does not dedicate within the state of no-mind by means of the state of no-mind. Thus, that which is no-mind is inconceivable; that which is inconceivable is no-mind. It is by dedicating within the state of no-mind by means of the state of no-mind that this becomes the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, Kauśika.
Thus is the establishment of the sixteen aspects based on the four truths of the path of the śrāvaka.
Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti:
“Excellent, excellent!”
“Excellent, Subhūti, truly excellent, Subhūti, that you thus instruct the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, in the perfection of wisdom and inspire them with enthusiasm.
Subhūti said:
“O Blessed One, I must be grateful and not ungrateful;

for, Blessed One, while formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, I was instructed, exhorted, and shown the way in the six perfections by those disciples in the presence of the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.”
Having been encouraged, gladdened, incited, settled, and established— since the Blessed One, while still a bodhisattva,
trained in the six perfections and thereby fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment— even so, Blessed One,
must we also instruct and admonish the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, in the six perfections.

"We ourselves must demonstrate, incite, inspire, gladden, establish, and settle the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; having been exhorted, instructed, demonstrated, inspired, gladdened, incited, established, and settled by us, they will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

"In that case, Kauśika, listen and pay close and careful attention; I shall speak of how a bodhisattva mahāsattva should stand in the perfection of wisdom and how they should practice. Kauśika, form is empty of form; feeling..."
Perception, mental formations, and consciousness, Kauśika, are empty of consciousness; a bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva.
For thus, Kauśika, that which is the emptiness of form and that which is the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—
And that which is the emptiness of a bodhisattva—this is non-dual and indivisible. For it is thus, Kauśika, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the eye is empty of the eye; likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the mind; and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
For thus, that which is the emptiness of the eye,
that which is the emptiness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind,
and that which is the emptiness of the bodhisattva—
This is non-dual and indivisible. Thus, Kauśika, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Kauśika, the earth element is empty of the earth element. Likewise, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element are empty of the consciousness element;
the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.

For thus, the emptiness of the earth element, the emptiness of the water element, the emptiness of the fire element, the emptiness of the wind element, the emptiness of the space element, the emptiness of the consciousness element, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva—these are non-dual and not divided into two. In this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika:

Ignorance is empty of ignorance. Likewise, the formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age and death are empty of old age and death. The cessation of ignorance is empty of the cessation of ignorance.
Likewise, the formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, and birth...
The cessation of old age and death is empty of the cessation of old age and death; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.

Thus, the emptiness of ignorance and the emptiness of the cessation of ignorance, up to the emptiness of old age and death and the emptiness of the cessation of old age and death, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva—these are non-dual and not divided into two. It is in this way, Kauśika, that by a bodhisattva...
A mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Kauśika, the perfection of giving is empty of the perfection of giving. Likewise, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are each empty of the perfection of wisdom.

A bodhisattva is empty of a bodhisattva; for indeed, the emptiness of the perfection of generosity and the emptiness of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the emptiness of the bodhisattva—these are non-dual and not divided into two. Furthermore, Kauśika, internal emptiness is empty of internal emptiness. Likewise, external emptiness and internal-external emptiness [are empty].

Up to the point where the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is empty by way of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and the bodhisattva is empty of being a bodhisattva—thus, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva: these are non-dual and not divided into two.

Furthermore, Kauśika, the applications of mindfulness are empty of the applications of mindfulness. Likewise, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the superknowledges, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.

For thus, the emptiness of the applications of mindfulness up to the emptiness of the unique attributes of a buddha, and the emptiness of the bodhisattva—these are non-dual and indivisible. Furthermore, Kauśika, concentration is empty of concentration; the gateways of mnemonic formulas are empty of the gateways of mnemonic formulas; and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva.
Thus, indeed, the emptiness of meditative concentration, the emptiness of the gateways of mnemonic formulas (dhāraṇī), and the emptiness of the bodhisattva—these are non-dual and indivisible.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the vehicle of the disciples is empty of the vehicle of the disciples; the vehicle of the solitary buddhas is empty of the vehicle of the solitary buddhas;
the Great Vehicle is empty of the Great Vehicle; the disciple is empty of being a disciple; and the solitary buddha is empty of being a solitary buddha.

The bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva; the Buddha is empty of Buddhahood. Thus, the emptiness of the Śrāvaka vehicle up to the emptiness of the Mahāyāna, and the emptiness of the Śrāvaka up to the emptiness of the Buddha—these are non-dual and indivisible. It is in this way, Kauśika, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [should practice] in the perfection of wisdom.
"One must abide [in this way]. This was the "Heat" stage (*uṣmagata*).
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the elder Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)?"
Subhūti said:

"In this regard, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in form, nor in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations, nor in consciousness by way of apprehension. One should not abide in the eye, nor in form."
One should not abide in eye-consciousness; one should not abide in eye-contact; one should not abide in the feeling born of eye-contact.
Likewise, one should not abide in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; one should not abide in mental objects; nor should one abide in mind-consciousness.

One should not abide in mental contact; one should not abide in the feeling born of mental contact by way of apprehension. One should not abide in the earth element; one should not abide in the water element; one should not abide in the fire element; one should not abide in the wind element; one should not abide in the space element; one should not abide in the consciousness element.

One should not abide by way of apprehension in the applications of mindfulness. Likewise, one should not abide by way of apprehension in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the superknowledges, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the specific perfect knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha. One should not abide in the fruit of stream-entry; likewise, one should not abide in the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood, or even in Buddhahood itself—by way of apprehension. This is the stage of the summits (*mūrdhagata*).
One should not abide in the thought that "form is permanent," nor likewise that it is "impermanent," "pleasant," "painful," "self," "non-self," "peaceful," "unpeaceful," "secluded," or "unsecluded.

One should not abide in the thought that "form is empty" or "not empty," "with signs" or "signless," "wished for" or "wishless," by way of apprehension. [The same applies to] feeling, perception, and mental formations.

One should not abide in the notion that consciousness is permanent; likewise, one should not abide in the notions that it is impermanent, pleasant, painful, self, non-self, peaceful, unpeaceful, secluded, or unsecluded. Consciousness is empty.

Thus, one should not abide by way of apprehension in [the notions] "it is empty," "it is non-empty," "it has signs," "it is signless," "it is with aspiration," or "it is aspirationless. Likewise, one should not so abide in the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and factors of dependent orignation—whether taken individually or collectively; nor in the perfections, the factors conducive to awakening, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the truths, the superknowledges, the meditative absorptions, or in all the doors of the dhāraṇīs.
Regarding the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, up to and including omniscience—

one should not abide in the notion that any of these are permanent; likewise, one should not abide in the notions that they are impermanent, pleasant, painful, self, non-self, peaceful, unpeaceful, secluded, or unsecluded.
One should not abide in the thought that "it is empty," "it is non-empty," "it has signs," "it is signless," "it is with aspiration," or "it is without aspiration," by way of apprehension.

Furthermore, Kauśika, one should likewise not abide in the thought that "the fruit of stream-entry is characterized by the unconditioned," nor should one abide in the thought that "the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or the state of a pratyekabuddha is characterized by the unconditioned."

One should not abide in the thought that "Buddhahood is characterized by the unconditioned. One should not abide in the thought that "the stream-enterer is worthy of offerings," nor likewise for the once-returner or the non-returner.

One should not abide in the notion that "the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Tathāgata are worthy of offerings," by way of apprehension. Furthermore, Kauśika, regarding the stage of patience (*kṣāntigata*), a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in the first bhūmi;
likewise, he should not abide in the second bhūmi, the third bhūmi, the fourth bhūmi, the fifth bhūmi, or the sixth bhūmi.

One should not abide in the seventh ground, the eighth ground, the ninth ground, or the tenth ground by way of apprehension. One should not abide [thinking], "Abiding in the first production of the thought of awakening, I shall fulfill the perfection of generosity.

Likewise, one should not abide [thinking], "I shall fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, or the perfection of wisdom."

One should not abide in the thought, "I shall fulfill [them]," by way of apprehension. Likewise, one should not abide in the thought, "I shall fulfill the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path," by way of apprehension. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in the thought, "I shall enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva," by way of apprehension. Nor should one abide in the thought, "Having entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva, I shall stand upon the stage of non-retrogression."

Even so, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide by way of apprehension. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide by way of apprehension with the thought, "I shall fulfill the five superknowledges. Having stood in the five superknowledges of a bodhisattva, one should not think, "I shall approach incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite Buddha-fields."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in the apprehension of a referent when thinking, "Having heard that I shall go to see, pay homage to, worship, attend upon, and listen to the Dharma from the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and having heard it, I shall practice in accordance with suchness and teach the Dharma to others. And as for the nature of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones...

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in the thought, "I shall bring such buddha-fields into existence," by way of apprehension. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in the thought, "I shall bring sentient beings to maturity for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening," by way of apprehension. Having gone to immeasurable and incalculable world-systems...
Thinking, "I shall honor, revere, and respect the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones," one thinks,
"I shall worship those Tathāgatas with hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and fine cloths."

Even so, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in the thought, "I shall establish immeasurable and incalculable beings in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. He should not abide in the thought, "I shall produce the five eyes"—
that is, "I shall produce the flesh eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the Buddha eye."

One should not abide with the thought, "I shall accomplish all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). Nor should one abide with the thought, "Whichever meditative concentration I desire to sport with, by that very concentration I shall sport. One should not abide with the thought, "I shall accomplish all gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇīmukha*). One should not abide with the thought, "I shall accomplish the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). [Likewise, one should not abide with the thought of accomplishing] the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in the thought, "I shall accomplish [the powers]," nor should they abide in the thought, "I shall accomplish the four grounds of self-confidence," nor should they abide in the thought, "I shall accomplish the four analytical knowledges," nor should they abide in the thought, "I shall fully accomplish the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha," by way of apprehending them as real entities. [Likewise, they should not abide in the thought,] "I shall [accomplish] great loving-kindness..."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in the thought, "I shall bring about great compassion," nor should he abide in the thought, "I shall bring about the thirty-two marks of a great man upon my body. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in the thought, "I shall bring about the eighty secondary characteristics," by way of apprehension. [This applies to] the follower by faith, the follower of dharma, and the eighth-rank practitioner.

One should not dwell on the thought that "the stream-enterer has seven births at most. One should not dwell on the thought that "he is a family-to-family practitioner" or "a one-interval practitioner. One should not dwell on the thought that "this person is one who has reached the same level [as the Buddhas]. One should not dwell on the thought that "at the exhaustion of life and the exhaustion of afflictions [I shall attain parinirvāṇa].

One should not dwell on the thought that "the stream-enterer is by nature not subject to falling into the lower realms. [Likewise,] regarding the once-returner who, having come to this world but once...

One should not abide in the thought, "I shall bring an end to suffering. One should not abide in the thought, "I am a non-returner practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning. One should not abide in the thought, "As a non-returner, I shall attain final nirvana right there. One should not abide in the thought, "I am an arhat practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship. An arhat... [should not abide in such thoughts].

One should not abide in the thought, "I shall attain final nirvana right here in the realm of nirvana without remainder. One should not abide in the thought, "I am a pratyekabuddha. One should not abide in the thought, "Having transcended the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha, I shall abide on the stage of the bodhisattva. One should not abide in the knowledge of the knowledge of the paths by way of apprehension. In every respect...

One should not dwell on the thought: "Having fully awakened to all phenomena, and through the exhaustion of all afflictions along with their latencies and continuities, I, as a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, having realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, shall turn the wheel of Dharma.
Nor should one dwell on the thought: "Having performed the deeds of a Buddha, I shall lead immeasurable and incalculable beings to final nirvāṇa."

Even so, one should not abide [therein]. Having stood in the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and the faculties (*indriya*), one should not abide with the thought, "I shall enter such a concentration (*samādhi*) that by means of that concentration I will remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges," for this is by way of apprehension (*upalambha*). One should not abide with the thought, "My lifespan will be immeasurable," for this is by way of apprehension.

One should not dwell on the thought: "Each single mark among the thirty-two marks of a great man will be perfected by a hundred merits. Nor should one dwell on the thought: "As many world-systems as there are in the east, equal in number to the sands of the river Ganges, and likewise as many world-systems in the south, west, and north, equal in number to the sands of the river Ganges—so many shall be my single Buddha-field."
One should not dwell [on the thought]: "My trichiliocosm shall become composed of adamant. One should not dwell [on the thought]:
"From my Bodhi tree such a fragrance shall issue forth that for whoever smells that fragrance, passion shall not afflict their entire body."
Hatred would not afflict them, delusion would not afflict them,
and no one would possess the mind of a śrāvaka or the mind of a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, one should not dwell even on the thought: "All those beings will become fixed in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and as for those beings who smell that fragrance, no disease whatsoever shall afflict them. And in that buddha-field, there shall be no [concept of] form, nor of sensation.

One should not abide in the thought, "The term 'perception' will not exist," nor "the term 'formative factors' will not exist," nor "the term 'consciousness' will not exist. One should not abide in the thought, "The term 'perfection of generosity' will not exist."

In this way, one should not abide with the thought, "There will be no sound of the perfection of ethical discipline, nor of the perfection of patience, nor of the perfection of vigor, nor of the perfection of meditative concentration, nor of the perfection of wisdom. One should not abide with the thought, "There will be no sound of the applications of mindfulness," nor of the sounds of the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the noble truths, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
In this way, one should not abide in the thought that even the terms "stream-enterer," "once-returner," "non-returner," "arhat," "pratyekabuddha," "bodhisattva," or "buddha" will exist;
this should be applied in detail. Why is that?
Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment...
"All dharmas are non-apprehendable. For this reason, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not abide in the perfection of wisdom by means of apprehension.
Then, it occurred to the venerable Śāriputra:
"But how, then, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide in the perfection of wisdom?"
Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti, having known with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the venerable Śāriputra, said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"What do you think, venerable Śāriputra? Where does the Tathāgata abide?"
Śāriputra said:

"Venerable Subhūti, the Tathāgata does not abide anywhere. Indeed, that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has a mind that is non-abiding; he does not abide in form, nor in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations."

He does not abide in consciousness; he does not abide in the conditioned realm, nor does he abide in the unconditioned realm. Likewise, he does not abide in the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, or the members of dependent origination, whether taken individually or collectively; nor does he abide in the perfections, nor in the factors conducive to enlightenment, nor in the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, or the formless attainments; nor in the superknowledges, nor in the truths, nor in any of the emptinesses.

He does not abide in all the samādhis, nor does he abide in all the doors of dhāraṇī; he does not abide in the powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha, nor does he abide in omniscience.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
In this way, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should stand in the perfection of wisdom. Just as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not stand in form, nor does he not stand;

he does not stand in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he not stand. In this way, Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should stand in the perfection of wisdom, with the thought "I shall stand" by means of the yoga of non-standing.
Thus has been explained the path of the śrāvaka, culminating in the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
Then, in that assembly, this thought occurred to certain sons of the gods:
"Those which are known as the yakṣa-sounds, yakṣa-words, yakṣa-conversations, and yakṣa-utterances of the yakṣas—"
While they were thus conversing, this was not understood: that which the noble elder Subhūti speaks, proclaims, teaches, and instructs regarding the perfection of wisdom.
Then the venerable Subhūti, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those sons of the gods, addressed those sons of the gods:
“O sons of the gods, why is that which is being discussed not understood?
The sons of the gods replied,
“It is not understood, Noble Subhūti.”
Subhūti said: "For indeed, O sons of the gods, not even a single syllable is uttered here, nor is it heard."
That is not understood.
Why is that?
For the perfection of wisdom is indeed beyond letters; therefore, there is no knower, no hearer, and no teacher, as the Tathāgatas are beyond letters.

The enlightenment of Arhats and Perfectly Enlightened Ones is as follows: O sons of gods, it is as if a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One were to create a magical emanation of a Buddha, and also create the fourfold assembly of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; having created them, he would teach the Dharma to those fourfold assemblies.
"What do you think, sons of gods? Was anything at all taught there, or heard, or understood?
The sons of gods replied:
"No, Venerable One.
Subhūti said: "It is just so, sons of the gods. All phenomena are like magical illusions; therein, nothing has been taught by anyone, nor has anything been heard by anyone."

It was not heard by anyone, nor understood. It is just as if, O sons of gods, a man were asleep and, while in a dream, were to see a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, teaching the Dharma. What do you think, sons of gods? Was anything at all taught there, or heard, or understood?
The sons of the gods said: "No, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said:

In this way, sons of gods, all phenomena are like a dream; therein, nothing has been heard by anyone, nothing has been taught by anyone, and nothing has been understood by anyone. It is just as if, sons of gods, two men standing in a mountain cave were to speak the praises of the Buddha, speak the praises of the Dharma, and speak the praises of the Saṅgha.
Then, from both of them, the sound of an echo would issue forth. What do you think, O sons of gods? Would that second echo-sound be made known by that [first] echo? The sons of gods replied:
"No, Venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said: "It is just so, O son of the gods. All dharmas are like echoes; therein nothing at all is taught, nor is anything heard."

It is not perceived. Devaputras, it is just as if a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice were to create at a crossroads a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and the fourfold assembly; having manifested them, he would teach the Dharma to those four manifested assemblies. What do you think?
“O sons of the gods, was anything taught, heard, or understood there by anyone?
The sons of the gods replied, “No, venerable Subhūti.”
Subhūti said:
"In this very way, O sons of the gods, all phenomena are like an illusion; therein there is no teacher, no listener, and no cognizer. Thus, instruction by another is purposeless."
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to those sons of the gods:
"Ah, this noble Subhūti will surely clarify the Perfection of Wisdom!
Yet, he teaches that which is even more profound than the profound.
He teaches that which is subtler than the subtle. Such is the profundity of knowledge.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said this to those sons of the gods:
"O sons of the gods, form is neither profound nor subtle."
Feeling is neither deep nor subtle; perception is neither deep nor subtle; mental formations are neither deep nor subtle; consciousness is neither deep nor subtle. Why is that?

Because the intrinsic nature of form is neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither deep nor subtle. The intrinsic nature of the eye is neither deep nor subtle.
The intrinsic nature of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind is neither profound nor subtle. The intrinsic nature of the earth element is neither profound nor subtle;

[the same applies to] the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element—their intrinsic nature is neither profound nor subtle. The intrinsic nature of the perfection of generosity is neither profound nor subtle.

The intrinsic nature of the perfection of ethical discipline is neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of the perfection of patience is neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of the perfection of vigor is neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of the perfection of meditative concentration is neither deep nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom is neither deep nor subtle. The intrinsic nature of internal emptiness is neither deep nor subtle;

the intrinsic nature of external emptiness, the intrinsic nature of internal and external emptiness, and so on, up to the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, is [neither deep nor subtle].

It is neither profound nor subtle. The intrinsic nature of the applications of mindfulness is neither profound nor subtle. Likewise, [it is neither profound nor subtle] for the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the truths, the superknowledges, the four immeasurables, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

The intrinsic nature of the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is neither profound nor subtle; the intrinsic nature of all the gateways of meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs is neither profound nor subtle;
and so on, up to the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all aspects, which is neither profound nor subtle.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to those sons of the gods:

"In this teaching of the Dharma, form is not designated; nor is feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness designated; and so on, up to: neither the elements, nor the sense bases, nor dependent origination is designated; neither the perfections are designated, nor the factors conducive to awakening are designated."
The immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments have not been designated;
neither all the emptinesses, nor all the samādhis, nor all the doors of dhāraṇī;
nor the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor the fearlessnesses, nor the analytical knowledges, nor the unique qualities of a Buddha have been designated.

Furthermore, in this teaching of the Dharma, the fruit of stream-entry has not been designated, nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the fruit of non-returning, nor arhatship, nor the state of a pratyekabuddha, nor the state of a bodhisattva; neither enlightenment has been designated, nor have syllables been designated.
Then the venerable Subhūti addressed those sons of the gods:
"So it is, sons of the gods, so it is; the awakening of the Tathāgatas is ineffable and inexpressible."

It has not been taught by anyone, it has not been heard by anyone, and it has not been understood by anyone. Therefore, O sons of the gods, those who wish to abide in the fruit of stream-entry, and those who wish to realize the fruit of stream-entry, cannot do so without relying on this patient acceptance (*kṣānti*); nor can those who wish for the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship.
Those who wish to abide in the state of a pratyekabuddha,
and those who wish to attain the state of a pratyekabuddha, cannot do so without relying on this patient acceptance (kṣānti). Thus, O sons of the gods,
from the first production of the thought of awakening onward, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom by means of non-discourse and non-hearing.
Thus [is described] the abandonment of the conceptualization of the apprehended object by the Pratyekabuddhas.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to those sons of the gods:
"What kind of listeners to the Dharma should be expected for the Elder Subhūti?"
Then, the venerable Subhūti, having known with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those sons of the gods, said this to them:

"O sons of the gods, my listeners for the Dharma should be regarded as like an illusion; my listeners for the Dharma should be regarded as like a magical creation. They will not hear anything at all, nor will they master it, nor will they even think about it.
Then those sons of the gods said this to the venerable elder Subhūti:

"But further, Venerable Subhūti, are those beings like an illusion, and are those listeners of the Dharma like an illusion? Are those beings like a magical creation, and are those listeners of the Dharma like a magical creation?
Subhūti replied:
"So it is, O sons of the gods; so it is."
Those sentient beings are like an illusion; those listeners of the Dharma are like an illusion.
Those sentient beings are like a magical creation; those listeners of the Dharma are like a magical creation. O sons of the gods, even form is like a dream, like an illusion;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, O sons of the gods, are also like a dream, like an illusion. Even the eye...

O sons of the gods, [the eye] is like a dream, like an illusion. In the same way, O sons of the gods, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind are also like a dream, like an illusion. Form, too, O sons of the gods, is like a dream, like an illusion. In the same way, O sons of the gods, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are also like a dream, like an illusion.

Eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and feeling born of eye-contact are like a dream, like an illusion. Likewise, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind-consciousness, mind-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact are like a dream, like an illusion. Even the perfection of generosity is like a dream, like an illusion; likewise the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of vigor.

The perfection of meditation and the perfection of wisdom are like a dream and like an illusion. Likewise, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal and external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, are also like a dream and like an illusion. The foundations of mindfulness are also like a dream.

In the same way, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the immeasurables, the meditations, and the formless attainments [are like a dream].

The superknowledges, the truths, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are like a dream, like an illusion. The fruit of stream-entry is also like a dream, like an illusion; the stream-enterer is also like a dream, like an illusion. Likewise, the fruit of once-returning, the once-returner, the fruit of non-returning, [the non-returner, the fruit of arhatship, and the arhat] are all like a dream, like an illusion.
Even the non-returner, even the fruit of arhatship, even the arhat, is like a dream, like an illusion; even pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is like a dream, like an illusion;
even a pratyekabuddha is like a dream, like an illusion; even the state of a bodhisattva is like a dream, like an illusion.
The bodhisattva, too, is like a dream, like an illusion. Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, too, is like a dream, like an illusion;
even a Buddha is like a dream, like an illusion.
Then those sons of the gods said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti, you say that even Buddhahood is like a dream and like an illusion. What do you think?
Is even Nirvāṇa like a dream and like an illusion?
Subhūti replied:
"O sons of the gods, I say that even nirvāṇa is like a dream, like an illusion.
O sons of the gods, if I were to know any dharma whatsoever as more distinguished than nirvāṇa, I would say that too is like a dream, like an illusion. Why is that?"
For it is thus, O sons of the gods: a dream, an illusion, and nirvāṇa—these are non-dual and not divided into two.
Thus is the non-abandonment of the conceptualization of a grasper among the Pratyekabuddhas.
Then indeed, the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila...
The venerable Mahākātyāyana, the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, the venerable Mahākāśyapa,

and many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of deities said this to the elder, the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, who [is capable] of [receiving] this profound perfection of wisdom, which is thus beyond reasoning, thus beyond the sphere of reasoning, and thus so subtle?"

"Thus subtle, thus difficult to see, thus difficult to understand, thus peaceful, thus sublime, thus perfectly noble, and thus to be realized by the wise and the learned—when this [Perfection of Wisdom] is being taught, who will have faith in it?
Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to those great Śrāvakas and those sons of the gods:
"Venerable ones, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who are irreversible from this Perfection of Wisdom so profound..."

Thus, when this which is beyond reasoning, beyond the sphere of reasoning, so subtle, so precise, so difficult to see, so difficult to realize, so peaceful, so sublime, so perfectly noble, and to be experienced by the wise and the learned is being taught, there will be those who accept it— whether they be individuals who have seen the truths, or Arhats whose outflows are exhausted and whose intentions are fulfilled.

Those sons of good family and daughters of good family have performed services for previous Victors, have planted roots of merit under many millions of Buddhas, or have been sustained by spiritual friends. To this very Perfection of Wisdom— so profound, so beyond ratiocination, so outside the sphere of ratiocination, so subtle, so precise, so difficult to see, and so difficult to realize— they [will respond].

When this teaching— which is thus peaceful, thus sublime, thus sufficient for the noble, and thus to be experienced by the wise and the learned— is being proclaimed, they will accept it. Furthermore, they will not conceptualize that "form is empty."
They will not conceptualize emptiness as form;
they will not conceptualize feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as empty;
they will not conceptualize emptiness as consciousness. They will not conceptualize form as signless.

They will not conceptualize form as signless; they will not conceptualize feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as signless, nor will they conceptualize consciousness as signless. They will not conceptualize form as wishless, nor will they conceptualize form as wishless.

They will not conceptualize feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as "wishless," nor will they conceptualize consciousness as "wishless. Likewise, they will not conceptualize them as "non-arising" or "non-ceasing."

They will not conceptualize it as "peaceful" or "secluded. Likewise, they will not conceptualize the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and the factors of dependent origination, whether individually or collectively; nor the perfections;
nor internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.

In this way, [he cultivates] the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the truths, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all meditative concentrations, and all doors of dhāraṇī.

Thus, they will not conceptualize that the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, the state of a pratyekabuddha, or omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) is empty;

nor will they conceptualize emptiness as omniscience. They will not conceptualize omniscience as signless (*ānimitta*); nor will they conceptualize the signless as omniscience. They will not conceptualize omniscience as wishless (*apraṇihita*).

They will not conceptualize that "the wishless is omniscience. They will not conceptualize that "omniscience is non-arising," nor will they conceptualize that "non-arising is omniscience. They will not conceptualize that "omniscience is non-ceasing," nor will they conceptualize that "non-ceasing is omniscience. They will not conceptualize that "omniscience is peace."

They will not conceptualize that "all-aspect omniscience is peaceful. They will not conceptualize that "all-aspect omniscience is secluded," nor will they conceptualize that "seclusion is all-aspect omniscience. They will not conceptualize that "the conditioned realm is empty," nor will they conceptualize that "emptiness is the conditioned realm. They will not conceptualize that "the conditioned realm is signless," nor...

They will not conceptualize that the signless is the conditioned realm; they will not conceptualize that the conditioned realm is the wishless, nor will they conceptualize that the wishless is the conditioned realm.

They will not conceptualize that the conditioned realm is non-arising, nor will they conceptualize that non-arising is the conditioned realm. They will not conceptualize that the conditioned realm is non-ceasing...
They will not conceptualize the unconditioned realm as "cessation.

They will not conceptualize the conditioned realm as "peace," nor will they conceptualize peace as the conditioned realm. They will not conceptualize the conditioned realm as "secluded," nor will they conceptualize seclusion as the conditioned realm. They will not conceptualize the unconditioned realm as "empty."

They will not conceptualize emptiness as the unconditioned realm; they will not conceptualize the unconditioned realm as signlessness, nor will they conceptualize signlessness as the unconditioned realm. They will not conceptualize the unconditioned realm as wishlessness, nor will they conceptualize wishlessness as the unconditioned realm. They will not conceptualize the unconditioned realm as non-arising.

They will not conceptualize non-arising as the unconditioned realm; they will not conceptualize the unconditioned realm as non-ceasing, nor will they conceptualize non-ceasing as the unconditioned realm. They will not conceptualize the unconditioned realm as peace, nor will they conceptualize peace as the unconditioned realm. They will not conceptualize the unconditioned realm as secluded.
They will not conceptualize that the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*) is secluded.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti said this to those sons of the gods:

"O sons of the gods, for this Perfection of Wisdom—so profound, and so on, up to being worthy of the noble ones and to be experienced by the wise and the learned—there will be no one at all who accepts it. For what reason?"
For indeed, herein no dharma whatsoever is taught, nor indicated, nor illuminated;
and just as herein no dharma whatsoever is taught, nor indicated, nor illuminated, even so herein there will be no one at all to comprehend it.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra said this to the Venerable Subhūti, the Elder:

"Venerable Subhūti, is it not the case that here in this Perfection of Wisdom the three vehicles are taught in detail— namely, the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and the vehicle of the perfectly enlightened Buddha— and that the complete support of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas,

is taught from the first production of the thought of awakening up to the tenth production of the thought of awakening, and that the path of the bodhisattva is also taught, namely, the perfection of generosity and the perfection of ethical discipline?"

The perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of wisdom; the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path; the four immeasurables, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the superknowledges, the truths, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the four grounds of self-confidence.
The four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all the emptinesses, all the meditative concentrations,
and all the doors of dhāraṇī—
these are taught as the complete support for bodhisattva mahāsattvas; thus is a bodhisattva mahāsattva [established].

Practicing the perfection of wisdom, he will not be born by spontaneous generation. Likewise, through the higher knowledges, he will possess the quality of non-retrogression and travel from buddhafield to buddhafield;
and whatever roots of merit he desires in order to honor, revere, respect, and worship the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, those roots of merit of his will reach fulfillment.

And whatever Dharma they shall hear in the presence of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, all that Dharma shall never be interrupted until they have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; and they shall always be concentrated,
with undistracted minds, through the practice of meditative concentration.
He will possess unattached eloquence;

he will possess uninterrupted eloquence, concentrated eloquence, appropriate eloquence, coherent eloquence, meaningful eloquence, and an eloquence that is preeminent and distinguished above all the world.
Subhūti said:

"So it is, Venerable Śāriputra; so it is. It is exactly as you have said in detail here in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: three vehicles have been taught, namely, the vehicle of the śrāvakas and the support for bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, up to the point where bodhisattvas mahāsattvas will possess a distinguished eloquence that transcends the entire world. And that is by way of non-apprehension."

By way of the non-apprehension of a self, a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, and a seer; by way of the non-apprehension of form, by way of the non-apprehension of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; by way of the non-apprehension of the eye, and likewise by way of the non-apprehension of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and by way of the non-apprehension of eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling born of eye-contact.

In this way, by means of non-apprehension, there is [non-apprehension] of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness; of mind-contact; and of the feeling born of mind-contact. In this way, by means of non-apprehension, there is [non-apprehension] of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharma*). By means of non-apprehension, there is [non-apprehension] of the earth element;

likewise, by means of non-apprehension, there is [non-apprehension] of the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element. By means of non-apprehension, there is [non-apprehension] of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

In this way, [he dwells] through the yoga of non-apprehension regarding the perfection of ethical discipline; the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom. Through the yoga of non-apprehension of internal emptiness, up to the yoga of non-apprehension of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence. Through the yoga of non-apprehension of the applications of mindfulness.

In this way, by means of non-apprehension, [there is the cultivation] of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path; by means of non-apprehension, [there is the cultivation] of the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, and the noble truths; and of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
By way of non-apprehension. By way of the non-apprehension of all samādhis, all doors of dhāraṇī, and omniscience. Then, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"For what reason, venerable Subhūti, are the three vehicles taught in detail here in the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension?"
"For what reason is the complete embracing of the bodhisattva mahāsattva taught, such that the bodhisattva mahāsattva will come to possess a distinguished eloquence that transcends all the world?
Subhūti replied:

"Venerable Śāriputra, it is by taking internal emptiness as a basis that the three vehicles are taught in detail through the application of non-apprehension. It is by taking external emptiness and internal-external emptiness as a basis [that they are taught]."

Ranging from [the emptiness of] the conditioned up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, the three vehicles are taught in detail by way of non-apprehension; and ranging from [the emptiness of] the conditioned up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, the complete support of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is taught,
until the bodhisattva mahāsattva will possess a distinguished eloquence that transcends the entire world by way of non-apprehension.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"While this vision of the Dharma is being spoken by the Elder Subhūti, as many gods as there are in the great trichiliocosm— from those of the Realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha gods—
the following thought occurred to them:"
While this vision of the Dharma was being spoken by the Elder Subhūti, [the gods thought]: "What if we were to manifest flowers and,
with those flowers, scatter them over the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Bodhisattvas, the community of monks, the Elder Subhūti, and this Perfection of Wisdom?"
Then Śakra, lord of the gods, having manifested divine māndārava flowers throughout this trichiliocosm— from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha gods—
scattered those flowers over the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, the community of monks, the Elder Subhūti, and this Perfection of Wisdom.
They scattered [flowers],
and as soon as those flowers were scattered by Śakra, the lord of the gods, and by the gods up to the Akaniṣṭha realm, [they remained suspended].
Then, indeed, the entire great trichiliocosm was strewn with a carpet of flowers. And above, in the sky, a pavilion of flowers came into being.
Then, Subhūti the Elder thought to himself:
"Never before have I seen such flowers circulating in all the abodes of the gods as these flowers which have been scattered by the sons of the gods; these flowers are emanated."
"These flowers which have been scattered by the sons of the gods are mind-made; these flowers scattered by the sons of the gods are not produced from trees, shrubs, or creepers.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the elder Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti, these flowers are unproduced; these flowers are not produced from the mind, nor [are they produced from anything else]."
[They] are produced from trees, shrubs, and creepers.
Subhūti said: "Kauśika, as for what you have said..."

"These flowers have not been produced; they are not produced from the mind, nor are they produced from trees, shrubs, or creepers. Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "Kauśika, those things which are unproduced are not flowers. But, Venerable Subhūti, are only these flowers unproduced, or is form also unproduced, and are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness also unproduced?"
The Elder Subhūti said:
"Kauśika, it is not only these flowers that are unproduced;
form (*rūpa*), Kauśika, is also unproduced, and that which is unproduced is not form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness [are likewise unproduced]."
O Kauśika, that which is unproduced is not consciousness. O Kauśika, the eye is unproduced, and that which is unproduced is not the eye;

likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, O Kauśika, are unproduced, and that which is unproduced is not the mind. O Kauśika, the earth element is unproduced, and that which is unproduced is not the earth element; likewise, the water element, the fire element, the space element, and the consciousness element, O Kauśika, are unproduced, and that which is unproduced is not the consciousness element. O Kauśika, the perfection of generosity is unproduced, and that which is unproduced—

That perfection of giving, Kauśika, is unproduced; likewise, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are unproduced. And that which is unproduced is not the perfection of wisdom. Inner emptiness, Kauśika, is unproduced; and that which is unproduced—

That which is the emptiness of the internal, up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, Kauśika, is unproduced; and that which is unproduced is not the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
The applications of mindfulness, Kauśika, are unproduced; and those which are unproduced are not the applications of mindfulness.
In this way, Kauśika, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path are unproduced;

and that which is unproduced is not the path. Likewise, the superknowledges, the truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha [are unproduced].
Kauśika, those which are unproduced are not the Buddha-dharmas. Kauśika, the fruit of stream-entry is unproduced;
and that which is unproduced is not the fruit of stream-entry.
In the same way, Kauśika, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, the state of a pratyekabuddha, and omniscience are unproduced.
And that which is unproduced is not omniscience. Kauśika, a stream-enterer is unproduced; and that which is unproduced is not a stream-enterer.
The same applies to a once-returner and a non-returner.

"An Arhat, a Pratyekabuddha, and a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, O Kauśika, are not born; and that which is not born is not a Samyaksaṃbuddha. This refers to the lineage as the basis for realization.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said this to the Blessed One:
"How profound is the wisdom of the Venerable Subhūti! For this Elder neither contradicts conventional designation nor fails to teach the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā)."
Then the Blessed One said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"So it is, Kauśika, so it is!
Deep indeed is the wisdom of this noble elder Subhūti, in that he does not contradict conventional designation while yet teaching the true nature of phenomena."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:
“How, Blessed One, does the Elder Subhūti neither contradict conventional designation nor teach the true nature of phenomena?
The Blessed One replied:
"Kauśika, form is a mere designation; and that which is a mere designation is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

And the Elder Subhūti does not contradict that, but teaches it. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, Kauśika, are mere designations; and that which is a mere designation is the true nature of phenomena.
And the Elder Subhūti does not contradict that, but teaches it. For what reason?"
That which is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not contradicted; and that which is not contradicted, the Elder Subhūti teaches it and does not contradict it—

thus, with respect to the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and the factors of dependent origination, both individually and collectively, and likewise with respect to the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.

In this way, it is so regarding internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence; likewise regarding the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the truths, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

In this way, regarding the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, the state of a pratyekabuddha, and omniscience—Kauśika, "stream-enterer" is a mere designation. That which is a mere designation is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the Elder Subhūti does not contradict it, but teaches it. It is the same for the once-returner.

"Kauśika, the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, and the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly enlightened one—these are mere designations. And that which is a mere designation is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā). The Elder Subhūti does not contradict this, but teaches it. For what reason?"
Kauśika, that which is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not contradicted;
and that which is not contradicted is what the Elder Subhūti teaches without contradicting it.
For in this way, Kauśika, the Elder Subhūti does not contradict conventional designation (prajñapti) and yet teaches the true nature of phenomena.
Subhūti said:

"So it is, Kauśika, so it is. Just as all phenomena have been taught by the Blessed One as being mere designations, even so, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having understood all phenomena as mere designations, [should train] in the perfection of wisdom."

One must train in this way. Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training thus does not train in form, nor in feeling, nor in perception, nor in mental formations, nor in consciousness. Why is that?
Because he does not perceive form as something in which to train; [he does not perceive] feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

He does not perceive that in which he trains. Kauśika, when training in this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not train in the perfection of generosity. Why is that? Because he does not perceive that perfection of generosity in which he trains. Likewise, he does not [train] in the perfection of ethical discipline.
He does not train in the perfection of patience, nor in the perfection of vigor, nor in the perfection of meditation, nor in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?

Because he does not perceive that perfection of wisdom in which he might train. He does not train even in internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
For what reason?

Because he does not perceive internal emptiness, nor does he perceive anything up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, wherein he trains. He does not even train in the applications of mindfulness; likewise, he does not train in the right efforts.

He does not train in the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold paths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the truths, the powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, nor even in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He does not train for the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, nor for arhatship.
He trains for the state of a pratyekabuddha, yet he does not train even for omniscience. Why is that?
Because he does not perceive that omniscience in which he might train.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the elder Subhūti:

For what reason, venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not perceive form, nor perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness? In this way, he does not perceive the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, the perfections, or the factors conducive to awakening, whether individually or collectively. He does not perceive the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, or the truths.

He does not perceive the superknowledges, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, wherein he trains; nor does he perceive even omniscience, wherein he trains?
Subhūti said:
For in this way, Kauśika, form is empty of form;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of consciousness. Likewise, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields—both individually and collectively—the factors of dependent origination, the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the meditative concentrations, all the doors of dhāraṇī, and the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening [are empty].

The dharmas—the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the truths, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, up to and including omniscience—are empty of omniscience. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, the emptiness of form does not perceive the emptiness of form, and so on, until the emptiness of omniscience does not perceive the emptiness of omniscience.
He perceives thus: "Kauśika, he who trains here in emptiness trains in the emptiness of form without making a duality;

he trains in the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness without making a duality. In this same way, he trains in the individual and collective aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, in dependent origination, in the perfections, and in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."

He trains without duality in the immeasurables, the meditations, the formless attainments, the truths, the superknowledges, all the emptinesses, all the samādhis, all the doors of dhāraṇī, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, the unique qualities of a Buddha, and so on, up to the emptiness of omniscience. Kauśika, he who trains without duality in the emptiness of form, up to the emptiness of omniscience—

He trains without dualism; he also trains without dualism in the perfection of generosity. Likewise, he trains without dualism in the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom. He also trains without dualism in internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.

He trains without duality: he trains without duality in the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. He trains without duality in the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the superknowledges, the truths, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
He trains without duality. He trains without duality in all meditative concentrations and in all gateways of dhāraṇīs.

He trains without duality in the incalculable and immeasurable qualities of a Buddha. He trains without duality in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, and the state of a pratyekabuddha. [He trains without duality] in the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
One trains in the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) without duality.

Thus, regarding the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*), which is part of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgiya*) on the path of the Pratyekabuddha, one does not train for the diminution of form (*rūpa*), nor does one train for its increase. Nor [does one train] for the diminution or increase of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

He trains neither for decrease nor for increase. Thus, he trains neither for the decrease nor for the increase of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, whether considered individually or collectively.

He trains neither for the decrease nor for the increase of dependent origination. He trains neither for the decrease nor for the increase of the perfection of generosity. Likewise, [he trains] in the perfection of ethical discipline.

One trains neither for the decrease nor for the increase of the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom. One trains neither for the decrease nor for the increase of the applications of mindfulness. Likewise, one trains neither for the decrease nor for the increase of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.

He does not train for the sake of the decrease or the increase of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, or the formless attainments. He does not train for the sake of the decrease or the increase of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence. [He does not train for the sake of the decrease or the increase] of the truths, the superknowledges, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha.

One does not train for the sake of the decrease or the increase of the Buddha-qualities, up to and including omniscience. One who trains for neither the decrease nor the increase of form, up to and including training for neither the decrease nor the increase of omniscience, does not train for the appropriation of form, nor does he train for its disappearance. This is also true for feeling, perception, and mental formations.

One does not train for the sake of grasping consciousness, nor does one train for its disappearance. In this way, one does not train for the sake of grasping or for the sake of the disappearance of the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and dependent originations, whether considered individually or collectively. Likewise, [one does not train for the sake of grasping or the disappearance] of the perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, and the truths.
He does not train for the sake of grasping nor for the sake of the disappearance of the superknowledges, all meditative concentrations, and all gateways of dhāraṇīs.

He does not train for the sake of grasping nor for the sake of the disappearance of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, up to and including omniscience.

Thus, in that very place, Śāriputra, having reached the stage of the Summits, said: "For what reason, Venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva not train for the sake of grasping form, nor for its disappearance?"

"He does not train for the sake of grasping or for the sake of the disappearance of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to and including omniscience; he does not train for the sake of grasping or for the sake of the disappearance of omniscience.
Subhūti said:
"For indeed, venerable Śāriputra, there is no grasping of form. Why is that?"

Form does not grasp form. Neither feeling, nor perception, nor mental formations [grasp themselves], for in this way, O Venerable Śāriputra, there is no grasping of consciousness. Why is that? Because consciousness does not grasp consciousness. Thus it is for the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination, whether taken individually or collectively.

There is no grasping of the perfections, the factors conducive to awakening, the truths, the superknowledges, all the emptinesses, all the meditative concentrations, all the doors of dhāraṇī, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique qualities of a Buddha, or the Buddha-dharmas. Why is that?
