He becomes conceited because of that. As that bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into worldly meditative concentration, it occurs to him:
"I am practicing the perfection of meditation; I am fulfilling the perfection of meditation."
He becomes conceited because of that. As that bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the mundane perfection of wisdom, through a lack of skillful means, it occurs to him:
"I am practicing the perfection of wisdom."

"I am fulfilling the perfection of wisdom," he thinks, and because of that, he becomes conceited. While that bodhisattva mahāsattva remains in the cultivation of the mundane applications of mindfulness, it occurs to him:
"I possess the applications of mindfulness."
I cultivate the right efforts; I [cultivate] the bases of psychic power.
I am the faculties, I am the powers, I am the factors of enlightenment.
I cultivate the noble eightfold path; I cultivate the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; I cultivate all meditative absorptions.
I [cultivate] all the gateways of dhāraṇīs;
I cultivate the immeasurable meditative absorptions and formless attainments;
I cultivate the four noble truths.
I am the superknowledges; I am the ten powers; I am the grounds of self-confidence.
"I shall cultivate the analytical knowledges; I shall cultivate the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
I shall bring sentient beings to maturity."
"I shall purify a buddha-field;

I shall attain the knowledge of all modes"—through such attachment to the notions of "I" and "mine," he becomes conceited. It is in this way, Blessed One, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva [becomes conceited].

Practicing among worldly phenomena, one falls into arrogance through the attachment of "I-making" and "mine-making. However, for such a person, the perfection of wisdom stands ready as a means of subduing and transforming that [attachment].
Furthermore, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices among supramundane phenomena and gives a gift, he does not apprehend a donor.

He does not apprehend a recipient, nor does he apprehend that which is to be given. For it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, becomes established for the sake of self-subduing and dedication. Thus guarding ethical discipline and accomplishing patience, [he exerts] vigor...

Beginning with meditative concentration, while practicing meditation and cultivating the perfection of wisdom, one does not apprehend wisdom. Likewise, while cultivating the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path, one does not apprehend them. While cultivating the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the noble truths, and the superknowledges, one does not apprehend them. [One likewise does not apprehend] the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and the analytical knowledges.

Cultivating the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), he does not apprehend them. Cultivating all the emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), all the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), and all the gateways of dhāraṇī (*dhāraṇīmukha*), he does not apprehend them. Likewise, cultivating great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he does not apprehend them, up to and including cultivating the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he does not apprehend it. In this way, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices] in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
He practices, being present for the sake of self-subduing and for the sake of dedication. Such is the activity of subduing and bowing in every respect.
Then the Blessed One said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Kauśika, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family takes up this profound perfection of wisdom..."
Whether he is upholding it, reciting it, mastering it, propagating it, studying it, or attending to it with wise reflection—
whether he has ascended to the front of a battle, is engaged in battle, has entered into battle, or whether he is lying down, passing by, sitting, or standing— [he would be protected].

It is impossible, Kauśika, it is out of the question, that anyone should throw a stick, a weapon, or a clod of earth at that son of good family or daughter of good family who takes up, bears in mind, recites, masters, sets in motion, and studies this perfection of wisdom, or who attends to it properly; or that such things, once thrown, should even strike their body.
It is impossible that weapons should fall upon him, or that his life should be endangered by the assault of another; for what reason?
Because that son of good family or daughter of good family has long practiced this perfection of wisdom.

One’s own sections of passion and the weapons of passion have been conquered; the sections of passion and the weapons of passion of others have also been conquered. One’s own sections of hatred and the weapons of hatred, the sections of delusion and the weapons of delusion have been conquered; the sections of hatred and the weapons of hatred, the sections of delusion and the weapons of delusion of others have also been conquered. One’s own sections of speculative views...

The arrows of speculative views and the weapons of speculative views belonging even to others have been conquered. The outbursts of one's own obsessions and the weapons of those obsessions have been conquered; the outbursts of obsessions and the weapons of obsessions belonging even to others have been conquered. The latent tendencies of one's own [mind] and the weapons of those latent tendencies have been conquered; [those of] others...

Even the arrows of the latent tendencies and the weapons of the latent tendencies have been conquered. By this method, Kauśika, whatever arrow or weapon is hurled at the body of that son of good family or daughter of good family does not fall. Thus is the activity of conquering the afflictions.
Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or daughter of good family shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and propagate this perfection of wisdom...

If he attends to it properly and remains never separated from the mind set on omniscience, then even if someone were to sprinkle him with non-medicinal substances, or perform sorcery against him, or cast him into a pit of fire, or strike him with a weapon, or give him poison, or throw him into water— all these things will not affect him. Why is that?
This, Kauśika, is the great knowledge, namely the perfection of wisdom;
this, Kauśika, is the unsurpassed knowledge, namely the perfection of wisdom. For, Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family training in this does not intend harm to themselves.
One does not intend for the harm of others,
nor does one intend for the harm of both.
Thus is the function of enduring the onset [of suffering].
For what reason?
Because he does not perceive a self; he does not perceive others, nor both together. He does not perceive form;
he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive them individually or collectively, up to and including all of them.

He does not apprehend the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, dependent origination, the perfections, the factors conducive to enlightenment, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, all the emptinesses, all the samādhis, all the doors of dhāraṇī, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the specific perfect knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so on, up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Not apprehending these, he does not intend his own harm, nor does he intend the harm of others.
One does not intend for the affliction of both [self and others]. One attains unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and beholds all sentient beings. Why is that?

For it was by training in this very science (*vidyā*) that the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas awakened to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and so too will those who are to become Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas in the future.
They too, training here in this perfection of wisdom, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who are currently present now in the world-systems of the ten directions—
they too, training here in this perfection of wisdom, are fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Thus is the conduct of one seeking perfect complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, Kauśika, wherever they shall write down this perfection of wisdom, and take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and set it in motion, and practice it with wise reflection (*yoniśas*), there neither a human nor a non-human who looks for an opportunity or seeks an opening will find an opportunity. Why is that?

For in this Prajñāpāramitā, for the sake of worship, there are the sons of the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm, the Trayastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin realms; the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and the Brahmapārṣadya realms, up to the Akaniṣṭha realm— these sons of the gods within the trichiliocosm mahāsāhasra world-system.

Furthermore, those sons of gods belonging to the realm of the Four Great Kings, up to and including the sons of gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven, who reside in other immeasurable and incalculable world-systems, they too will provide protection, shelter, and defense for those sons of good family or daughters of good family.
Those sons of the gods who, having no other recourse, shall honor, revere, respect, and worship this Perfection of Wisdom after they have written it down and retained it,
or read it— having worshipped it, they shall depart; and for those who, having written down this Perfection of Wisdom, shall retain it or read it, these [benefits] will belong.

There will be benefits and advantages pertaining to this present life. For example, Kauśika, just as those who have gone to the seat of awakening, or to the vicinity of the seat of awakening, or to the interior of the seat of awakening—even including those belonging to the animal realm—cannot be harassed or harmed by either humans or non-humans. Why is that?

For it was here that those former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas sat and fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Future Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas will also fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and those of the present are also fully awakening to it. Having fully awakened, [they...]
And they establish all sentient beings in happiness, fearlessness, freedom from agitation, absence of enmity, lack of terror, non-affliction, and the absence of adversaries.

Having established immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings in happiness, fearlessness, freedom from agitation, lack of terror, absence of enmity, non-affliction, and the absence of adversaries, they establish them in the excellence of divine and human bodies, as well as in the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of once-returning.
They dedicate [the merit] toward the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, and unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. For what reason?

Because by this very perfection of wisdom, Kauśika, that spot of earth is made into a shrine for all beings, worthy of being saluted, honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, adored, and venerated with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
Thus has been described the activity consisting in making the place of its support worthy of worship.
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family writes down this Perfection of Wisdom and places it in the form of a book..."

Moreover, having written it down, one should preserve it and honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags, as well as with rows of lamps all around and various kinds of offerings;
and whoever shall establish the relics of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, who has entered final nirvāṇa, within stupas.

Having established them, one should receive them, uphold them, and recite them; and one should honor, revere, esteem, and worship them with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
Of these two, which generates more merit?

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "In that case, Kauśika, I shall question you in turn regarding this matter; you should answer as you see fit. What do you think?"
"Kauśika, regarding this omniscience of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, and this physical body of the Tathāgata that has been manifested—
on which practice was the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, training himself, that he awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and manifested this physical body?
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"In this very world, Blessed One, while training in the perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and this physical body was brought forth.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is."

It was by training in the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and brought this physical body into being.

Therefore, Kauśika, it is not by the acquisition of this physical body that a Tathāgata comes to be designated as a "Tathāgata"; rather, it is when omniscience has been attained that a Tathāgata comes to be designated as a "Tathāgata."

Kauśika, this omniscience is born from the perfection of wisdom. Likewise, because this acquisition of the physical body of the Tathāgata is born from the perfection of wisdom, it becomes the basis for the knowledge of omniscience. And by relying on such a basis, there occurs the manifestation of the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience, the manifestation of the Buddha, the manifestation of the Dharma, and the manifestation of the Saṅgha.

Thus, this acquisition of his physical body has its cause in the knowledge of the Omniscient One. Because it serves as the basis for all sentient beings, he has become like a shrine (caitya)—worthy of being saluted, honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, adored, and venerated. And even after I have passed into final nirvana, there will be worship of these relics in this same manner.

Therefore, Kauśika, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family shall write down this perfection of wisdom, make it into a book, and recite it with reverence, preserve it, and honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and with many kinds of lamp-rows and various offerings; [that person shall produce much merit].
This very person generates far more merit than that.
For what reason? Because, Kauśika, by that son of good family, the knowledge of the omniscient one [is sought].

Or a daughter of good family would have performed an act of worship. Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to place the body of the Tathāgata after his final nirvāṇa in a stūpa made of the seven precious gems, or having placed it in a casket made of the seven precious gems,
were to carry it about, and honor it, and so forth, even worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
And whoever here should show honor, respect, reverence, worship, veneration, and homage to this Perfection of Wisdom while it is being written down or when it has entered into a book,
this person would generate much more merit than that.
Why is that?
By that, worship of the knowledge of the omniscient one will have been performed; for from this the five perfections are born,
from this internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature is born,

and from this the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the superknowledges, and the noble truths are born.

From this are born the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments; from this are born the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
from this are born all samādhis and all gateways of dhāraṇī;
from this is born the ripening of all sentient beings.
From this is born the purification of the buddha-field;
from this is born the excellence of family, the excellence of wealth, and the excellence of retinue for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas;
from this are born great loving-kindness and great compassion.
From this have emerged the great śāla-tree clans of kṣatriyas, the great śāla-tree clans of brahmins, and the great śāla-tree clans of householders;

from this have emerged the sons of the gods belonging to the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin realms, as well as the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, the Mahābrahmā,
up to the Akaniṣṭha sons of the gods.
From this have emerged the stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats;
from this have emerged the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas;
from this have emerged the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
From this has emerged the omniscience of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), which is inconceivable, incomparable, unsurpassed, peerless, unequaled, and equal to the unequaled.
Thus ends the stage of weak-weak resolve for one's own welfare.
Then, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, as for these humans of Jambudvīpa who do not honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, or venerate this perfection of wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags— will they, Blessed One, know that such an offering made to the perfection of wisdom will be of such great supernatural power?"
"Will they not know that by doing so, a worship of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) will have been performed with such great benefit?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

What do you think, Kauśika, how many of those humans in Jambudvīpa are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Buddha, who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Dharma, and who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Saṅgha?
"Those who are free from doubt regarding the Buddha, those who are free from doubt regarding the Dharma, and those who are free from doubt regarding the Saṅgha;
those who have reached certainty regarding the Buddha, those who have reached certainty regarding the Dharma, and those who have reached certainty regarding the Saṅgha?
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One in this way:

"Few, O Blessed One, are those humans of Jambudvīpa who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Buddha, who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Dharma, and who are endowed with verified clarity regarding the Saṃgha;
few are those who are free from doubt regarding the Buddha, free from doubt regarding the Dharma, and free from doubt regarding the Saṃgha;
few are those who have reached certainty regarding the Buddha, reached certainty regarding the Dharma, and reached certainty regarding the Saṃgha."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Kauśika? How many among the humans of Jambudvīpa are possessors of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment?
How many among the humans of Jambudvīpa are possessors of the three gateways to liberation?"
How many among the humans of Jambudvīpa are attainers of the eight liberations? How many among the humans of Jambudvīpa are attainers of the nine successive meditative attainments?
How many among the humans of Jambudvīpa are attainers of the four analytical knowledges?
How many among the humans of Jambudvīpa are possessors of the six higher knowledges?
How many among the humans of Jambudvīpa, through the abandonment of the three fetters, are stream-enterers?
How many among the humans of Jambudvīpa, through the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion, are once-returners?
How many among the humans of Jambudvīpa are non-returners (*anāgāmin*) through the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)?
How many among the humans of Jambudvīpa are arhats through the abandonment of the five higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)?
How many among the humans of Jambudvīpa have set out for the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabodhi*)?
"How many are those Jambudvīpa humans who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
Śakra replied: "Blessed One, those Jambudvīpa humans who have attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are very few;
even fewer than those are they who have attained the three gateways to liberation."
Fewer still are those who have attained the eight liberations; fewer still are those who have attained the nine successive meditative attainments;
and fewer still are those who have attained the four analytical knowledges.

Even fewer than those are the ones who have attained the six superknowledges. Even fewer than those are the people of Jambudvīpa who, through the abandonment of the three fetters, are stream-enterers;
even fewer than those are the ones who, through the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion, are once-returners.

Even fewer than those are the non-returners who, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters, have reached that state; even fewer than those are the arhats who, through the abandonment of the five higher fetters, have attained that state; and even fewer than those are the humans of Jambudvīpa who have set out for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Therefore, those humans of Jambudvīpa who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment are very few.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is."
Few are those humans of Jambudvīpa who possess verified clarity of faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
few are those who are free from doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;

and even fewer than those few are those who have reached certainty regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Even rarer than those few are those who practice the ten paths of wholesome action.
Among those few, even fewer are those who are engaged in the cultivation of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Among those few, even fewer are those who cultivate the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment. Among those few, even fewer are those who cultivate the three gateways to liberation. Among those few...

Fewer still are those who cultivate the eight liberations; fewer than those few are those who cultivate the nine successive meditative attainments; and even fewer than those few are those who cultivate the four analytical knowledges.
Among those, even fewer cultivate the six superknowledges; fewer still are those who have entered the stream; fewer still are those who are once-returners;
and fewer still are those who are arhats.
Fewer still are those who are pratyekabuddhas; fewer still are those who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Even fewer than those few are those who course toward awakening.
For what reason is that?

For thus it is that while wandering in saṃsāra, they have not seen the Buddha, nor heard the Dharma, nor attended upon the Saṅgha. They have not given gifts, nor guarded their ethical discipline, nor cultivated patience, nor exerted vigor,
nor practiced meditative concentration, nor cultivated wisdom.

The perfection of generosity has not been heard; likewise, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom have not been heard.

Skill in means has not been heard; neither internal emptiness, nor external emptiness, nor internal-and-external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, has been heard.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment have been heard, yet not the concentrations, nor the gateways of all the dhāraṇīs, nor the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments;

the noble truths have not been heard, nor the superknowledges, the powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, nor the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; omniscience has not been heard, nor cultivated, nor practiced extensively.

For this reason, Kauśika, those beings who are endowed with verified clarity toward the Buddha, those who are endowed with verified clarity toward the Dharma, and those who are endowed with verified clarity toward the Saṅgha are few;
those beings who are free from doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are few.
Rare are those beings who have reached certainty in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
rare are those humans of Jambudvīpa who practice the ten paths of wholesome action;
rare are those who are devoted to the cultivation of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Few are those who cultivate the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening. Few are those who cultivate the three gateways to liberation.
Few are those who cultivate the eight liberations. Few are those who cultivate the nine successive meditative attainments.
Few are those who cultivate the four analytical knowledges. Few are those who possess the six superknowledges.
They cultivate [these paths]. Rare are those humans of Jambudvīpa who, through the abandonment of the three fetters, are stream-enterers;
rare are those who, through the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion, are once-returners;
and rare are those who, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters, are non-returners.

They are Arhats because of the abandonment of the five higher fetters. Few are those humans of Jambudvīpa who have set out upon the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas. Even fewer than those few are those who have set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Even fewer than those few are those who practice for the sake of awakening. From among them...

Fewer still are those who increase the thought of awakening. Fewer still are those who apply themselves to the yoga of the perfection of wisdom. Fewer still are those who course in the perfection of wisdom. Fewer still are those who, having established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

"Here, Kauśika, with my unobstructed Buddha-eye, I see in the eastern direction immeasurable and incalculable beings who, having generated the mind for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, are practicing the perfection of wisdom but are devoid of skill in means; from among them,
perhaps only one or two bodhisattva mahāsattvas would remain in the state of non-retrogression."
For the most part, they remain on the level of a śrāvaka or on the level of a pratyekabuddha.
Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, unexcelled perfect enlightenment is difficult to realize for those who are indolent, lacking in vigor, and of inferior resolve.

By beings of inferior nature and poor wisdom. In this way, Kauśika, with my unobstructed Buddha-eye, I see in the southern direction, the western, the northern, above, below, and in the intermediate directions, immeasurable and incalculable beings who,
having generated the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and practicing for the sake of awakening, are nevertheless devoid of skillful means.
Only one or two bodhisattva mahāsattvas might remain in the state of non-retrogression;
for the most part, they settle on the level of a śrāvaka or the level of a pratyekabuddha.
For what reason is that?

For, Kauśika, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is indeed difficult to realize for those who are indolent, lacking in vigor, having inferior resolve, being of inferior character, and possessed of poor wisdom.
Thus ends the section on the weak and middling resolve regarding one's own welfare.

Therefore, Kausika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who desires to quickly and easily awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should repeatedly hear, take up, bear in mind, recite, master, propagate, inquire about, and attend to this very perfection of wisdom in a systematic manner.
They should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags;

and whatever other wholesome qualities are included herein within this perfection of wisdom, those too should be taken up, retained, recited, mastered, promulgated, and properly attended to by reflection— just as follows:
Namely: the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, the perfection of wisdom;
internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
all meditative absorptions, all doors of dhāraṇī, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the four right efforts.
The four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path,

the four immeasurables, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the six supernormal knowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical insights, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, and great compassion.

Furthermore, those other immeasurable qualities of a Buddha that are included within the perfection of wisdom should also be taken up, and so on, until they are properly attended to with right reflection.
Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family will understand it thus: "In this very place is the Tathāgata."
While formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, he was trained in what is to say, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of concentration,

the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity; and in internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, and in all meditative absorptions.

In all the gateways of dhāraṇī, in the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, in the four immeasurables, in the four formless attainments, in the six superknowledges, in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, in the four grounds of self-confidence, in the four analytical knowledges,
in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, in great loving-kindness, in great compassion, and in others...
Furthermore, we too, while training in this perfection of wisdom, should train ourselves in the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha;
for whether the Tathāgata remains or has passed into parinirvāṇa, it is precisely this perfection of wisdom that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas must rely upon.
Thus is the weak-strong conviction regarding one's own welfare.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:
"How much more merit, Blessed One, does that son of good family or daughter of good family produce, who will honor, revere, respect, and worship this perfection of wisdom?"

The Blessed One said: "Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of honoring the Tathāgata after his parinirvāṇa, should have a stūpa made of the seven precious gems built one yojana in height, and having had it built, should honor it throughout their life with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags— "

And if one were to honor, revere, respect, and worship it on all sides—what do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate a great deal more merit on that account?
Śakra said: "A great deal, Blessed One; a great deal, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will produce much greater merit who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and propagate this Perfection of Wisdom."

And he will reveal and teach it in detail to others, attend to it with wise reflection, and remain never separated from the mind of omniscience; and having written it down, he will honor, revere, respect,
and worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags.
Thus, Kauśika, let alone the middling miraculous power consisting of conviction in one’s own welfare;

suppose, Kauśika, that a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of performing an act of worship after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, were to fill this Jambūdvīpa with stupas made of the seven precious gems, each one yojana in height.
And one should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate them with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate a great deal more merit on that account?
Śakra said: "A great deal, Blessed One; a great deal, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will generate much greater merit who shall take up this Perfection of Wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, propagate it, and attend to it with wise reflection."

Not separated from the mind of omniscience, he will write it down and honor it, revere it, respect it, and worship it; he will worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags, and with many kinds of offerings. Thus, Kauśika, let Jambudvīpa remain filled with stūpas of the Tathāgata for those who possess medium-middling conviction in their own welfare. Furthermore, Kauśika, if this world-system of four great continents—

Suppose one were to fill an entire world-system with stūpas made of the seven precious gems, each a yojana in height, for the purpose of honoring the Tathāgata after his parinirvāṇa; and suppose one were to revere, honor, esteem, worship, adore, and venerate them with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate a great deal of merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate even more merit than that."
Whoever should take up this Perfection of Wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and even go so far as to preserve it in the form of a book,

and should honor, revere, and worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags— this person alone would, on that account, generate much greater merit.
Thus, the conviction regarding one’s own welfare is middling-superior.

Let it be, Kauśika, that a world-system of four great continents is filled with reliquaries of the Tathāgata; yet if, Kauśika, someone were to fill a thousandfold world-system with reliquaries made of the seven precious gems for the purpose of honoring the Tathāgata after his final nirvāṇa—
If one were to fill [the world] with [stūpas] a yojana high, and having filled it, were to honor, revere, respect, worship, adore,

and venerate them with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags— what do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate a great deal of merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate even more merit than that."

Whoever, having made this Perfection of Wisdom even as far as a mere book, should take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection; and should honor, revere, respect, and worship it, adorning it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags,
and should celebrate, revere, and venerate it—

This very person would generate much more merit than that. Thus, let alone the supreme resolve for one's own welfare being of superior power, Kauśika, suppose there were a thousandfold world system completely filled with stupas made of various jewels; and suppose, Kauśika, some man were to [fill] a second-order intermediate thousandfold world system [with them] after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa.

For the sake of worship, one should have a land filled with stupas made of various jewels; and having had them made, one should honor, revere, respect, and worship them, worshipping, adoring, and venerating them with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate a great deal of merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate even more merit than that."

If someone were to honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate this Perfection of Wisdom—even by making it into a book—offering flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags, this person alone would generate far more merit than that. Let this stand, Kauśika, as the middling-high degree of conviction regarding one's own welfare: suppose there were a second-order intermediate world-system filled with stūpas made of various jewels. Suppose, Kauśika, someone...

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, for the sake of honoring the Tathāgata after his parinirvāṇa, were to fill this trichiliocosm with stūpas made of the seven precious substances, each one yojana in height, and having filled it, were to revere, honor, esteem, worship, adore, and venerate them with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags;
"What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate a great deal more merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much greater merit who, having made this Perfection of Wisdom even as a book, should take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, honor it, revere it, respect it, worship it, adore it, and venerate it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
Thus, Kauśika, let alone the conviction regarding one's own welfare being of the highest degree; suppose this trichiliocosm were filled with stupas made of various jewels and worshipped.
As for all those beings included within the category of "beings" in the trichiliocosm, Kauśika—

Suppose each single being were to have stupas made of the seven precious gems—each one a yojana in height—for the sake of honoring the Tathāgata after he has passed into parinirvāṇa; and suppose they were to revere, honor, respect, worship, adore, and venerate them with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory-pennants.
What do you think, Kauśika, would those beings generate a great deal of merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One! Much, Sugata!
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit on that account."

Whoever, having even made this Perfection of Wisdom into a book, should take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and attend to it with proper mental application, remaining never parted from the mind set on omniscience, and should honor, revere, and worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags—
This person alone would produce much more merit than that.
When this was said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.”

“Blessed One, by honoring, respecting, revering, and worshiping the perfection of wisdom, the Blessed Buddhas of the past, future, and present are honored, respected, revered, and worshipped. Furthermore, Blessed One,

as for those beings in the world systems of the eastern direction— worlds as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in each of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems— if every single one of those beings were to create [stūpas] made of the seven precious gems for the purpose of worshipping the Tathāgata after his final nirvāṇa...”

Suppose one were to establish stūpas a yojana in height and honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate them for an eon or the remainder of an eon, with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory standards—
would those sons of good family or daughters of good family, Blessed One, generate a greater amount of merit on that basis?

In the same way, in the south, the west, the north, above, below, and in the intermediate directions— in each single direction, across world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— if every single sentient being among them were to establish stupas made of the seven precious gems, one yojana in height, for the purpose of honoring the Tathāgata after his parinirvāṇa, and were to maintain them for an eon or the remainder of an eon;

Or if one were to honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate them with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory standards—
would those sons of good family or daughters of good family, O Blessed One, generate a greater amount of merit on that account?
The Blessed One said:
"It is so, Kauśika, it is so.

Śakra said: 'Therefore, Blessed One, that son of good family or daughter of good family generates much more merit on that account who, having had this perfection of wisdom written down in a book, should take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and attend to it properly, as well as those [who honor it].'"

One should honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate them, and one should worship, adore, and venerate them with divine flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory standards; O Blessed One, this son of good family or daughter of good family would generate far more merit than that previous son of good family or daughter of good family.
For in this way, Blessed One, all wholesome dharmas are included within this perfection of wisdom. That is to say:

the ten paths of wholesome action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gateways to liberation, the four noble truths, and the six superknowledges.

The eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of wisdom, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal and external emptiness,
up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, all samādhis, all doors of dhāraṇī, and the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
The four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,

great loving-kindness, great compassion, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, omniscience, and the knowledge of all aspects— this is that teaching of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, having trained in which the Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas of the past, future, and present have emerged, are emerging, and will emerge.
Then the Blessed One said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"So it is, Kauśika, so it is!
On that account, those sons of good family or daughters of good family will produce much more merit—immeasurable merit."

Incalculable, inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable is the merit of those who, having written down this *prajñāpāramitā* and made it into a book, shall take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection;
and who, furthermore, shall honor it, revere it, respect it, worship it, adore it, and venerate it.
With flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, the five perfections of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are born from the perfection of wisdom.
All the emptinesses, all the meditative concentrations, all the doors of dhāraṇī, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening,

the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the noble truths, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the five eyes, the six superknowledges, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the ripening of sentient beings, and the excellence of the buddha-field.
For, Kauśika, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, all-knowledge, and the knowledge of all aspects are born from the perfection of wisdom;
for, Kauśika, the vehicle of the śrāvakas and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas are born from the perfection of wisdom.
For, Kauśika, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is born from the perfection of wisdom.

Therefore, Kauśika, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family shall write down this perfection of wisdom, make it into a book, and take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and reflect upon it correctly—
And if one should attend to it, and honor, revere, respect, worship, adore,
and venerate it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory standards,
then that former accumulation of merit would not approach even a hundredth part of this accumulation of merit.
It does not approach even a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part, up to and including a hundred-thousand-koṭi-niyuta-part;
it does not admit of any calculation, fraction, reckoning, comparison, resemblance, or proximity.
For what reason?

Kauśika, as long as this perfection of wisdom remains in Jambudvīpa, so long will there be no disappearance of the Jewel of the Buddha, no disappearance of the Jewel of the Dharma, and no disappearance of the Jewel of the Saṅgha; for that long,

the ten paths of wholesome action will exist in the world, as will the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditation.
Of the perfection of wisdom; of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;

of the noble truths; of the six supernormal knowledges; of the eight liberations; of the nine successive meditative attainments; of the four analytical insights; of the ten powers of a Tathāgata; of the four grounds of self-confidence; and of the eighteen unique qualities [of a Buddha].

The appearance in the world of the Buddha-qualities, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, omniscience, and the knowledge of all aspects; and the appearance in the world of the great kṣatriya clans, the great brahmin clans, and the great householder clans; and of the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.
There occurs the manifestation in the world up to the realm of the Akaniṣṭha gods;
there occurs the full realization of the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, of the pratyekabuddhas,
and of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as well as the unsurpassed Buddha-knowledge and the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
The ripening of sentient beings and the purification of the Buddha-field are made known.
Thus, the weak-weak stage of conviction regarding one's own and others' welfare is established.
Then, those belonging to the assembly of the Four Great Kings in this trichiliocosm...
Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the sons of the gods as far as those of the Akaniṣṭha heaven:
"Friends, the perfection of wisdom should be taken up; friends, the perfection of wisdom should be retained, recited, mastered, and properly attended to.
Why is that?"

Friends, when the perfection of wisdom has been taken up, maintained, recited, and mastered, all unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase; the divine hosts increase and the asura hosts diminish. Friends, when the perfection of wisdom has been taken up, maintained, recited, and mastered, the lineage of the Buddha is not cut off, nor is the lineage of the Dharma or the lineage of the Saṅgha cut off.
Friends, for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Three Jewels is not interrupted, there appears in the world the manifestation of all the perfections (*pāramitā*),

the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣyadharma*), the noble truths (*āryasatya*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*),
the eight gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), the six superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and the ten powers of a Tathāgata (*tathāgatabala*).
The manifestation in the world of the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha occurs;

the manifestation in the world of all the emptinesses, all the meditative concentrations, all the doors of dhāraṇī, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, omniscience, and the knowledge of all aspects occurs.
The appearance of the bodhisattva practice in the world occurs;
the appearances in the world of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are made known.
Then the Blessed One said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Take up, Kauśika, this perfection of wisdom; bear it in mind, recite it, and master it, Kauśika, this perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, when such thoughts arise among the asuras as, 'We shall wage war against the gods of the Thirty-three,' [they will be overcome]."
Therefore, Kauśika, at that time you should bring this perfection of wisdom to mind and recite it; thus those manifestations of the asuras will disappear,
and they will no longer give rise to those thoughts of hostility.

And for those sons of the gods or daughters of the gods whose time of death has come, you should recite this before them; if they should perceive their own rebirth in a state of woe, as they listen to this Perfection of Wisdom, those mental states leading to rebirth in a state of woe will vanish, and they will be reborn right there in that celestial abode. For such is the great power of the hearing of this Perfection of Wisdom for any son of good family or daughter of good family, Kauśika.

Whether it be a son of the gods or a daughter of the gods, this perfection of wisdom will come within the range of their hearing. By that root of virtue, they shall all, in due course, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. For indeed, Blessed One, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones who appeared in the past, and whose disciples were established in the realm of nirvana without remainder—they too, by relying on this very perfection of wisdom, fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. And those, Blessed One, who will appear in the future..."
"In the past time, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, together with their assemblies of disciples, by relying on this very perfection of wisdom, fully awakened to unsurpassed,

perfect enlightenment. And those Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, together with their assemblies of disciples, who now currently reside, stay, and maintain themselves in the world throughout the ten directions in the present time [also do so by relying on this very perfection of wisdom]."
All of them, having trained right here in the perfection of wisdom, attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is that?
Because all the qualities of a Buddha, all the qualities of a bodhisattva, all the qualities of a pratyekabuddha, and all the qualities of a śrāvaka are contained within the perfection of wisdom.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"So it is, Kauśika, so it is! This is a great vidyā, Kauśika, namely the perfection of wisdom."
This, Kauśika, is the unsurpassed lore, namely the perfection of wisdom; this, Kauśika, is the peerless lore, namely the perfection of wisdom.
For what reason?

For it is thus, Kauśika: all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who, in the ten directions of the world, have been, are, or will be, have relied upon this very perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) to have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi). It is by relying upon this very perfection of wisdom that the ten paths of wholesome action (daśakuśalāḥ karmapathāḥ) are made known.

The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, all the perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, all the emptinesses, all the samādhis,
all the doors of dhāraṇī, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, and the four analytical knowledges.

The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) are known. The three gateways to liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), the six superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), suchness (*tathatā*), non-falsity (*avitathatā*), non-otherness (*ananyatathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), and the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*) are known in the world. The five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*), the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), and the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) [are also known].

The fruit of non-returning, arhatship, the state of a pratyekabuddha, and omniscience are known in the world. Furthermore, Kauśika, it is by depending upon the bodhisattva that the ten wholesome paths of action, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble truths are manifested in the world.
The immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the three gateways to liberation,

the six superknowledges, all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the samādhis, all the gateways of dhāraṇī, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

The knowledge of the aspects of the path, the knowledge of all things, and the knowledge of all aspects are known in the world. The realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), suchness (*tathatā*), non-falsity (*avitathatā*), non-other-suchness (*ananyatathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), and the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*) are known in the world.
The five eyes, the fruit of stream-entry and the stream-enterer, the fruit of once-returning and the once-returner, and the fruit of non-returning...

The non-returner, arhatship, the arhat, pratyekabodhi, the pratyekabuddha, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment— the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha— is manifested in the world. Just as, Kauśika, by means of the lunar disk, all medicinal herbs and the hosts of stars are manifested, even so, Kauśika, [is the Tathāgata manifested].

Having relied upon the lunar orb of the bodhisattva, there arise the ten paths of wholesome action; all wholesome conduct, right conduct, and all the perfections; the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening; the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments;
the noble truths, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the six superknowledges, and all meditative concentrations.
All the emptinesses and all the gateways of the dhāraṇīs are manifested as the medicinal herbs of the concentrations on emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

The medicinal herbs of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are manifested. All the stars and constellations of the learners, the non-learners, and all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are made known. Omniscience is manifested. The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are manifested.

Even when the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have not awakened in the world and there is no arising of Tathāgatas, even then those Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, teach beings both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
For what reason?
For the vehicle of gods, the vehicle of humans, the vehicle of śrāvakas, and the vehicle of pratyekabuddhas are all born from the bodhisattva;

and that skill in means of the bodhisattva mahāsattva is born from the perfection of wisdom, by which skill in means he fulfills the six perfections, cultivates all emptinesses, and [cultivates] all samādhis.
And he enters [these meditative states], attains all the gateways of the dhāraṇīs, and enters the immeasurable dhyānas and formless attainments;

he cultivates the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, cultivates the noble truths, cultivates the eight liberations, enters the nine successive meditative attainments, and cultivates the three superknowledges.

He cultivates the gates of liberation; he attains the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; he attains the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks.

Yet he does not personally realize the stage of a śrāvaka or the stage of a pratyekabuddha. Rather, he brings sentient beings to maturity, purifies the buddha-field, acquires the excellence of a bodhisattva, and attains omniscience.
Furthermore, Kauśika, any son of good family or daughter of good family who shall take up this perfection of wisdom...
"He who shall uphold it, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection will be endowed with these qualities pertaining to the present life.
When this had been said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Blessed One, with what qualities pertaining to the present life will sons of good family or daughters of good family be endowed who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to this perfection of wisdom?"
The Blessed One said:

"In that case, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family shall not die by poison, nor by fire, nor by weapon, nor by water; indeed, they shall not die from any disease whatsoever, with the exception of [the natural end of their lifespan]."
There will be no suffering from the ripening of past karma, nor will there be calamities arising from the royal court. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family,
while reciting this Perfection of Wisdom, enters a royal court, those who watch for an opening, who seek an opening, shall find no opening against them.
For what reason?

It is because of the very power of this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). If, Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family, while reciting this perfection of wisdom, should approach a royal court, the kings there, or the princes, or the high ministers, will think that they should first address him and think that they should speak with him.
For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, for those sons of good family and daughters of good family, a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings has become present;
a mind of compassion, a mind of sympathetic joy, and a mind of equanimity have become present. By these, Kauśika...

A son of good family or a daughter of good family who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to this perfection of wisdom will be endowed with qualities pertaining to the present life. Furthermore, Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family [will be endowed] with these qualities pertaining to future lives.

One who shall take up, uphold, recite, master, and properly attend to this perfection of wisdom will be endowed with these qualities; that is to say, they shall never be separated from the ten paths of wholesome action.

Nor by the four dhyānas, nor by the four immeasurables, nor by the four formless attainments, nor by the perfections, nor by the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, nor by the truths, nor by the eight liberations, nor by the nine successive meditative attainments,
nor by the three gateways to liberation, nor by the superknowledges, nor by all the emptinesses, nor by all the samādhis.

He will never be devoid of all the gateways of dhāraṇī, nor of the ten powers, nor of the fearlessnesses, nor of the analytical knowledges, nor of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He will never be devoid of the primary marks and secondary characteristics. He shall never be reborn in the hells, among animals, or in the world of Yama; he shall never have impaired faculties.

He shall never be deficient in limb; he shall never be reborn in poor families, nor in families of bamboo-workers, nor in families of outcasts, nor in families of boxers, nor in families of Caṇḍālas, sheep-butchers, or fowlers, nor in Śūdra families;
rather, he will be reborn in great Kṣatriya families, or in great Brāhmaṇa families, or in great householder families.

Or he will be reborn in sublime and most exalted states. From that time forth, his body will be constantly and perpetually adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the secondary characteristics.

In whichever world-system there are Buddhas, Blessed Ones, he will be born spontaneously upon a lotus in the presence of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. He will never be deprived of the superknowledges (abhijñā). Desiring...

He will travel from buddha-field to buddha-field in order to attend upon those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and to hear the Dharma; and as he travels from buddha-field to buddha-field, he brings sentient beings to maturity and purifies the buddha-fields.

Therefore, Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to this perfection of wisdom, remaining never parted from the mind set on omniscience. He will not be deprived of these qualities pertaining to the present life and the qualities pertaining to future lives.
"Until he fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Then, a hundred wandering mendicants of other sects, with the intention of finding fault, approached the place where the Blessed One was.
At that time, this thought occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

This hundred of wanderers from other sects, with the intention of finding fault, is approaching the place where the Blessed One is; therefore, I should now recite as much of the perfection of wisdom as I have received from the presence of the Blessed One, so that this hundred of wanderers from other sects will not approach the Blessed One and will not create an obstacle to the perfection of wisdom.
Then indeed Śakra, the lord of the gods, recited as much of the Perfection of Wisdom as he had received from the Blessed One.
Then those wanderers of other sects, having circumambulated the Blessed One from a distance, departed by the very same path by which they had come.
Then this thought occurred to the venerable Śāriputra:

"What is the reason here, by which these wanderers of other sects, with the intention of finding fault, circumambulated the Blessed One from afar and returned by the very same path by which they had come?
Then the Blessed One, knowing the reflection in the mind of the venerable Śāriputra with his own mind, addressed the venerable Śāriputra:
"Śāriputra, this Perfection of Wisdom was brought to mind by Śakra, the lord of the gods, by which these followers of other sects [were turned back]."
The wandering mendicants, having circumambulated the Blessed One from afar, returned by the very same path by which they had come.
Indeed, Śāriputra, I do not perceive even a single wholesome quality (*śukladharma*) in those wandering mendicants of other sects;
all these wandering mendicants of other sects have hostile minds and intend to find fault, thinking that they should approach [the Buddha].

Śāriputra, I do not perceive anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, who could approach this Perfection of Wisdom with the intention of finding fault or with a hostile mind; such a thing is impossible.
For what reason? Because, Śāriputra, those here in this triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system— the Cāturmahārājika, Trāyastriṃśa,
Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, as well as the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Brahmapārṣadya gods— [all approach].
Even the gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven, as well as the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattva mahāsattvas—they too have taken up this perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
Because they are born from the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, together with their assemblies of śrāvakas, and along with the bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, who reside in each of the ten directions in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— up to all the world-systems in the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— by them...
Moreover, this perfection of wisdom has been embraced by all of them. For what reason?
Because they have all been born from this perfection of wisdom.
Then, it occurred to Māra, the Evil One:
These four assemblies of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, stand here in his presence.

These sons of the gods of the desire realm and the form realm also stand in his presence; without doubt, the bodhisattvas, the great beings, will here receive their prophecy regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
"What if I were now to approach the Blessed One in order to cause him to lose his sight?
Then Māra the Evil One, having conjured up a fourfold army, desired to approach the place where the Blessed One was.
Then it occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Surely this is Māra the Evil One who, having conjured up a fourfold army, desires to approach the Blessed One.
Such is the array of this fourfold army of Māra the Evil One; such an array does not belong to King Bimbisāra’s fourfold army."
Such an array as this has never been seen in the fourfold army of Prasenajit, nor in the fourfold army of the Śākyas, nor in the fourfold army of the Licchavis.
The Mallas do not possess such an array of their fourfold army as this fourfold army which has been conjured up by Māra, the Evil One; for indeed,
for a long time Māra, the Evil One, has been seeking an opportunity, searching for an opening against the Blessed One, with the intention of harassing sentient beings.
"What if I were now to bring this Perfection of Wisdom to mind and recite it from memory?
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, brought the Perfection of Wisdom to mind and recited it from memory.
And in whatever way Śakra, the lord of the gods, recited this Perfection of Wisdom from memory, in that very same way Māra, the Evil One, [returned] by that same path and through that same door.

Thus he turned back. Then, indeed, those gods in this assembly, from the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods up to the Akaniṣṭha gods, having manifested divine flowers, while remaining in the sky, cast them toward the Blessed One and scattered them over him.
And they spoke these words:

"Ah, may this Perfection of Wisdom long circulate among the humans of Jambudvīpa! As long as this Perfection of Wisdom shall circulate among the humans of Jambudvīpa, for so long there will be no disappearance of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The True Dharma will endure for a long time,
and the appearance of the Saṅgha will manifest in the world. In this way, throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system,
and likewise in all Buddha-fields in the ten directions, the distinguished conduct of the bodhisattvas will become known.
And in whichever direction those sons of good family or daughters of good family shall write down, preserve, recite, or even keep this Perfection of Wisdom after having it committed to a book,
that direction will become filled with light.
"This direction where this perfection of wisdom shall circulate will become possessed of a protector and freed from the darkness of ignorance.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"So it is, Kauśika, so it is!

In whichever direction, throughout the expanse of world-systems, this Perfection of Wisdom shall circulate— whether written in a book or existing as a manifestation of light— that direction shall become filled with light."
"This direction shall become possessed of a protector and free from the darkness of ignorance.
Then those sons of the gods, having manifested divine flowers, scattered them over the Blessed One and spoke these words:
Whosoever, whether a son of good family or a daughter of good family, shall take up this Perfection of Wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it,

and attend to it with wise reflection— for such a person, neither Māras nor the gods belonging to the host of Māra will find an opportunity to harm them. We too, O Blessed One, [will protect] that son of good family or daughter of good family...
Or we shall constantly and continuously provide protection, shelter, and defense; O Blessed One,
we shall regard that son of good family or daughter of good family as the Teacher himself— whoever shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to this perfection of wisdom.
Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who will take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to this perfection of wisdom will not be endowed with meager roots of virtue."

And they will attend to it with proper mental attention. Blessed One, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who will take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and attend to this perfection of wisdom with proper mental attention must have performed services for previous Victors. Those sons of good family must have attended upon many Buddhas and been sustained by spiritual friends.
And there will be daughters of good family.
Why is that?
For omniscience is born from this, namely, it is born from the perfection of wisdom; and the perfection of wisdom is born from omniscience.
For what reason?
Because there is no other perfection of wisdom and no other omniscience; for omniscience and the perfection of wisdom are non-dual and indivisible.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "So it is."

"Kauśika, it is just as you say: omniscience and the perfection of wisdom are non-dual; they are not divided into two. Thus ends the section on the weak-middling conviction regarding one's own and others' welfare.
Then, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
For thus the Blessed One does not proclaim the name of the perfection of giving, nor the perfection of ethical discipline,
nor the perfection of patience, nor the perfection of vigor, nor the perfection of meditative concentration, in the same way that he proclaims the name of the perfection of wisdom;
he does not proclaim the names of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
He does not proclaim the names of the noble truths, nor of the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, or the formless attainments;
he does not proclaim the names of the eight gates of liberation, nor of the nine successive dwellings and attainments;
he does not proclaim the names of the six superknowledges, nor of all the emptinesses, nor of the concentrations, nor of all the gateways of dhāraṇīs.

He does not proclaim the names of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor of the grounds of self-confidence, nor of the analytical knowledges, nor of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, in the same way that he proclaims the name of the perfection of wisdom. When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:

Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom is the precursor and the leader of the six perfections; it is the precursor and the leader of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments; it is the precursor and the leader of the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and the six superknowledges.

The perfection of wisdom is the precursor and leader of all emptinesses, all samādhis, and all doors of dhāraṇī; it is the precursor and leader of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; it is the precursor and leader of all the qualities of a Buddha.
What do you think, Ānanda? Does a gift that has not been dedicated toward omniscience receive the designation of a "perfection"?
What do you think?
“Unconsecrated morality, unconsecrated patience, unconsecrated vigor, unconsecrated meditation, and unconsecrated wisdom do not receive the designation ‘perfection’ with respect to omniscience.
Ānanda said: “Certainly not, Blessed One; certainly not, Sugata.
But how, Blessed One, does a gift that is consecrated to omniscience receive the designation ‘perfection’?”
"But how, Blessed One, do morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom, when dedicated toward omniscience, receive the designation 'perfection'?
The Blessed One replied:
"Ānanda, it is by way of non-duality that giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom, when dedicated toward omniscience..."

When dedicated [to awakening], it receives the name "perfection" (*pāramitā*). When giving, up to wisdom, is dedicated by way of non-arising and by way of non-apprehension, it receives the name "perfection" for the sake of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Ānanda said: "How, Blessed One, does giving, when dedicated by way of non-duality, receive the name 'perfection' for the sake of omniscience?"

"In this way, Blessed One, how do morality, patience, vigor, and meditation—when dedicated through the yoga of non-duality with regard to wisdom—attain the designation of 'perfection' (pāramitā) for the sake of omniscience?

The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, it is through the yoga of non-duality with regard to form; through the yoga of non-duality with regard to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to awakening."
Ānanda said: "How, Blessed One, is there the application of non-duality to form; how is there the application of non-duality to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
"How is it that [this applies] up to enlightenment through the yoga of non-duality?
The Blessed One said:

"For in this way, Ānanda, form is empty of form; feeling is empty of feeling; perception is empty of perception; mental formations are empty of mental formations; and consciousness is empty of consciousness."
For what reason?
Because form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as the perfections, are non-dual and not divided; even up to awakening and the perfections, these are non-dual.
Therefore, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom is the precursor and the leader of all the perfections and all the emptinesses.
Of all samādhis, all doors of dhāraṇīs, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments,

the noble truths, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the three doors of liberation, the six superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities...

For the unique qualities of a Buddha, up to awakening and omniscience, the perfection of wisdom is the precursor and the leader. Just as, Ānanda, seeds grow depending upon the great earth by the power of their causal totality, even so, Ānanda, all the perfections, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, and [all other qualities] depend upon and come from the perfection of wisdom.

The immeasurable meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the noble truths, the six superknowledges, and all the gateways of the dhāraṇīs grow forth. The ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha grow forth, up to and including omniscience. Relying upon omniscience, all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the samādhis, and all the gateways of the dhāraṇīs [grow forth].
The thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges,
and even the unique qualities of a Buddha grow from it. Therefore, Ānanda, the perfection of wisdom alone is the leader of these perfections,
up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and even up to the knowledge of all aspects.
