Thus, Śakra spoke regarding the weak-to-strong conviction in one’s own and others’ welfare: “Furthermore, Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One has not indeed fully proclaimed all the qualities of the perfection of wisdom that a son of good family or a daughter of good family acquires by grasping this [perfection].”

“Blessed One, by taking up, maintaining, reciting, mastering, and attending to the perfection of wisdom in a proper manner, through the perfection of wisdom being thus taken up, maintained, recited, mastered, and attended to in a proper manner, there occurs in the world the manifestation of the ten paths of wholesome action, as well as the four meditative concentrations and the four immeasurables.”

of the four formless attainments, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the six superknowledges, the three gateways to liberation, all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the samādhis, all the gateways of dhāraṇīs, and the ten powers of a Tathāgata;

The manifestation in the world of the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha occurs through the Perfection of Wisdom, Blessed One— when it has been taken up, maintained, recited, mastered, and correctly attended to by mind. It is through this that great wealthy merchant families are known.
The great śāla clans of kṣatriyas are known; the great śāla clans of brahmins are known;
and the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha gods are known.
“Blessed One, it is through the perfection of wisdom—when it has been taken up, and so on, up to when it has been properly attended to—that stream-enterers are known;
that once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas are known; and that bodhisattvas are known.”

“Blessed One, it is through the Perfection of Wisdom—when it has been taken up, maintained, recited, mastered, and properly attended to—that Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas become known in the world.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

“Furthermore, Kauśika, for those sons of good family or daughters of good family by whom this Perfection of Wisdom has been maintained, recited, mastered, and properly attended to, it is not merely by that much [that they have accomplished].”
For what reason?

Because, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to this perfection of wisdom will indeed be endowed with an immeasurable aggregate of ethical discipline.

And they will attend to it with their minds and shall not be separated from the mind of omniscience. They who take up, preserve, recite, master, and properly attend to this perfection of wisdom will be endowed with the immeasurable aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.

And they will attend to it with their minds undiverted from the mind of omniscience. Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to this perfection of wisdom with a mind directed toward omniscience should be known as images of the Tathāgata.

And they will not be separated from it. Moreover, Kauśika, whatever aggregate of morality, aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation belongs to all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and whatever aggregate of morality, aggregate of concentration... belongs to those sons of good family and daughters of good family who dwell in the perfection of wisdom—
The aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation— Kauśika, compared to this aggregate of morality,
aggregate of concentration, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation,
the aggregates of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas [are infinitesimal].
It does not approach even a hundredth part,
nor a thousandth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part;
it does not admit of any calculation, nor any counting, nor any comparison, nor any resemblance, nor any analogy whatsoever.
For what reason?

Because the minds of those sons of good family and daughters of good family are liberated from the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and there is no dharma whatsoever that they have not penetrated or known. Those, Kauśika, who are sons of good family or daughters of good family [who] this...

Those sons of good family and daughters of good family who will honor, revere, respect, and worship the Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags— these qualities and benefits, pertaining both to this life and to future lives, are to be expected for them as well.

Thus, when the middling supernatural power associated with the inclination toward one's own and others' welfare had been spoken, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One,
I shall provide constant and continuous protection, shelter, and defense for that son of good family or daughter of good family."
I shall provide for whoever shall take up this perfection of wisdom, maintain it, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection;
whoever shall not be separated from the mind of omniscience and shall honor and revere this perfection of wisdom.
"He will honor and worship [this perfection of wisdom] with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Furthermore, Kauśika, for those sons of good family or daughters of good family who recite this perfection of wisdom..."

Many hundreds of thousands of sons of the gods will approach to hear the Dharma. Furthermore, those sons of the gods will think it their duty to provide eloquence associated with the perfection of wisdom to those sons of good family or daughters of good family. Even when those Dharma-preachers do not wish to speak, [the gods will assist them].
Even then, those sons of the gods will think that eloquence should be brought forth out of reverence for the Dharma.

Furthermore, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who shall take up, recite, master, and properly attend to this perfection of wisdom will obtain this very quality pertaining to the present life.
And having written it down, they will honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.

Furthermore, Kauśika, when these sons of good family or daughters of good family are reciting this Perfection of Wisdom in the presence of the fourfold assembly, their minds will not be cowed, thinking, "Who will apply themselves to me? Who will find fault with me?"
For what reason?
Because this very perfection of wisdom will provide protection, defense, and shelter for those sons of good family or daughters of good family;
for in this perfection of wisdom, all phenomena—whether mundane or supramundane—are undifferentiated and common.
And they are wholesome, conditioned and unconditioned, the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of buddhas. For what reason is that?

For it is because those sons of good family or daughters of good family, having established themselves in internal emptiness and so on, up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, do not perceive any ground for reproach in the perfection of wisdom,
nor do they perceive anyone who might be reproached.
For in this way, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who are sustained by the perfection of wisdom will be free from reproach.

Furthermore, Kauśika, the mind of that son of good family or daughter of good family who takes up, bears in mind, recites, masters, and correctly attends to this perfection of wisdom does not sink down, nor does it...
He does not shrink back, he is not terrified, he is not frightened, and he does not fall into terror.
For what reason?
Because that son of good family or daughter of good family does not perceive any objective basis upon which he might cling or shrink back.
Or he might be startled, or terrified, or fall into a state of dread. Moreover, Kauśika,

that son of good family or daughter of good family who will take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to this perfection of wisdom, and who will honor, revere, and respect it, shall obtain these very qualities pertaining to the present life.

"He will worship [her] with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags"— this is the middling-middling resolve for the benefit of oneself and others.
Furthermore, Kauśika, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family shall take up this *prajñāpāramitā*, retain it, recite it, master it, and attend to it properly (*yoniśas*), that...
And having written it down, he will honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags;
he will become beloved by his mother and father, by friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relatives, and by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas;
and even those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, bodhisattvas, and pratyekabuddhas who reside in all the world-systems throughout the ten directions of the world.

He will be dear to all Arhats, to all those in training (śaikṣas), and to all those beyond training (aśaikṣas); that Bodhisattva will also be dear and pleasing to the world with its gods, to the world with its Māras, to the generation of recluses and brahmins, and to the generation of gods, humans, and asuras. Thus [is] the medium and superior degree of success regarding the welfare of oneself and others.

He will be endowed with uninterrupted eloquence. He will be endowed with the uninterrupted perfection of generosity. Likewise, he will be endowed with the uninterrupted perfection of ethical discipline, the uninterrupted perfection of patience, the uninterrupted perfection of vigor, the uninterrupted perfection of meditative concentration, and the uninterrupted perfection of wisdom. He will be endowed with the uninterrupted emptiness of the internal.

He will be endowed with the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, which is indestructible. He will be endowed with the indestructible applications of mindfulness. He will be endowed with the indestructible right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path. [He will be endowed] with the indestructible noble truths and the indestructible immeasurables, meditative concentrations, and formless attainments.

By means of the eight gates of liberation that are indestructible; by means of the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling, the supernormal powers, the noble truths, all samādhis, and all dhāraṇī-gates that are indestructible;

by means of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha that are indestructible; and by means of the indestructible ripening of sentient beings and the indestructible...

Through the purification of the Buddha-field, he will become endowed with the unassailable knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). He will also be capable of suppressing, in accordance with the Dharma alone, the various doctrines of non-Buddhist teachers as they arise. Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who [upholds] this [perfection of wisdom] shall likewise acquire these qualities pertaining both to the present life and to future lives.
He will take up the *prajñāpāramitā*, uphold it, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).

He will remain never separated from the mind of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā-citta*), and having written it down, he will honor, revere, esteem, and worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.

Thus, there is the superior resolve for one’s own and others’ welfare, and superior miraculous power. Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having even written this Perfection of Wisdom in a book,
should uphold it, recite it, and master it— then, Kauśika, regarding those [beings] in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system...

In this world-system, the sons of the gods belonging to the assembly of the Four Great Kings, who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, will come there and take up, bear in mind, recite, master, attend to, and pay homage to this perfection of wisdom; and having paid homage and bowed down, they will depart once again. Thus...
The Trāyastriṃśas, Yāmas, Tuṣitas, Nirmāṇaratis, Paranirmitavaśavartins, Brahmapāriṣadyas, Brahmapurohitas,

Mahābrahmans, Parīttābhas, Apramāṇābhas, Ābhāsvaras, Parīttaśubhas, Apramāṇaśubhas, Śubhakṛtsnas, Anabhrakas, Puṇyaprasavas, Bṛhatphalas, Śuddhāvāsas, Avṛhas, Atapas, Sudṛśas, Sudarśanas, and Akaniṣṭhas.

In that regard, Kauśika, those Great Brahmās who have made the vow for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment will also come there, and having taken up, mastered, retained, recited, and paid homage to this perfection of wisdom, they will depart once again.

They will depart. Furthermore, those sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host—the Avṛhas, Atapas, Sudṛśas, Sudarśanas, and Akaniṣṭhas—they too, having come there, will take up, master, retain, recite, and pay homage to this Perfection of Wisdom, and then they will depart once again. Therefore, Kauśika, by that son of good family or daughter of good family...
One should generate this thought:

"Those sons of the gods in the world-systems of the ten directions, from the Cāturmahārājakāyikas up to the Bṛhatphalas, who have set their minds upon unexcelled perfect enlightenment; and also those sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realms; and whoever else there are—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas."
Let them also come here, take up this *prajñāpāramitā*, master it, retain it, recite it, and honor it, and then return;

let this gift of Dharma be given to them. And as for those sons of the gods, from the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods up to the Bṛhatphala gods, in the world-systems of the ten directions, who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—let this gift of Dharma be given to them as well.

Even those sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host will come there and take up, retain, recite, and master this perfection of wisdom; having bowed to it, paid homage to it, and worshipped it, they will think to depart once again. Furthermore, for that son of good family or daughter of good family who is here—
In this trichiliocosm, from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha gods,

and likewise in the world-systems of the ten directions, from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha gods— they all shall provide protection, defense, and guardianship for that son of good family or daughter of good family. Furthermore, no one [shall be able to harm them].
Seeking an opportunity and searching for an opening, Mara will find such an opportunity, except in the case of the ripening of past karma;
furthermore, Kauśika, this son of good family or daughter of good family also acquires these qualities pertaining to the present life.
For what reason is that?

For even those sons of the gods who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment will think that they too must go there. For, Kauśika, those sons of the gods have set out for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment for the sake of protecting, benefiting, and bringing happiness to all sentient beings. Thus, the conviction regarding the welfare of oneself and others is of the highest-middle degree.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, how will a son of good family or a daughter of good family know that the sons of the gods from the realm of the Four Great Kings have come, up to and including the sons of the gods from the Akaniṣṭha heaven?"
In this way, from all ten directions, one should seek to take up, bear in mind, recite, master, honor, revere, respect, and worship this Perfection of Wisdom.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
If, Kauśika,
a son of good family or a daughter of good family perceives a sublime radiance, they should come to the conclusion:
"Gods of great majesty and great power have arrived to recite, take up, master, and preserve this perfection of wisdom."
to honor, revere, respect, worship, praise, and pay homage to it.

Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family should smell a divine, non-human fragrance never smelled before, they must conclude: "Highly powerful, highly powerful sons of the gods have come here for the sake of the *prajñāpāramitā*."

to recite, hear, take up, master, retain, honor, revere, respect, and worship it. Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family will be pure in their conduct, the deities will come because of that purity of conduct and, having taken up this *prajñāpāramitā*, will preserve it.

Having recited it, they will treat it with respect, honor it, revere it, and worship it, becoming joyful in mind. And those deities of little power who may be in that region of earth will think they must depart from there, unable to endure the splendor and majesty of those gods of great power and great power.

To the extent that deities of ever-greater majesty approach, to that same extent those sons of good family or daughters of good family will possess noble resolve. Furthermore, one must not practice any form of impure conduct in that region of earth;
rather, that region of earth should be adorned with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.

"It should be adorned; it should be made fragrant with ointments and strewn with loose flowers. It should be hung with bundles of hanging cloth-festoons and covered with a canopy of fine cloth. And that area of ground should be decorated in many ways.
Furthermore, Kauśika, the body of that son of good family or daughter of good family shall not become weary."
There will be physical ease; he will practice for the welfare of many people and for the happiness of many people with lightness of body.

And that son of good family or daughter of good family, Kauśika, will experience lightness of body, fitness of body, and ease of body, as well as lightness of mind, fitness of mind, and ease of mind. With ease, he...

At night he will prepare his bed; contemplating this very Perfection of Wisdom with a resolute intention, he will not see evil dreams. Furthermore, in his dreams he will see Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas, their bodies adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, their forms of golden hue, surrounded by a community of monks and a host of Bodhisattvas, [teaching] the Dharma.

As they teach, he will hear from them only discourse connected with the six perfections; he will hear only discourse connected with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, up to and including those connected with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. And of those perfections...
He will hear the meaning of [the teachings], up to hearing the meaning of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He will see the Bodhi tree.

He will see the bodhisattva mahāsattva approaching the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa). He will see him fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Having awakened, he will see him turning the wheel of the non-dual Dharma.

He will see many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas who delight in the communal recitation of the Dharma, [thinking]: "In this way omniscience is to be acquired; in this way sentient beings are to be matured; in this way the buddha-field is to be purified.
He will hear the voices of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas in the eastern direction.

In this way, in the south, the west, the north, above, below, and in the intermediate directions, he will hear the voices of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas: "In such-and-such a world-system, a Tathāgata, Arhat,
Samyaksaṃbuddha named so-and-so is surrounded and honored by so many hundreds of thousands of millions of Bodhisattvas and so many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Śrāvakas."
He teaches the Dharma. In the eastern direction, he will see many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa;
likewise, in all ten directions, he will see many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas entering parinirvāṇa.
And he will see the stūpas containing the relics of those Tathāgatas, made of various jewels—many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of stūpas.
He will see them, and he will honor, revere, respect, and worship those stūpas with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.

Furthermore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will indeed see such auspicious dreams; he will sleep in peace and awaken in peace, and his body will be infused with vitality.

He will perceive it; he will perceive his body as light, not heavy. He will have no powerful greed for food, nor will he have greed for the requisites of robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, or medicinal herbs for the sick.
It is just as, Kauśika, when a monk who practices yoga has emerged from meditative concentration and is satisfied by his mental attention.
The mind does not become strongly attached to food.
In the same way, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will not have a strong attachment to food.
For what reason?
For in this way, non-human beings infuse vitality into his body.

Moreover, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the ten directions—along with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—also pour vitality into his body. Kauśika, this son of good family or daughter of good family possesses this visible-world benefit.

One who grasps this perfection of wisdom—taking it up, mastering it, retaining it, reciting it, and attending to it with proper mental focus, never being separated from the mind of omniscience—thereby acquires its qualities. Thus, the conviction regarding one's own and others' welfare is of the highest degree.
Furthermore, even if that son of good family or daughter of good family were not to take up or retain this perfection of wisdom...
One should not recite it, nor master it, nor attend to it properly, nor explain it to others;
rather, having written it down in a book, one should honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
And, Kauśika, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family should take up and bear this Perfection of Wisdom in mind...
If one were to recite it, master it, attend to it thoroughly, and reveal it to others;

and if one were to honor, revere, respect, and worship that written copy with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags— then, Kauśika, this son of good family or daughter of good family would, on that account, produce far more merit.

But it is not so for one who would honor, revere, respect, and worship the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones throughout all the world-systems in the ten directions, together with their communities of disciples, providing them with robes, alms-food, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick; and [who would do likewise] for those Tathāgatas,
Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, together with their communities of disciples, once they have entered final nirvana.

One should have stūpas made of the seven precious jewels, and one should honor, revere, respect, and worship them with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags. Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Chapter on Honoring Stūpas," which concerns the weak-weak level of conviction regarding the welfare of others.
Then the Blessed One said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

"Kauśika, suppose this Jambudvīpa were completely filled with the relics of the Tathāgata, heaped up to the very top, and some son of good family or daughter of good family were to offer them to you."
"And if someone were to offer this perfection of wisdom to you, which of these two portions placed before you would you take?
Śakra said: "Blessed One, if this Jambudvīpa, filled to the very crest with the relics of the Tathāgata, were offered to me..."

And if this Perfection of Wisdom were written down in a book and offered to me, then, making a comparison, of these two portions thus set before me, I would take the Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that?
Blessed One, it is not that I lack reverence for those relics of the Tathāgata.

"O Blessed One, it is not that I am unwilling to honor, revere, respect, or worship the relics of the Tathāgata. Rather, O Blessed One, it is because they think to me: 'The relics of the Tathāgata are born from the perfection of wisdom; it is by means of this that they are honored, revered, respected, and worshipped.'"
It is because the relics of the Tathāgata have been permeated by the perfection of wisdom that they receive such worship.
Then, the venerable Śāriputra said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is ungraspable, invisible, non-obstructive, and has but a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics. Thus it is.
How can you think that the perfection of wisdom— which is ungraspable, invisible, non-resistant, and of a single characteristic, namely, the characteristicless— is something to be grasped?
For what reason is that?
For the perfection of wisdom does not abide for the sake of grasping or favoring;
it is not for decrease or increase, not for elevation or dispersal, not for affliction or purification;
nor is it a giver of the qualities of a Buddha.

It is not the discarder of the dharmas of ordinary beings; it is not the giver of the dharmas of bodhisattvas, nor of pratyekabuddhas, nor of śrāvakas, nor of those in training (śaikṣa), nor of those beyond training (aśaikṣa);
it is not the giver of the conditioned realm (saṃskṛtadhātu).
It is not the giver of the unconditioned realm;
it is not the giver of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature;
nor is it the giver of the perfections, nor of the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the path.

It is not the giver of the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, or the formless attainments; it is not the giver of the powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
nor is it the giver of omniscience.
Śakra said: "It is so, venerable Śāriputra, just as you say: the perfection of wisdom is not the giver of the Buddha-dharmas, nor is it the giver of anything up to omniscience. For what reason?
Because the perfection of wisdom does not appear as a duality; for the perfection of wisdom is non-dual."
In this way, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline,
and the perfection of generosity do not appear as a duality;
for the perfection of generosity is non-dual.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Excellent, excellent, Kauśika! It is just as you have pointed out: the perfection of wisdom does not appear as a duality, for the perfection of wisdom is non-dual."
In this way, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline,
and the perfection of generosity do not appear as a duality.
For the perfection of generosity is non-dual.
O Kauśika, one who would seek duality in the perfection of wisdom would be seeking duality in the dharmadhātu. Why is that?
Because, O Kauśika, the dharmadhātu and the perfection of wisdom are one and the same.
And this is non-dual, without division:
thus the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of ethical discipline,
as well as the realm of phenomena and the perfection of generosity— this is non-dual, without division.
O Kauśika, whoever would desire duality in the perfection of wisdom would desire duality in suchness.
Why is that?
Because, O Kauśika, suchness and the perfection of wisdom are non-dual and indivisible.
In this way, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of ethical discipline,

as well as suchness and the perfection of generosity— these are non-dual and not divided into two. O Kauśika, one who would seek duality in the perfection of wisdom would be seeking duality in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the inconceivable realm.
For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) are non-dual and not divided;
likewise for the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of ethical discipline.
The limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), as well as the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), are non-dual; they are not divided into two.

Śakra said: "I pay homage, Blessed One, to the perfection of wisdom, which is honored by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, and having trained in which a bodhisattva mahāsattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

"Blessed One, when I am seated upon that throne of the lord of gods in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods, those sons of the gods who come there to attend upon me pay homage to me as I sit there. But when I am not present there on my own lion-throne, those sons of the gods, having paid homage to that seat of mine, depart once again."

"Here Śakra, the lord of the gods, seated upon the Dharma-throne, taught the Dharma to the Trāyastriṃśa gods. In the very same way, Blessed One, wherever this Perfection of Wisdom is written down and remains, or is recited, or is fully proclaimed to others, there those sons of the gods from the ten directions— along with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— who shall pay homage to that Perfection of Wisdom will then depart once more.
From this have emerged the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
from this has emerged the source of happiness for all sentient beings.

Even the relics of the Tathāgatas receive worship because they have been permeated by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Blessed One, for a bodhisattva practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, the perfection of wisdom is the foundation of omniscience.
"Because the Perfection of Wisdom is the cause and the sustainer;
therefore, O Blessed One, from between those two portions, I would choose the Perfection of Wisdom alone.
Having taken up this Perfection of Wisdom, one should recite it with a mind absorbed in the Dharma at whatever time."
"I direct my attention to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
At that time, Blessed One, I do not perceive any sign whatsoever of fear or paralysis. Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is signless (*animitta*), without characteristics (*aliṅga*), and inexpressible (*anabhilapyā*).
For the perfection of wisdom, Blessed One, is beyond verbal expression;
likewise are the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of ethical discipline.
For the perfection of generosity, Blessed One, is signless, without marks, ineffable, and beyond verbal expression; and so it is for everything up to omniscience.

If, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom were with signs, with characteristics, expressible, and communicable— and not signless, without characteristics, inexpressible, and non-communicable— then the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would not have known all dharmas as signless, without characteristics, inexpressible, and non-communicable, and thus attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having attained perfect awakening, he would have taught to sentient beings a Dharma that is signless, markless, ineffable, and beyond verbal expression; for, Blessed One, since this perfection of wisdom is signless, markless, ineffable,
and beyond verbal expression, the Tathāgata, having realized that all phenomena are signless, markless, ineffable, and beyond verbal expression, [attained] unsurpassed...
Having awakened to perfect enlightenment, he should teach to sentient beings the Dharma that is signless, markless, ineffable, and beyond verbal expression.
Thus, the resolve for the welfare of others is of middling-mild degree;
therefore, Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom should be honored and revered by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.
They should be honored and worshipped with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
One should not expect for them a rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama;
nor should one expect for them the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha, until they attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
He will become fully awakened. And he will never be separated from the vision of the Tathāgatas as he matures sentient beings;

that is to say, he approaches the Buddha-fields in order to honor, revere, respect, and worship those Tathāgatas with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags. Thus ends the section on the weak and intense degrees of conviction regarding the welfare of others.

Furthermore, Blessed One, if this great trichiliocosm world-system, filled to the very crest with the relics of the Tathāgata, were offered to me, and if this Perfection of Wisdom were also offered to me after being written down in a book—
of these two portions thus set before me, I would choose this very Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that?
For it is from this that the relics of the Tathāgata have emerged.

Therefore, those sons of good family and daughters of good family who honor, revere, respect, and worship them, do not fall into the lower realms or states of woe after having honored, revered, respected, and worshipped them.

Having experienced the prosperities of gods and humans, they will attain nirvāṇa according to their respective vows—either by way of the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna).
Furthermore, O Blessed One, the vision of the Tathāgata and the vision of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are equal;
for, O Blessed One, that which is the perfection of wisdom and that which is the Tathāgata are non-dual and not divided into two. Thus is the medium-superior resolve for the benefit of others.

Furthermore, Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha who teaches the Dharma through the three miracles—namely, the twelvefold division consisting of sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, up to avadāna and upadeśa—and that son of good family or daughter of good family who, having taken up and mastered this Prajñāpāramitā, should teach it extensively to others: these two are equal. Why is that?
For it is from this, Blessed One, that the three miracles have emerged;
from this have emerged the discourses (*sūtra*), the songs (*geya*), the prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), and so on, up to the edifying tales (*avadāna*) and instructions (*upadeśa*).

Furthermore, Blessed One, those Buddhas, Blessed Ones, in the eastern direction—numbering as many as the sands of the river Ganges—who teach the Dharma, namely the discourses, the songs, the prophecies, and so on, up to the edifying tales and instructions; [all these have emerged from this].

By means of the three miracles, in the same way in the southern direction, the western, the northern, above, below, and even in the intermediate directions, throughout world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma by means of the three miracles, namely: the miracle of the discourse (*sūtra*).

Whether it be the *geya*, the *vyākaraṇa*, up to the *avadāna* and *upadeśa*, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take up this *prajñāpāramitā* and extensively proclaim it to others, these two are equal. Why is that?
For, Blessed One, the three miracles (*prātihārya*) have issued from this; from this have issued the *sūtra*, the *geya*, the *vyākaraṇa*, up to the *avadāna* and *upadeśa*.

Furthermore, Blessed One, suppose someone were to honor, revere, respect, and worship as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are in each of the ten directions— in all world-systems throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags;

And whoever, having had this Perfection of Wisdom written down in a book, should honor it, revere it, respect it, and worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags—this is equal [to the former]. Why is that?
For from this have emerged the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Thus, O Blessed One, is the medium-of-the-medium resolve for the sake of others.

Furthermore, O Blessed One, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family shall take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, attend to it with wise reflection, and reveal it in detail to others—

For him, rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama is not to be expected; nor is the level of a Śrāvaka or the level of a Pratyekabuddha to be expected. This is because, Blessed One, that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva stands firmly on the stage of non-retrogression. Why is that?
Because that son of good family or daughter of good family, having written down this Perfection of Wisdom, takes it up, memorizes it, and maintains it.

He recites it, masters it, and attends to it with wise reflection; and having written it down, he honors, reveres, respects, and worships it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
For him, no fear from any quarter is to be expected. Lord, it is just as if a man, terrified by the fear of a creditor, were to seek refuge with a king.
While serving that king, he is served by those very ones from whom he previously had fear, and yet he does not fear them. For what reason?

Because, Blessed One, when there is a powerful support, fear does not arise. In the same way, Blessed One, the relics of the Tathāgata receive worship because they have been permeated by the perfection of wisdom. In this regard, Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom should be viewed as being like that king.

Just as that man who relies upon the king receives honor, even so the relics of the Tathāgata, being permeated by the perfection of wisdom, receive honor. Furthermore, Blessed One, that omniscient knowledge itself should be understood as being permeated by the perfection of wisdom; therefore, between those two parts set out for comparison, I would choose this very perfection of wisdom. For what reason?
For it is from this that the relics of the Tathāgata have emerged;
it is from this that the thirty-two marks of a Great Man have emerged;
it is from this that the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha have emerged.
From this have arisen great loving-kindness and great compassion;
from this have arisen the five perfections, which thereby receive the designation "perfection";
from this has arisen the omniscience of the Tathāgata.
Blessed One, in whatever place within this trichiliocosm world-system there are beings who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to this perfection of wisdom,
there those beings— whether humans or non-humans— who look for an opportunity and seek an opening to harm them, shall find no such opportunity.

And all those beings will, in due course, become subject to final nirvāṇa. Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom possesses such great supernatural power that, indeed, Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom stands present for the sake of performing the Buddha-work for all those beings within the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system.

“Blessed One, the arising of a Buddha is to be expected in that world system where this perfection of wisdom shall circulate. Blessed One, it is just as if there were a jewel that was priceless among all precious gems.”

Furthermore, that great maṇi-jewel would be endowed with these very same qualities. Wherever that great maṇi-jewel is placed, there non-human beings find no opportunity to enter. And wherever a woman or a man might be seized by a non-human being, if that great maṇi-jewel were introduced there, at the very moment it is introduced...
That non-human being would depart from the great precious gem, unable to endure its brilliance.
Or, if the body were burning with bile, if that great precious gem were placed there, it would suppress that bile; it would not increase, but would be pacified.
Or, if the body were overcome by wind, if that great precious gem were placed there, it would suppress that wind as well. [Or] by phlegm...

If that great maṇi-jewel were placed upon a body that has been propped up, it would pacify all phlegm. Or, if that great maṇi-jewel were placed before a son of good family or a daughter of good family whose body is overcome by a disorder of the humors (saṃnipāta), even their illness would be pacified. Furthermore, that great maṇi-jewel would provide illumination at night, and when the hot season is present, [it would provide coolness].

In whatever region of the earth that great maṇi-jewel is placed, that region of the earth will become cool. Even when it is the season of cold, in whatever region of the earth that great maṇi-jewel is placed, that region of the earth will become warm. And in whatever region of the earth that great maṇi-jewel is placed, that region of the earth will not be excessively hot.
It shall not be too cold, but pleasant according to the season.
In whatever region of the earth that great maṇi-jewel remains, in that region of the earth venomous snakes do not roam, nor scorpions or other crawling reptiles.
Should any son of good family or daughter of good family be bitten by a venomous snake, for them also that great maṇi-jewel [shall serve as a remedy].
Upon being shown, that poison would vanish at the very moment of its sight. Endowed with such qualities as these, that great jewel-gem would be;
and, Blessed One, if that great jewel-gem were placed upon the bodies of any men or women who are afflicted by various diseases, [those ailments would likewise be cured].

All those diseases of theirs would also be pacified. Furthermore, Blessed One, wherever that great maṇi-jewel might be placed in water, it would make all that water take on its own color. Blessed One, if that great maṇi-jewel were wrapped in a blue cloth and cast into water, it would make that water blue; if [wrapped] in a yellow one, or in a red cloth...

If that great maṇi-jewel were tied with a cloth of madder-red color or a cloth of crystal color and cast into water, the water would take on that color. Even if that great maṇi-jewel were tied with cloths dyed in various colors and cast into water, it would make that water many-colored. And wherever, Blessed One, in the water—

If that great maṇi-jewel were placed in turbid water, it would clarify all that water; such a great maṇi-jewel would be endowed with these and other such qualities. Then, the venerable Ānanda said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"What do you think, Kauśika? Is that great jewel a divine one, or does such a great jewel exist among the humans of Jambudvīpa?
Śakra replied: "Venerable sir, that great jewel is divine."
Those jewel-gems belonging to the humans of Jambudvīpa are small and heavy,
whereas those that are divine are large and light;
in such ways are the jewel-gems of the humans of Jambudvīpa completely surpassed by them, so that they do not [compare].

Furthermore, the well-perfected jewel-gems of Jambudvīpa do not approach even the number, the fraction, the calculation, the comparison, or the likeness of divine jewel-gems. Indeed, when that great jewel-gem is taken out from the casket in which it resides—
That casket becomes desirable, for it is there that the great jewel of a gem was situated.
It is even so, Venerable Ānanda; in whatever region of earth this Perfection of Wisdom shall circulate, there—

Whether for sons of good family or daughters of good family, there may arise physical or mental sufferings and calamities, whether caused by humans or non-humans. "Great jewel" (*mahāmaṇiratna*) is a designation for the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and for the knowledge of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*). How many qualities of the perfection of wisdom can possibly be [enumerated]?

For the qualities of the perfection of wisdom are indeed immeasurable to proclaim. In the same way, [the qualities] of the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity; of internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
and of the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the noble eightfold path.
Of the path, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, the formless attainments, the four noble truths, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments,

the six superknowledges, all samādhis, all dhāraṇī-doors, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and even the knowledge of omniscience.

These qualities belong to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*); by virtue of these, even the relics of a Tathāgata who has entered final nirvāṇa receive worship. These [qualities] belong to the wisdom of omniscience, which has abandoned all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies, which abides in constant equanimity, and whose nature of phenomena is never lost.
The relics of the Tathāgata became vessels; therefore, these relics of the Tathāgata receive worship.
Thus ends the medium and superior degrees of conviction regarding the welfare of others.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:

“Blessed One, these relics of the Tathāgata have become the vessel for the perfection of jewels. These relics of the Tathāgata are the vessel for the perfection of non-affliction and non-purification, for the perfection of non-arising and non-ceasing, and for the perfection of non-coming; they are the vessel for the perfection of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).”
The relics of the Tathāgata receive worship because they have been permeated by the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, Blessed One, let alone a trichiliocosm world-system filled to the brim with the relics of the Tathāgata; if, Blessed One, world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges were filled to the brim with the relics of the Tathāgata...

And if this Perfection of Wisdom were written down in a book and offered to me, O Blessed One, between these two things thus set before me, I would take up this very Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that?
For it is from this that the bodies of the Tathāgatas are born; having been permeated by the Perfection of Wisdom, they receive worship.

Furthermore, Blessed One, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to honor, revere, respect, and worship the relics of the Tathāgata, they would experience limited divine and human pleasures resulting from that root of merit,
and [be reborn] among great kṣatriya clans, or great brahmin clans, or great householder clans.

Or, having experienced happiness among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, or the Paranirmitavaśavartin realms, he will, by that root of merit, bring an end to suffering. Furthermore, for that son of good family or daughter of good family who takes up, bears in mind, recites, masters, and correctly attends to this perfection of wisdom—

The perfection of meditation is fulfilled; when the perfection of meditation is fulfilled, the perfection of vigor is fulfilled; when the perfection of vigor is fulfilled, the perfection of patience is fulfilled; when the perfection of patience is fulfilled, the perfection of ethical discipline is fulfilled. The perfection of ethical discipline [is fulfilled].

The perfection of giving, being fulfilled, brings the perfection of giving to completion. In this way, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, are fulfilled.

Having transcended the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, having entered the fixed course of a Bodhisattva, and having attained the superknowledges of a Bodhisattva, he will travel from Buddha-field to Buddha-field.

He will assume various bodies by which he will bring sentient beings to maturity— whether assuming the body of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), or assuming the body of one born into a great *kṣatriya* clan,
or assuming the body of one born into a great *brāhmaṇa* clan, or assuming the body of one born into a great *gṛhapati* clan.
Having taken hold of sentient beings, he will bring them to maturity. Therefore, Blessed One, it is not that I lack respect for the relics of the Tathāgata;

nor, Blessed One, is it that I have no desire to take them up. Rather, when the perfection of wisdom is honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped, the relics of the Tathāgata likewise become honored and revered.
They become honored and revered.

Furthermore, Blessed One, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who dwell, abide, and maintain themselves, and who teach the Dharma, in the countless and immeasurable world-systems in the ten directions— those [who honor this perfection of wisdom] also [honor them].
One who wishes to see [the Buddhas] by means of both the Dharma-body and the form-body should hear, take up, retain, recite, master, and extensively proclaim to others this very perfection of wisdom,
and should attend to it with proper mental attention. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family [wishes to see] those Tathāgatas, Arhats, in the ten directions...
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family who practices the perfection of wisdom should desire to see the perfectly awakened Buddhas, they should cultivate the recollection of the Buddha.
By the very nature of things, there are these two natures of the Blessed Ones. Which two?
Namely, the nature of conditioned phenomena and the nature of unconditioned phenomena.
In that regard, Blessed One, what is the nature of conditioned phenomena?
It is, namely, the knowledge of internal emptiness, the knowledge of external emptiness, the knowledge of internal and external emptiness, and so forth, up to—

The knowledge of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence is the knowledge regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, that which is regarding the noble truths, that which is regarding the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments, the knowledge regarding the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and that which is regarding the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

Knowledge regarding the roots of virtue—whether with outflows or without outflows, blameworthy or blameless, mundane or supramundane—and regarding the phenomena of affliction and purification: this is called the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharmatā*).
In that regard, what are called unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)?
They are those phenomena for which there is no arising, no cessation, no duration, and no change.

There is no alteration, no affliction, no purification, no decrease, and no increase, up to the point of the non-existence-intrinsic-nature of all phenomena. What is this non-existence-intrinsic-nature of all phenomena?
It is internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, and great emptiness.

Ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, beginningless-and-endless emptiness, non-dispersal emptiness, natural emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence,
the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, and the emptiness of other-nature. That which pertains to all phenomena...
The state of natural emptiness, non-apprehension, and the ineffability and inexpressibility of all phenomena— this is called the unconditioned nature of phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharmatā*).
Thus, the resolute conviction for the sake of others is the highest degree of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
Then the Blessed One said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:

"So it is, Kauśika, so it is. Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who appeared in the past also, having relied upon this very perfection of wisdom, fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. And those who..."

In the future time, they will become Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; they too, by relying on this very perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who currently reside, remain, and maintain themselves while teaching the Dharma in the world-systems of the ten directions—[they too have done so by relying on this very perfection of wisdom].
They too, having relied upon this very perfection of wisdom, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Those who were the disciples of the past and those who will be the disciples of the future, as well as those who are the pratyekabuddhas— they too, having relied upon this very perfection of wisdom, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and they will fully awaken to it.
Those who will attain or are attaining the fruit of stream-entry;

those who will attain or are attaining the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship; and those disciples who, in the worlds of the ten directions throughout incalculable world-systems, currently abide, persist, and maintain themselves as pratyekabuddhas—they too have attained the enlightenment of disciples and the enlightenment of pratyekabuddhas by relying on this very perfection of wisdom. For what reason is that?
For in this Perfection of Wisdom, the three vehicles are taught in detail; moreover,

they are [taught] through the yoga of signlessness, the yoga of non-arising and non-ceasing, the yoga of non-defilement and non-purification, the yoga of non-conditioning, the yoga of non-introduction and non-removal, the yoga of non-addition and non-subtraction, and the yoga of non-apprehension and non-abandonment.
Furthermore, that is according to worldly convention and not according to ultimate truth. Why is that?

Because in the perfection of wisdom there is neither the near shore nor the far shore, neither dry land, nor the deep, nor the level, nor the uneven, neither a sign nor the signless, neither the mundane nor the supramundane, and neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned.

Whether wholesome or unwholesome, past, future, or present, it is discerned. Yet, Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is not the giver of any dharma; it is not the giver of the dharmas of a Pratyekabuddha, nor the giver of the dharmas of an Arhat. Thus is the superior-middle conviction regarding the welfare of others.

Śakra said: "O Blessed One, this is a great perfection, namely, the perfection of wisdom. For herein, O Blessed One, bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom thoroughly understand the mental activities of all sentient beings, yet they do not apprehend a 'sentient being'."
They do not apprehend a living being, nor a person, nor a human, nor a man, nor an agent, nor an experiencer, nor a knower, nor a seer. They do not apprehend form;
they do not apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. They do not apprehend the earth element;
they do not apprehend the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, or the consciousness element. They do not apprehend the eye.
They do not perceive form,
they do not perceive visual consciousness,
and they do not perceive visual contact.

Furthermore, they do not apprehend that feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—which arises conditioned by eye-contact with forms. Likewise, they do not apprehend the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
they do not apprehend sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena; nor do they apprehend auditory consciousness, up to and including mental consciousness.

They do not apprehend auditory contact, up to and including mental contact; nor do they apprehend even that feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—which arises conditioned by mental contact with mental objects. They do not apprehend the foundations of mindfulness; they do not apprehend the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, or the path. [They do not apprehend] the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, or the formless attainments.
They do not apprehend them. They do not apprehend the noble truths, nor the eight liberations, nor the nine successive attainments, nor the six superknowledges.

They do not apprehend the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor the grounds of self-confidence, nor the analytical knowledges, nor the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. They do not apprehend internal emptiness.
They do not apprehend external emptiness, nor internal-and-external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.
They do not apprehend the meditative concentrations, nor the gateways of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*). They do not apprehend emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness.
They do not apprehend awakening, nor the Buddha, nor the qualities of a Buddha. For the perfection of wisdom does not function by way of apprehension.
It is present. For what reason?
Because intrinsic nature does not exist and is not apprehended—that by which one might apprehend, that which might be apprehended, or where it might be apprehended.
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Kauśika, so it is.
For in this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension does not apprehend even awakening, let alone the qualities of a bodhisattva."
Śakra asked: "But, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice only in the perfection of wisdom and not in the other perfections?
The Blessed One replied:
"Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in all the perfections, not merely in the perfection of wisdom."

And by way of non-apprehension, he does not apprehend the perfection of giving; he does not apprehend the giver, nor does he apprehend the recipient. He does not apprehend the perfection of ethical discipline; he does not apprehend the one possessed of ethical discipline, nor does he apprehend immorality. He does not apprehend the perfection of patience; he does not apprehend the patient person, nor does he apprehend that which is to be endured. He does not apprehend the perfection of vigor; he does not apprehend what is to be done, nor does he apprehend body or mind.
Furthermore, one does not apprehend it;
one does not apprehend the perfection of meditation, nor does one apprehend the mind, nor does one apprehend meditative concentration;
one does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor does one apprehend the wise person, nor does one apprehend wisdom itself.

Moreover, Kauśika, the perfection of wisdom is the precursor and the leader for a bodhisattva mahāsattva when he practices giving; the perfection of wisdom is the precursor for a bodhisattva mahāsattva when he guards morality,
cultivates patience, exerts vigor, enters meditative concentration, and discerns phenomena.
For the bodhisattva mahāsattva, the perfection of wisdom is the precursor and the leader of all dharmas by way of the non-apprehension of them.
Thus it is for the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and the factors of dependent origination, whether taken individually or collectively, by way of their non-apprehension.
[The same applies to] the thirty-seven [factors of enlightenment].

By way of the non-apprehension of the factors conducive to enlightenment; by way of the non-apprehension of the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments;

by way of the non-apprehension of the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the six superknowledges; [and] by way of the non-apprehension of the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four grounds of self-confidence.
By way of non-apprehension of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*);

by way of non-apprehension of all the emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), all the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), and all the gateways of dhāraṇīs (*dhāraṇīmukha*); by way of non-apprehension of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), up to and including by way of non-apprehension of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). It is just as if, Kauśika...

Among the trees of Jambudvīpa, which have various leaves and foliage, various flowers and fruits, and various heights, shapes, and circumferences, no distinction or difference whatsoever is perceived in their shade;
rather, it is simply designated by the term "shade. In the same way, Kauśika, regarding the five perfections when they are embraced by the perfection of wisdom...
For those [merits] dedicated toward omniscience, no distinction or differentiation is perceived by way of non-perception.
Thus, the mental engagement of resolute belief regarding the welfare of others is called "the highest of the high. This concludes the fourth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of Qualities.
Śakra said: "O Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is endowed with great qualities."

"Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom fulfills all qualities; it is endowed with immeasurable qualities, endowed with inconceivable qualities, endowed with incomparable qualities, endowed with infinite qualities, and endowed with boundless qualities. Blessed One, if any son of good family or daughter of good family [should] even [possess] this perfection of wisdom written in a book..."
Having written it down, he will uphold it, recite it, and master it;

and he will honor, revere, respect, and worship it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags; and he will attend to the Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught through systematic mental engagement.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to have this Perfection of Wisdom written down in a book and give it to another,
which of these two would generate the greater merit?
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, Kauśika, I shall question you on this matter; you should answer as you see fit. What do you think, Kauśika:

if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to honor, revere, respect, and worship the relics of the Tathāgata with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags;

and if another son of good family or daughter of good family were to give even a relic of the size of a mustard seed to another person, sharing it with them—[which of these two would generate more merit?]"

If that son of good family or daughter of good family were to honor, revere, respect, and worship that relic of the Tathāgata, even one the size of a mustard seed, with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags—
which of those two would generate the greater merit?
Śakra said: "Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to personally honor,

revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate the relics of the Tathāgata, and were also to give even a relic of the size of a mustard seed to another person, this latter [act] would produce far more merit than the former."

It would produce merit. Seeing such a purpose, the Tathāgata, having entered the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) and having split his own body which was like a diamond, empowered the relics of the Tathāgata out of great compassion for the mass of sentient beings—those beings who are to be disciplined by the relics of the Tathāgata. Why is that?

"Blessed One, for whoever shall worship even a relic of the size of a mustard seed from the Tathāgata who has entered final nirvāṇa, it will not be possible to reach the limit of their root of merit until their own final nirvāṇa.
The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Kauśika, so it is. Any son of good family or daughter of good family who shall honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and venerate this perfection of wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags, and who, having written it down, shall give it to another—this son of good family or daughter of good family produces far more merit. Thus ends the first [section] on mere praise."

Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to go to others and explain, teach, reveal, analyze, and clarify this Perfection of Wisdom exactly as it has been taught, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit than the former son or daughter of good family.
Or he should be regarded as the Teacher, or as some other fellow-practitioner who occupies the position of a teacher. Why is that?
Because this very Perfection of Wisdom is to be seen here as the Teacher; for the Teacher is not one thing and the Perfection of Wisdom another.
The perfection of wisdom itself is the Teacher, and the Teacher himself is the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?

For it is by training in this perfection of wisdom that sons of good family or daughters of good family have appeared in the world as the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.

Even those fellow practitioners of the holy life who possess the superknowledges and are established in one or another state of non-retrogression— those bodhisattva mahāsattvas have also awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by training in this very perfection of wisdom. It is in this very perfection of wisdom, Kauśika, that the śrāvakas have trained.
Arhats have attained arhatship;
Pratyekabuddhas have attained Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; and Bodhisattvas enter, have entered, and will enter the Bodhisattva-determination. Therefore...

Therefore, Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to honor, revere, respect, and worship the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones in their presence with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags— this very Prajñāpāramitā, written in a book, should be honored, revered, respected, and worshipped.

With flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags. Furthermore, perceiving this very purpose, after I had fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, this thought occurred to me:
"Upon what dharma should I rely while dwelling, so that I might honor it, revere it, esteem it, and worship it?"

Thus it was, Kauśika. When I did not see anyone equal to myself in the world with its gods, its Brahmās, and its Māras, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods, humans, and asuras—while I was thus searching for an equal—it occurred to me:
"What if I were to honor, revere, respect, and worship that very Dharma which I have fully awakened to?"
"I shall dwell relying solely upon the Dharma. Kauśika, this very True Dharma is this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Kauśika, it is I who honors, reveres, respects, and worships this perfection of wisdom;
having honored, revered, respected, and worshipped it, I dwell relying upon it. How much more so, then, Kauśika, for a son of good family?

Or by a daughter of good family who desires to fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, this very *prajñāpāramitā* should not be honored, nor revered, nor esteemed, nor worshipped with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags. Why is that?
Because it is precisely this [perfection] that has been practiced by sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the vehicles of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
The perfection of wisdom should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags. Why is that?
For it is from the perfection of wisdom that bodhisattvas are born, and from bodhisattvas that Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are born.

All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have also been born from the Tathāgata. Therefore, Kauśika, this very perfection of wisdom should be honored, revered, and esteemed by sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the Mahāyāna, as well as by those belonging to the Śrāvakayāna.

They should be honored with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags—having trained in which, sons of good family and daughters of good family have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is the second measure of praise:
Kauśika, by establishing even a single sentient being in the fruit of stream-entry, one generates immeasurable merit.
But it is not so when one establishes the beings of Jambudvīpa in the ten paths of wholesome action. Why is that?
Kauśika, beings established in the ten paths of wholesome action remain unliberated from the realms of hell, the animal womb, the world of Yama, and the state of the asuras;
however, one who is established in the fruit of stream-entry becomes liberated from all miserable destinies. This is the third measure of praise.

Having established even a single being in the fruit of a once-returner, one generates much more merit than by establishing all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the ten paths of wholesome action; this is the fourth measure of praise.
Likewise, having established a single being in the fruit of a non-returner, one generates much more merit [than by doing the same for all beings].
But it is not so when one establishes beings of Jambudvīpa in the ten paths of wholesome action. This is the fifth measure of praise:
establishing a single being in the state of an Arhat produces far more merit than establishing beings of Jambudvīpa in the ten paths of wholesome action. This is the sixth measure of praise.

Thus, having established even a single sentient being in pratyekabodhi, one generates far more merit than by establishing all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa in the ten paths of wholesome action. This is the seventh measure of praise:
"Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa in the fruit of stream-entry."

Or, if another son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish even a single sentient being in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, he would generate much more merit than that. Why is that?
Because he has set himself up for the non-interruption of the Buddha’s lineage. This is the eighth measure of praise.
Likewise, if one were to establish all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa in the fruit of a once-returner...

Or if another were to establish even a single being in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment, this latter person generates far more merit than that. This is called the ninth [level], "mere praise" (*stutimātra*). Likewise, if one were to establish all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), yet another were to establish even a single being in unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment, this latter person generates far more merit than that. This is the first [level of] "mere glorification" (*stobhamātra*).

Thus, if someone were to establish all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the state of arhatship, and another were to establish even a single being in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, the latter generates far more merit than the former. This is the second measure of praise.
Likewise, if someone were to establish all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the awakening of a pratyekabuddha...
Or, if another son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish even a single being in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, this person would produce far more merit than that.

This is because, for the sake of the non-interruption of the Buddha’s lineage, one who would establish even a single being in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening becomes established in its preservation. Why is that?
For, Kauśika, as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are, they are all born from the Bodhisattva.
Therefore, Kauśika, by this very reasoning it should be understood that the Bodhisattva, too, is to be honored by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. This is the third measure of praise.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the ten paths of wholesome action. What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit who, having written out this Perfection of Wisdom in a book, should give it to another, even for the purpose of copying or reading it. For what reason?"
For herein, in this Perfection of Wisdom, the untainted dharmas are taught in detail;
having trained in them, sons of good family and daughters of good family have entered, will enter, and are entering the fixed course of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Likewise, they have attained, will attain, and are attaining up to the state of an Arhat and Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.

They have attained, they will attain, and they are attaining [the state of a Bodhisattva]. Bodhisattvas who have entered, will enter, and are entering the fixed course of a Bodhisattva; those who have fully awakened, will fully awaken, and are fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. And what, Kauśika, are those untainted dharmas? They are as follows: the perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four noble truths, and the four immeasurables.
The four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges,
internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence,
all samādhis, all doors of dhāraṇī, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, and the four [fearless confidences].

The analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and even the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha have been taught in detail by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones within the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Therefore, Kauśika, by this very method you should understand it thus: whichever son of good family or daughter of good family [takes up] this *Prajñāpāramitā*...
Even having written it down in a book, one should give it to others for the purpose of copying or for the purpose of reciting; thereby, one would generate much more merit. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, herein in this Prajñāpāramitā all dharmas are taught in detail.
By means of those dharmas, the great śāla clans of kṣatriyas, the great śāla clans of brahmins, and the great śāla clans of householders are made known;
the gods of the Four Great Kings are made known;

and the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmapārṣadya, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahmāṇa, up to the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, are made known.
The gods are known,
all the perfections are known,
and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are known.
The noble truths, the eight liberations, and the nine successive meditative attainments are discerned; emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, as well as the six superknowledges, are discerned;
all the emptinesses, all the concentrations, and all the doors of dhāraṇī are discerned.

The ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are discerned; great loving-kindness and great compassion are discerned;
and all forms of omniscience are discerned.
Stream-enterers are known;
once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas are known;
and Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are known. Let alone, Kauśika, those of Jambudvīpa.

As for those beings established in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha— Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in a world system of four great continents in the ten paths of wholesome action, and so on,
