up to establishing them in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. What do you think?
"Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate a greater amount of merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit on that account who, having had this Perfection of Wisdom written down in a book, should give it to another, even for the purpose of copying or reading it. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, all the dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are born from the Perfection of Wisdom.

And the qualities of a Buddha as well. Let alone, Kauśika, the beings in a world-system of four great continents who are established in the ten paths of wholesome action, up to being established in the state of a pratyekabuddha;
rather, Kauśika, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in a thousandfold world-system in the ten paths of wholesome action—
[If someone were to] establish others in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or the state of a pratyekabuddha;

and if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take this perfection of wisdom— even if only as a written book— and give it to another, even for the sake of copying or reading it, the latter would produce far more merit than the former.
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One! Much, Sugata!
The Blessed One said:
"Let alone, Kauśika, the beings in a thousandfold world-system who have been established even in the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha."

Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in the two-thousandfold world-system in the ten paths of wholesome action, up to and including the state of a pratyekabuddha. What do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces even more merit than that."

If one were to have this Perfection of Wisdom written down in a book and give it to another, even for the sake of merely copying or reading it, that person would generate far more merit. Let alone, Kauśika, those beings in a two-thousandfold world system who have been established in Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment.

Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings whatsoever in the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system in the ten paths of wholesome action, and even were they to establish them in the state of a pratyekabuddha;
yet, if another son of good family or daughter of good family were to do no more than write this Perfection of Wisdom in a book—

If one were to give it to others, even for the purpose of copying or reciting it, then, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family generates much more merit. Let alone, Kauśika, the beings in a trichiliocosm who have been established in the state of a Pratyekabuddha; as many as there are beings, Kauśika, in worlds as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the ten directions—

If some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in the world-systems in the ten paths of wholesome action, or even establish them in the state of a pratyekabuddha;
and if another son of good family or daughter of good family were to do no more than have this perfection of wisdom written down in a book—
One should give this to another, even for the purpose of copying it or reading it; by doing so, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family generates much greater merit. Why is that?
Because herein, in this Prajñāpāramitā, the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are taught in detail.
Therein, sons of good family and daughters of good family, having trained, have entered, will enter, and are entering the fixed course of rightness (*samyaktvaniyāma*);

they have attained, will attain, and are attaining up to arhatship; they have attained, will attain, and are attaining individual enlightenment (*pratyekabodhi*); and bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas have entered, will enter, and are entering the fixed course of a bodhisattva (*bodhisattvaniyāma*).
And they enter [the path]; they have awakened, are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. And what, Kauśika, are those untainted phenomena?

Namely: the perfections; the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening; the four truths; internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence;
the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments; the ten powers of a Tathāgata, up to the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha.
This has been taught in detail by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones in the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Therefore, Kauśika, you should understand it by this very method:

if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to have this *Prajñāpāramitā* written down in a book and give it to others—even for the sake of copying or reading—it would be far more [meritorious] than that.
He generates merit.
For what reason?
Because here, Kauśika, all dharmas are taught in detail within this perfection of wisdom.
By means of those dharmas, the great śāla clans of kṣatriyas, the great śāla clans of brahmins, and the great śāla clans of householders are known;
the gods of the Four Great Kings are known, up to the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
the perfections are known, up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that are known.
Omniscience is known; stream-enterers are known;
once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas are known.

The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are known [through this]. Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the four dhyānas, in the four immeasurables, and in the four formless attainments.
One should establish them in the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*). What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family generates much more merit on that account who, having written down this Perfection of Wisdom and made it into a book, should give it to others, even for the purpose of copying or reading it. Why is that?"
For herein, in this Perfection of Wisdom, the untainted dharmas are taught in detail.
Furthermore, Kauśika, any son of good family or daughter of good family who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and correctly attend to this Perfection of Wisdom—

That son of good family or daughter of good family will generate far more merit than one who would establish all beings in Jambudvīpa, or in the four continents, or in a thousandfold, two-thousandfold, or three-thousandfold world system, in the ten paths of wholesome action, in the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, and the formless superknowledges.

In this regard, one who possesses such appropriate mental attention and does not engage in duality toward awakening will take up, retain, recite, master, and appropriately attend to the perfection of wisdom;
likewise, one who does not engage in duality toward awakening [will do so with] the perfection of meditative concentration.

One who does not practice dualism regarding awakening will take up, maintain, recite, master, and properly attend to the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of ethical discipline; as well as the perfection of generosity. One who does not practice dualism regarding awakening [will likewise take up] internal emptiness and external emptiness.
He will correctly attend to internal-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.

Not practicing duality regarding awakening, he will correctly attend to the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path. Not practicing duality regarding awakening, [he will correctly attend to] the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and the knowledge of all aspects.
He will attend to it with wise attention. This is the fourth measure of praise.

Furthermore, Kauśika, if any son of good family or daughter of good family should, in many ways, teach the perfection of wisdom to others, explain it in detail, cultivate it, analyze it, and clarify it;
He will teach the meaning. In this regard, this is the meaning of the perfection of wisdom: one will not see the perfection of wisdom in non-duality, nor in duality;
not through signs, nor through signlessness; not through accumulation, nor through removal;
not through addition, nor through subtraction.

Neither from the perspective of affliction nor from the perspective of purification; neither from the perspective of arising nor from the perspective of cessation; neither from the perspective of grasping nor from the perspective of relinquishing.
Neither from a standpoint nor from a non-standpoint,
neither from reality nor from unreality,
neither from conjunction nor from non-conjunction.
Neither in its entirety nor not in its entirety; neither part by part nor not part by part; neither as dharma nor as non-dharma;
neither from suchness nor from non-suchness.

Neither from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) nor from the non-limit of reality. This very son of good family or daughter of good family will generate much greater merit on that account, who shall extensively proclaim this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to others, recite it, teach it, cultivate it, clarify it, and explain its meaning; but not so one who merely takes it up for oneself alone.
"He will uphold it, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection. This is the fifth measure of praise.

Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family themselves takes up, upholds, recites, masters, and attends to the Perfection of Wisdom with wise reflection, and furthermore explains it in detail to others, makes it known, establishes it, elucidates it, clarifies it, and teaches its meaning—
This very person will produce far more merit than that.
Śakra said: "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
In this way, Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should teach the perfection of wisdom with its meaning and its phrasing.

Teaching it in this manner, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family will be endowed with a mass of merit that is immeasurable, incalculable, and limitless. Thus ends the sixth measure of praise.

If, Kauśika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family were for as long as life lasts to honor, revere, respect, and worship with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags immeasurable, innumerable, and infinite Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in each of the ten directions, one after another;

Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach this perfection of wisdom extensively to others in many ways, making its meaning known, illuminating it, analyzing it, investigating it, and clarifying it—
this very son of good family or daughter of good family would generate far more merit than that. Why is that?
For it is by training in this perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past, future, and present have awakened,
are awakening, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is the seventh measure of praise.

Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to extensively proclaim, explain, and even indicate to others the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom for incalculable and immeasurable eons, doing so by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*),
they would thereby generate a much greater amount of merit. In this regard, Kauśika, what is apprehension (*upalambha*)?
When a bodhisattva gives a gift by way of apprehension, it occurs to him:
"I am giving a gift."
"I give this gift;
for one who gives a gift to another, there will be only the gift itself, not the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). This is ethical discipline (śīla)..."
"I am virtuous; I protect these beings"—this is not the perfection of ethical discipline. "I undertake patience;
I endure this [insult] from another"—[this is not the perfection of patience].
"I shall abide in this patience;
this is not the perfection of patience. I shall exert vigor;
this vigor is for the sake of these [beings]."
"I shall abide in this vigor;
this is not the perfection of vigor. I shall enter into meditative concentration;
I shall enter into this meditative concentration for the sake of these beings."
"I shall abide in this meditation;
this is not the perfection of meditation. I cultivate wisdom;
this wisdom is for their sake."
"I shall abide in this wisdom;

this is not the perfection of wisdom. For in this way, Kauśika, for a son of good family or a daughter of good family who courses in apprehension, the perfection of giving is not fulfilled, nor the perfection of ethical discipline, nor the perfection of patience, nor the perfection of vigor, nor the perfection of meditative concentration.
The perfection of wisdom is not fulfilled.
Śakra said: "Blessed One, how is the perfection of generosity fulfilled for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices?
How is the perfection of ethical discipline fulfilled?"
How is the perfection of patience fulfilled?
How is the perfection of vigor fulfilled?
"How is the perfection of meditation fulfilled?
How is the perfection of wisdom fulfilled?
The Blessed One said:
In this regard, Kauśika, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift, he does not perceive a giver, he does not perceive a recipient, and he does not perceive that which is given;

this is called the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). He does not perceive morality, nor one who possesses morality, nor a sentient being; this is called the perfection of morality (*śīlapāramitā*). He does not perceive patience, nor that which is to be endured, nor one who is patient.

This is called the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*). One does not apprehend vigor, nor does one apprehend body or mind; this is called the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*). One does not apprehend meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), nor the meditator, nor that which is to be meditated upon;

this is called the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*). One does not apprehend wisdom (*prajñā*), nor the wise person, nor that which is to be known, for the sake of which one cultivates [these practices].

This is called the perfection of wisdom. For a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in this way, Kauśika, the perfection of giving is fulfilled, the perfection of ethical discipline is fulfilled, the perfection of patience is fulfilled, the perfection of vigor is fulfilled, the perfection of meditative concentration is fulfilled, and the perfection of wisdom is fulfilled. It is in this manner, Kauśika, that for a son of good family or a daughter of good family...

Or rather, this Perfection of Wisdom should be taught with its meaning and its phrasing through non-apprehension. In the same way, this Perfection of Meditation, Perfection of Vigor, Perfection of Patience, Perfection of Ethical Discipline, and Perfection of Giving should be taught with their meanings and their phrasings through non-apprehension. Why is that?
Kauśika, in a future time there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who [will produce] a counterfeit of the Perfection of Wisdom.

They will teach it. In that regard, for a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, this Perfection of Wisdom— both in its meaning and its letter— should be taught, lest they be ruined by hearing a counterfeit version of the Perfection of Wisdom.
Śakra asked: "Blessed One, what is that counterfeit perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One replied:
"In this case, Kauśika, when sons of good family or daughters of good family intend, 'We shall teach this perfection of wisdom,' yet they teach a counterfeit perfection of wisdom."
They will teach as follows: this is a counterfeit perfection of wisdom. They will teach that form is impermanent;

they will teach that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent. And they will teach thus: "Whoever practices in this way, he practices in the perfection of wisdom. To whichever sons of good family or daughters of good family they will teach this...

Or they will seek [to understand] that form is impermanent; likewise, they will seek that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent. They will teach a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom. They will practice according to that counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom. They will teach that the eye is impermanent; likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

They will teach that "it is permanent. They will teach that "form is impermanent. Likewise, they will teach that sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are impermanent. They will teach that the earth element is impermanent;
[they will teach that] the water element, the fire element, and the wind element are impermanent.
They will teach that the space element and the consciousness element are impermanent. They will teach that the eye element is impermanent;
they will teach that the ear element, the nose element, the tongue element, the body element, and the mind element are impermanent.
They will teach that the form element is impermanent; they will teach that the sound element is impermanent; [and] the odor element...

They will teach that the taste element, the tangible element, and the mental-object element are impermanent. They will teach that the eye-consciousness element is impermanent. They will teach that the ear-consciousness element, the nose-consciousness element, the tongue-consciousness element, the body-consciousness element, and the mind-consciousness element are impermanent. [They will teach that] the eye-contact element...

They will teach that [the eye-contact element] is impermanent. They will teach that the ear-contact element, the nose-contact element, the tongue-contact element, the body-contact element, and the mind-contact element are impermanent. They will teach that feeling conditioned by eye-contact is impermanent; likewise for those conditioned by ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.
They will teach that feeling is impermanent. They will teach that form is suffering, impermanent, non-self, and impure.
They will teach that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering, impermanent, non-self, and impure.
They will teach that the earth element is suffering, non-self, and impure; [and likewise] the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.

They will teach that the element of space and the element of consciousness are suffering, selfless, and impure. They will teach that visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are suffering, selfless, and impure. They will teach that the eye is suffering, selfless, and impure; and that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are suffering, selfless, and impure.

They will teach that the form-element, the sound-element, the odor-element, the taste-element, the tangible-element, and the mental-object-element are suffering, are selfless, and are impure. They will teach that the eye-element is suffering, is selfless, and is impure.
They will teach that the ear-element, the nose-element, the tongue-element, the body-element, and the mind-element are suffering... [and so forth].
Thus they will teach: "It is non-self; it is impure. They will teach that the eye-consciousness element is suffering, non-self, and impure;

they will teach that the ear-consciousness element, the nose-consciousness element, the tongue-consciousness element, the body-consciousness element, and the mind-consciousness element are suffering, non-self, and impure. They will teach that the eye-contact element and the condition of eye-contact...

They will teach that feeling is suffering, is selfless, and is impure. Likewise, they will teach that the sphere of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact, as well as the feelings conditioned by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, are suffering, are selfless, and are impure. In this way, they will teach a counterfeit perfection of wisdom. In this way, they will teach a counterfeit perfection of meditative concentration.

They will teach a counterfeit perfection of vigor, a counterfeit perfection of patience, a counterfeit perfection of ethical discipline, and a counterfeit perfection of generosity. They will teach that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure; and so on, up to the eye, forms, and the eye-consciousness element.

They will teach that [the eye] is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure. In this same way, they will teach that the elements of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure. Likewise, they will teach that the perfection of wisdom is impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure. In the same way, they will teach that the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity [are likewise].

They will teach that [the aggregates] are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure. Likewise, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, they will teach that the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure. They will teach that the applications of mindfulness are impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

They will teach that "these are impure. Thus, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, they will teach that the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure; and so on, up to omniscience, they will teach that it is impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure. And they will say: "Whoever practices in this way, that person is practicing the perfection of wisdom."
Kauśika, this is a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who teach the perfection of wisdom will teach it in this way:
"Come, son of good family, cultivate the perfection of wisdom; as you cultivate the perfection of wisdom, [you will enter] the first..."

You will abide on the stages until you abide on the tenth stage. Likewise, while cultivating the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity, you will abide on the first stage until you abide on the tenth stage. And that [cultivation] is by way of signs, by way of apprehension, and by way of the perception of all aspects.
"Kauśika, one who will cultivate this [perfection of wisdom]— this, Kauśika, is a counterfeit perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family will instruct them in this way:"

"Come, son of good family, cultivate the perfection of wisdom. As you cultivate the perfection of wisdom, you will transcend the level of the śrāvakas and you will transcend the level of the pratyekabuddhas.
This, Kauśika, is that counterfeit perfection of wisdom."

Furthermore, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who teach the perfection of wisdom to those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the Mahāyāna will instruct them thus:
"Come, son of good family, cultivate the perfection of wisdom; by cultivating the perfection of wisdom, you will enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva.
This, Kauśika, is a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family, while teaching the perfection of wisdom, will instruct thus:

"Come, son of good family, cultivate the perfection of wisdom; as you cultivate the perfection of wisdom, you will attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);
having attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena, you will stand firm in the superknowledges (abhijñā) of a bodhisattva."
Abiding in the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), you shall travel from buddhafield to buddhafield to honor, revere, respect, worship, adore, and pay homage to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;

thus will they instruct you. But, Kauśika, when those sons of good family or daughters of good family are being instructed in this way, they will instead teach a counterfeit version of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family will instruct those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle as follows:
"That son of good family who shall take up, bear in mind, recite, master, and properly attend to the perfection of wisdom will produce an incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite mass of merit."
And while teaching in this manner, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family will teach a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-prativarṇikā*).
Furthermore, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family will instruct those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, saying:
"Come, son of good family, [study] the past, future, and present Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones."

"Having rejoiced in all that root of merit— from the first production of the thought of awakening until their final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder— and having gathered it all together as one mass, they dedicate it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening. Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who teach in this way will be teaching a counterfeit perfection of wisdom."

Śakra asked: "How do those sons of good family or daughters of good family teach so that they do not [teach] a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom to those sons of good family or daughters of good family who have set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle?
The Blessed One said:

"In this case, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family will teach the perfection of wisdom to those sons of good family or daughters of good family who have set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle."
Come, son of good family, while cultivating the perfection of wisdom, do not view form as impermanent. Why is that?
Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; and that which is the intrinsic nature of form is non-existence.
That which is non-existence is the perfection of wisdom;
that which is the perfection of wisdom is not designated therein as "form is permanent" or "form is impermanent. For what reason?
Because form itself does not exist there. How then could it be either permanent or impermanent?

And teaching in this way, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family will not teach a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom. "Do not view feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as impermanent. Why is that?
Because consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness.
That which is the intrinsic nature of consciousness is non-existence;
that which is non-existence is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
In that perfection of wisdom, consciousness is not designated as either permanent or impermanent. For what reason?
For in that case, consciousness itself does not exist; how then could it be either permanent or impermanent?

Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who teach in this way will not be teaching a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*. This applies likewise to the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and the factors of dependent origination, both individually and collectively, as well as to all the *pāramitās*.

In all the emptinesses, in all the samādhis, in all the doors of dhāraṇī, in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, in the truths, in the eight liberations, in the nine successive meditative attainments, in the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments,
in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, in the six superknowledges, and in the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four fearlessnesses.

One should apply oneself to the four analytical knowledges and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Come, son of good family, cultivate the perfection of wisdom, and do not, son of good family, view omniscience as impermanent. Why is that?
Because omniscience is empty of the intrinsic nature of omniscience.
That which is the intrinsic nature of omniscience is non-existence;
that which is non-existence is the perfection of wisdom;
and in that perfection of wisdom, neither permanence nor impermanence of omniscience is predicated. For what reason?
For in this way, even omniscience itself does not exist. How, then, could there be either permanence or impermanence?
And by teaching in this manner, Kauśika, sons of good family or daughters of good family will not teach a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Kauśika, sons of good family or daughters of good family [will not teach] such a counterfeit of the perfection of wisdom to those sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the Mahāyāna.
"Come, son of good family, cultivate the perfection of wisdom; do not perceive any dharma whatsoever, and do not abide in any dharma. Why is that?
Because within the perfection of wisdom, that dharma which is to be perceived or in which one should abide does not exist. Why is that?"
For in this way, Kauśika, all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature;
and that phenomenon which is empty of intrinsic nature is a non-entity,
and that which is a non-entity is the perfection of wisdom.
That which is the perfection of wisdom does not involve for any dharma either addition or subtraction, arising or cessation,

annihilation or permanence, identity or difference, coming or going. Teaching in this way, Kauśika, those sons of good family or daughters of good family will not teach a counterfeit perfection of wisdom.

Therefore, Kausika, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should explain the meaning of the perfection of wisdom in this way. By teaching in this manner, that son of good family or daughter of good family will generate far more merit than those aforementioned sons and daughters of good family. This is the eighth measure of praise.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the fruit of stream-entry. What do you think, Kauśika, would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit who, in many ways, would explain, teach, and elucidate this Perfection of Wisdom to others, together with its meaning and its phrasing."

He will clarify and fully reveal it. And they will say: "Come, son of good family, take up the perfection of wisdom, master it, retain it, recite it, attend to it with wise reflection, and practice according to the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught. For what reason?

For it is from this perfection of wisdom, Kauśika, that the stream-enterer and the fruit of stream-entry are manifested. Let alone, Kauśika, all the beings in Jambudvīpa established in the fruit of stream-entry; let alone all the beings in the four-continent world system trained in the fruit of stream-entry; let alone all the beings in a thousandfold world system trained in the fruit of stream-entry.

Let alone all the beings in a dichiliocosm who have been disciplined in the fruit of stream-entry. Let alone all the beings in a trichiliocosm, Kauśika, who have been disciplined in the fruit of stream-entry.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish in the fruit of stream-entry all the beings in as many world systems in the eastern direction as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges; and likewise in the southern, western, northern, intermediate, and upward directions.

Suppose there were beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges below, and some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish them all in the fruit of stream-entry. What do you think,
Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One! Much, Sugata!
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family produces much more merit who [upholds] this perfection of wisdom."
To others, he should speak it in detail, both in its substance and its phrasing; he should teach it, illuminate its meaning, analyze it, clarify it, investigate it, make it plain, and reveal it.

And he should say: "Come, noble son, take up this perfection of wisdom, master it, retain it, recite it, attend to it with wise reflection, and act according to the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught."
Practice it. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, it is from this perfection of wisdom that the stream-enterer is distinguished.
Thus, the ninth [section] is called "mere praise," and the praise has been stated.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in Jambudvīpa in the fruit of a once-returner. This is the first measure of praise. Suppose they were to establish them in the fruit of a non-returner; this is the second measure of praise.
Suppose they were to establish them in arhatship. What do you think?
"Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much more merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:

Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit who would teach, speak, illuminate, analyze, clarify, investigate, and explain this Perfection of Wisdom in detail, together with its meaning and its phrasing; and who would say:
"Come, son of good family, take up this Perfection of Wisdom, master it, retain it, recite it, attend to it properly, and practice according to the Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught."
For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, it is from this perfection of wisdom that the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, and arhatship are known.
Let alone, Kauśika, the beings of Jambudvīpa who have been disciplined in the state of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat—whosoever [they may be].

A son of good family or a daughter of good family might establish all sentient beings in the four continents in arhatship; they might establish all sentient beings in a thousandfold world system in arhatship; they might establish all sentient beings in a two-thousandfold world system in arhatship; [and they might establish all sentient beings] in a three-thousandfold world system in arhatship.
Suppose one were to establish all sentient beings in a single world-system in the state of arhatship;

or, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all those sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in as many world-systems in the eastern direction as there are—up to establishing them all in the state of arhatship. In this same way...

In the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, in the intermediate directions, and above and below—in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā—he would establish all those sentient beings in the state of arhatship. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would produce even more merit than that."
Whoever should thoroughly proclaim, teach, explain, analyze, investigate, and clarify this Perfection of Wisdom, complete with its meaning and its phrasing, to others;

and who should speak thus: "Come, son of good family! Take up this Perfection of Wisdom, master it, retain it, recite it, attend to it with wise reflection, and practice according to the Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught"—this [person] alone, compared to that...
He would generate much greater merit. Why is that?
Because, Kauśika, it is from this perfection of wisdom that the once-returners, non-returners, and arhats are known. This is the third mere praise.
Furthermore, Kauśika, as many world systems as there are in the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā...

If some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all those beings in every direction in the state of a Pratyekabuddha—what do you think, Kauśika, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate a great deal of merit on that account?
Śakra said: "A great deal, Blessed One; a great deal, Sugata."

The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit who, for those who are seekers and desirous, should extensively teach, speak, reveal, analyze, investigate, and clarify this Perfection of Wisdom, together with its meaning and its phrasing."

And he should speak thus, he should say: "Come, son of good family, take up the perfection of wisdom, master it, retain it, recite it, attend to it with wise reflection, and practice according to the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, it is from this perfection of wisdom that the Pratyekabuddha is manifested. This is the fourth mere praise.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to encourage all the beings in Jambudvīpa toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. What do you think, Kauśika, would that son or daughter of good family generate a great deal of merit on that account?
Śakra said: "A great deal, Blessed One; a great deal, Sugata."

The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit who, for others, should extensively teach, speak, explain, reveal, analyze, investigate, and clarify this Perfection of Wisdom, together with its meaning and its phrasing."

One should say this: "Come, son of good family, take up the perfection of wisdom; retain it, recite it, teach it, proclaim it, master it, attend to it with wise reflection, and practice according to the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught.
To the extent that you, son of good family, practice according to the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, to that same extent..."

"Son of good family, you shall become an attainer of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). And to the extent that your omniscience reaches fulfillment, to that same extent will your cultivation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) reach fulfillment to a still greater degree.
And to the extent that your cultivation of the perfection of wisdom reaches fulfillment, to that same extent you [shall attain] the unsurpassed..."
"You shall fully awaken to perfect enlightenment. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, it is from this [perfection of wisdom] that the bodhisattvas who have first produced the thought of awakening are born, as well as all those bodhisattvas in each of the ten directions, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā."
For all of them as well, the stage of the first production of the thought of awakening is born from the perfection of wisdom. This is the fifth mere praise.
"As many beings as there are in the four continents"—this is the sixth mere praise. "As many beings as there are in a thousandfold world-system"—this is the seventh mere praise.
However many beings there may be in a two-thousandfold or three-thousandfold world system;

furthermore, Kauśika, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all those beings in the worlds of the ten directions— each direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
One should encourage them to do so. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate much more merit on that account?
Śakra said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, Kauśika, that son of good family or daughter of good family would produce much more merit who, having taught this perfection of wisdom to others in detail— along with its meaning and its phrasing— should even go so far as to illuminate it."

And he should say this: "Come, son of good family, take up the perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, teach it, elucidate it, master it, attend to it with proper mental attention, and practice according to the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught.
Just as [he is instructed], so...

Noble son, in whatever measure you practice according to the Prajñāpāramitā as it has been taught, in that same measure you will become an attainer of omniscience. To the extent that your omniscience reaches fulfillment, to that same extent your cultivation of the Prajñāpāramitā will reach fulfillment to an even greater degree. To the extent that your cultivation of the Prajñāpāramitā reaches fulfillment...
In that very manner you shall go on until you fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that?

Because, Kauśika, it is from this [perfection of wisdom] that all those bodhisattvas who have first produced the thought of awakening, as well as all those bodhisattvas in every single direction throughout world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, have emerged.
The stage of the first production of the thought of awakening is born from the perfection of wisdom. This is the eighth mere praise.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in Jambudvīpa on the stage of non-retrogression, and another son of good family or daughter of good family were to [establish] this perfection of wisdom...
He would teach all those beings the meaning and the phrasing, and even illuminate it fully;
and he would say: "Come, son of good family, take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and attend to it properly.

And as you practice according to the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught—just as you proceed in accordance with the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught—so, training yourself in the perfection of wisdom, you will stand in the state of non-retrogression."
And you shall gradually awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;

this son of good family or daughter of good family, Kauśika, would generate much more merit than all the beings in a world system of four continents, or all the beings in a thousandfold world system, up to...

Suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in a two-thousandfold world system, as many as there are beings in a three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, and even all the beings in as many world systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges in each of the ten directions, upon the stage of non-retrogression.

And if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach this perfection of wisdom to those beings, and even to illuminate it— both in its meaning and its phrasing— and were to say: "Come, son of good family, take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, teach it, illuminate it, master it, attend to it properly, and act according to the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught."
Practice this, for by practicing it you will stand upon the stage of non-retrogression;
you will gradually awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This alone would produce far more merit than that.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in Jambudvīpa in the state of non-retrogression toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening,
and were to teach, proclaim, analyze, investigate, and clarify the perfection of wisdom to them.
Suppose one were to analyze [the Dharma] with its meaning and its phrasing, and say to some among them, "I shall quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Then,
if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to teach, explain, illuminate, clarify, analyze, and set forth in detail this Perfection of Wisdom with its meaning and its phrasing;

This person would generate even more merit than that: suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in each of the ten directions in the state of non-retrogression;
and suppose someone else were to teach this Perfection of Wisdom to them; and suppose yet another were to say this to them:

"I shall swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment"— if someone were to instruct, teach, illuminate, analyze, examine, clarify, and explain this perfection of wisdom to such a person, providing both its meaning and its phrasing, this latter person would generate far more merit than the former. Why is that?

"For the Dharma must be taught with extreme intensity to irreversible Bodhisattvas, for they are fixed upon supreme enlightenment and shall no longer turn back from unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening; these ones are truly yearning for [liberation] from cyclic existence and are tormented by great compassion. Having said this, he spoke the ninth [verse], which is merely a praise.

Śakra said: "Blessed One, to the extent that a bodhisattva mahāsattva draws near to unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening, to that same extent should the bodhisattva mahāsattva be exhorted and instructed in the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of concentration, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity; he should be exhorted and instructed therein."
He should be instructed and exhorted regarding all the emptinesses;
he should be instructed and exhorted regarding the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path;
and he should be instructed and exhorted regarding the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the noble truths, and emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
He should be instructed and exhorted regarding the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the superknowledges;

he should be instructed and exhorted regarding all samādhis, all doors of dhāraṇī, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and he should be supported with the requisites of robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal provisions for the sick.

And that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be assisted by means of both the gift of the Dharma and material gifts. This very one who assists with the gift of the Dharma and material gifts would generate far more merit than that. Why is that?
Because it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is instructed and exhorted in the perfections and in all the emptinesses.

He is awakened to and instructed in all the factors conducive to enlightenment, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the noble truths, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the superknowledges, the samādhis, all the doors of dhāraṇī, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Excellent, excellent, Kauśika! It is well that you give encouragement to those sons of good family and daughters of good family who belong to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas;
it is exactly as you have done. Those noble disciples who desire to benefit sentient beings likewise provide assistance to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas."
They favor [beings] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and protect them through both the favor of the Dharma and the favor of material gifts. Why is that?
For from this [enlightenment] proceeds the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of Śrāvakas;

from this proceeds the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, and from this proceeds the Mahāyāna. For if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva had not produced the thought of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, [the Saṅgha would not exist].

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva would not have trained in the six perfections, nor in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, nor in the noble truths, nor in the eight liberations, nor in the nine successive meditative attainments, nor in the immeasurables, the dhyānas,
and the formless attainments, nor in the six perfections, nor in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, nor in internal emptiness, nor in external emptiness.

He would not have trained in internal-external emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature; nor in all meditative concentrations, nor in all doors of dhāraṇī, nor in the powers of a Tathāgata, nor in the grounds of self-confidence, nor in the analytical knowledges, nor in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
Since he would not have trained, and while not training, in those dharmas, he would not [attain] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If he were not to awaken, then neither unexcelled perfect enlightenment, nor the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, nor the enlightenment of a śrāvaka would be known. Therefore, Kauśika, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva [practices] in the six perfections, in all the emptinesses, in all the concentrations, in all the doors of dhāraṇī, and in the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—

He trains in the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, in the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments; in the noble truths, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the six superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so on, up to all dharmas.

Therefore, having awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the bodhisattva mahāsattva eradicates the hells from all world-systems; he eradicates the animal realm and the domain of the hungry ghosts. He appears in great kṣatriya families; he appears in great brahmin families;
he appears in great householder families. He appears among the gods of the Four Great Kings.
It occurs among the Trāyastriṃśas, the Yāmas, the Tuṣitas, the Nirmāṇaratis, the Paranirmitavaśavartins,
the Brahmapārṣadyas, the Brahmapurohitas, the Mahābrahmans, the Parīttābhas, the Apramāṇābhas, the Ābhāsvaras, the Parīttaśubhas, and the Apramāṇaśubhas.

In the world of the Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, and the Śuddhāvāsa gods— namely the Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha gods; and of the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space, the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness,
the gods who have reached the sphere of nothingness, and the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There is an appearance. There is the appearance of the perfection of generosity in the world. There is the appearance of the perfection of ethical discipline in the world.

There is the appearance of the perfection of patience in the world. There is the appearance of the perfection of vigor in the world. There is the appearance of the perfection of meditative concentration in the world. [There is the appearance] of the perfection of wisdom in the world.

The manifestation of things occurs in the world. The manifestation of internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, up to the emptiness of the nature of non-existence, occurs in the world. The manifestation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the four noble truths occurs in the world. [Likewise] the manifestation of the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments [occurs in the world].

The manifestation in the world of the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and the six supernormal powers occurs. The manifestation in the world of all samādhis, all doors of dhāraṇīs, and the bodhisattva stages occurs. [The manifestation] of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the four...

The manifestation of the analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and omniscience occurs in the world. Furthermore, the manifestation of the vehicle of the disciples, the vehicle of the solitary buddhas, and the Great Vehicle occurs in the world.
Thus was the summary of the subject matter, beginning with praise, concluded.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Elder Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti, as for that basis of meritorious action associated with the sympathetic joy of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva..."
Having made it common to all sentient beings, it is dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by way of non-apprehension.
And as for the basis of meritorious action associated with the sympathetic joy of all sentient beings,
and that of those who have set out in the vehicle of the hearers (śrāvakayāna), [it is likewise dedicated].

And compared to the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving, the basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline, and the basis of meritorious action consisting of cultivation belonging to those who have set out in the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, the basis of meritorious action associated with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s rejoicing—
having made it common to all sentient beings and dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment— is declared to be supreme.
It is called the best; it is called the eldest; it is called the excellent; it is called the most eminent;
it is called the sublime; it is called the supreme; it is called the unsurpassed. It is called the unequaled; it is called the equal to the unequaled. This is the distinguished dedication.
For what reason?

Because all the bases of meritorious action consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation belonging to those of the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas— all that is for the sake of self-taming, self-pacification, and the parinirvāṇa of the self, up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

The dharmas— emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the four noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the four analytical insights, and the six superknowledges— serve for the taming of the self, the calming of the self, and the parinirvāṇa of the self. Furthermore, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, that which is accompanied by rejoicing...

The basis of meritorious action is dedicated for the taming, the pacification, the parinirvāṇa, and the unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening of all sentient beings. This is the function of dedication.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:
Furthermore, Maitreya, as for those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who in the eastern direction reside in world-systems that are incalculable,

immeasurable, and infinite— and likewise in the south, west, north, the intermediate directions, above, and below— in each and every direction there are Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who have passed into parinirvāṇa, as incalculable, immeasurable, and infinite as they are.
From the first production of the thought of awakening until they have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,

and until they have passed into final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder, and as long as the true Dharma has not disappeared— in this interval, whatever root of merit is associated with the six perfections, [that is dedicated to awakening].

Whatever basis of meritorious action consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation belongs to those of the Śrāvaka vehicle and those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, as well as those untainted roots of goodness belonging to those in training (śaikṣa), [all these he surpasses].
And those roots of merit which are beyond training and untainted,

as well as the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to those Tathāgatas,
and their benevolence—
That which is great loving-kindness, that which is great compassion,
and the immeasurable and incalculable qualities of a Buddha—
And whatever Dharma was taught by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; and whoever, through that teaching of the Dharma, attained the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning,
the fruit of non-returning, the state of arhatship, or attained solitary awakening, or entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva— whatever roots of merit they possess;
And whatever roots of merit have been planted there by those toward the Tathāgatas or Arhats, whether they are still present or have already entered final nirvāṇa—
all that, having condensed it together, one should rejoice with the foremost, the eldest, the best, the most excellent, the preeminent, the supreme,
the unsurpassed, the incomparable, and the peerless rejoicing.
He rejoices with sympathetic joy;

having rejoiced, he makes the root of merit associated with that sympathetic joy common to all sentient beings and dedicates it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, thinking, "May it become a bringer of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Furthermore, when this follower of the Mahāyāna thus dedicates his mind— by means of those objects and those entities by which that mind was generated—
do those entities and those objects exist and are they perceived in the same way as they were conceptualized as signs by those sons of good family of the Mahāyāna?
Maitreya replied:

"Venerable Subhūti, those things and those objects are not perceived in the way that those sons of good family belonging to the Mahāyāna have conceptualized them and dedicated [the merit] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Subhūti said:

If those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were first made into signs by means of non-existent entities and non-existent objects, then [consider] whatever roots of merit those [Buddhas] possess— beginning from their first production of the thought of awakening until they reach unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening— whoever they may be, abiding, remaining, and maintaining themselves throughout the expanse of the world-systems in all ten directions.
From the time they attained full enlightenment until their final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder, and for as long as the true Dharma remains—
whatever roots of merit belong to those persons belonging to the vehicle of the disciples, and whatever roots of merit belong to those persons belonging to the vehicle of the solitary buddhas.

Furthermore, all those untainted roots of virtue belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those untainted roots of virtue belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), having condensed them all together, were dedicated toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment by means of the yoga of the signless (*animitta*). May there be no perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) for him; namely, the perversion of perception that takes the impermanent to be permanent.
There was a perversion of mind and a perversion of view. Regarding what is suffering as happiness,
regarding what is not-self as self,
and regarding what is unpeaceful as peace— this is the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view.

Furthermore, is it the case that just as the thing is, just as the objective support is, so too is awakening, so too is the mind, so too are the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom; so too are the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, and so too are the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments?

Likewise the noble truths; likewise internal emptiness, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; likewise emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; likewise the eight liberations; likewise the nine successive meditative attainments; likewise the six superknowledges; likewise all samādhis; likewise all doors of dhāraṇī; likewise the ten powers of a Tathāgata; likewise the grounds of self-confidence; and likewise the analytical knowledges.
Likewise, there are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), as well as omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

If, for instance, awakening (*bodhi*) is just as the thing itself, just as the objective support (*ālambana*), so too are the mind (*citta*), form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*);
likewise the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and likewise internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

Likewise the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; likewise the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments;

likewise the noble truths; likewise the eight liberations; likewise the nine successive meditative attainments; likewise the three gateways to liberation; likewise the six superknowledges; likewise all samādhis; and likewise all gateways to the dhāraṇīs.
Likewise, there are the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
In that regard, what is the entity? What is the objective referent?
What is awakening? What is the mind?
What are the roots of goodness?
"What is that basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing which one dedicates toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Maitreya said: "If, Reverend Subhūti, bodhisattvas had practiced the six perfections..."
They would have attended upon many Buddhas,
they would have planted roots of merit,
and they would have been sustained by spiritual friends.
If they had trained in phenomena that are empty of intrinsic characteristics,

they would not have taken those things as signs— neither those objects, nor those focal points, nor those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, nor those roots of merit, nor those bases of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing— and thereby dedicated them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Moreover, they will indeed dedicate [the merit] in such a way that it is neither by way of duality nor by way of non-duality; neither by way of signs nor by way of signlessness; neither by way of apprehension nor by way of non-apprehension; neither by way of affliction nor by way of purification;
and neither by way of arising nor by way of cessation.
If, however, these bodhisattvas had not trained in the six perfections,

had not attended upon the Buddhas, had not planted roots of merit, had not been sustained by spiritual friends, and had not trained in the fact that all phenomena are empty of their own intrinsic characteristics,

they would have taken those things, those objects, those roots of merit, and those productions of the thought of awakening accompanied by sympathetic joy as signs, and dedicated them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, Reverend Subhūti, this Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught should not be spoken in the presence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the vehicle. Likewise, the Perfection of Meditation, the Perfection of Vigor, the Perfection of Patience, the Perfection of Ethical Discipline, the Perfection of Generosity, and everything from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence should not be so taught.
This [teaching] should be taught in the presence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the vehicle.
Why is that?
Because he may possess only a measure of faith, a measure of serene confidence, a measure of affection, and a measure of reverence.

Even if [this teaching] were to vanish while being spoken and taught before an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva— up to and including the teaching and instruction on the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence— he, having heard this, would not tremble, would not be terrified,
and would not fall into fear. This is provided that he has been taken hold of by a spiritual friend and has performed services for previous Victors.
"One who has planted roots of merit and attended upon many Buddhas—

furthermore, Reverend Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should thus dedicate the basis of meritorious action associated with sympathetic joy toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. And as for that mind by which one rejoices and dedicates— "
The mind has ceased, been suppressed, departed, and transformed;
those objects, those focal points, and those roots of merit have also ceased, been suppressed, departed, and transformed.
What, then, is the mind associated with rejoicing?
What are the bases? What are the objects of focus?
What are the roots of goodness that he dedicates toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
Does one mind transform another mind?
Since there is no simultaneous conjunction of two minds,
and since that which is the intrinsic nature of mind cannot be transformed, how could it be so?

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, understands in this way: "The perfection of wisdom is non-existence," and likewise understands that the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity are non-existence;

and that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existence; and that the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment are non-existence—[then he practices the perfection of wisdom].
The meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the noble truths, the eight liberations, and the nine successive meditative attainments are non-existence;
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are non-existence;
the six superknowledges are non-existence.
All the emptinesses, all the meditative concentrations, and all the gateways of the dhāraṇīs are non-existent;
the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are non-existent.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should dedicate the basis of meritorious action associated with sympathetic joy toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"If one dedicates in this way, it becomes dedicated to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Elder Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti, how should those [merits] be dedicated by a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has newly set out in the vehicle?"
The roots of virtue are dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. And how is the basis of meritorious action associated with rejoicing grasped and dedicated?
Subhūti said:

If, Maitreya, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the vehicle shall practice the perfection of wisdom, he will grasp that perfection of wisdom through the yoga of non-apprehension and not through the yoga of signs. In the same way, he will grasp the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity through the yoga of non-apprehension and not through the yoga of signs. [He will do so] regarding internal emptiness...

He will abound in resolute faith. He will abound in resolute faith in external emptiness, internal-external emptiness, and so on, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence. He will abound in resolute faith in the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, and the noble truths. He will abound in resolute faith in the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments.

He will abound in resolute conviction regarding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. He will abound in resolute conviction regarding the superknowledges, all meditative concentrations, and all gateways of dhāraṇī. He will abound in resolute conviction regarding the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He will be sustained by spiritual friends.

And they will come to be his spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), who will teach him this very perfection of wisdom, the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity, together with their meaning and their phrasing. And they will teach them in such a way that he will never be separated from the perfection of wisdom, nor likewise from all the perfections.

He will not be separated from [these], up to and including all the emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, emptiness, the signless, the wishless, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, all samādhis, all doors of dhāraṇī, and the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

He will not be separated from the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. This will continue until he has entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, he will point out the works of Māra;
upon hearing of those works of Māra, there will be for him neither loss nor increase. Why is that?

For indeed, the intrinsic nature of those deeds of Māra is not perceived. He shall never be separated from the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, until he has entered the fixed course of a bodhisattva. And therein he will plant roots of merit; by those roots of merit he will grasp the lineage of the bodhisattvas, and by that lineage of the bodhisattvas he shall never be separated.
This shall continue until he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the vehicle [should reflect upon] those Buddhas,
the Blessed Ones, whose paths have been cut off, whose tracks have been obliterated, who have severed the net of conceptual proliferation and existence, and who have exhausted all tears.

Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones who reside in the ten directions— in immeasurable and incalculable numbers— who have crushed the thorns [of defilement], laid down the burden, attained their own goal, exhausted the fetters of existence, whose minds are rightly liberated through perfect knowledge, and who have reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states.
Regarding those Blessed Buddhas who currently abide, maintain themselves, and teach the Dharma, together with their assemblies of śrāvakas—
whatever accumulations of merit belong to them, or whatever roots of virtue have been planted there among the great kṣatriya clans,
the great brahmin clans, the great householder clans, or among the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm;
Or among the gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven, or the Yāma heaven, or the Tuṣita heaven, or the Nirmāṇarati heaven, or the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven;

or among the Brahmapārṣadya gods, or the Brahmapurohita gods, or the Mahābrahmans; or among the Parīttābha gods, or the Apramāṇābha gods, or the Ābhāsvara gods; or among the Parīttaśubha gods, or the Apramāṇaśubha gods, or the Śubhakṛtsna gods, or the Anabhraka gods.

Or whatever roots of merit have been planted among the gods of the Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Śuddhāvāsa, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, or Akaniṣṭha realms— all of these, having condensed, gathered, and weighed them together,
with the foremost, most excellent, eldest, best, preeminent, and supreme rejoicing;

One should rejoice with the unsurpassed rejoicing; having rejoiced, one should dedicate the root of merit associated with that rejoicing toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is the dedication through non-apprehension.
Maitreya said:

If, Reverend Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has newly set out in the vehicle, having brought to mind all the roots of merit of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, together with their assemblies of śrāvakas, rejoices with the foremost rejoicing, and having rejoiced up to the unsurpassed rejoicing, dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; [then he would produce a great deal of merit].
How is it that for a bodhisattva mahāsattva there is no perversion of perception, no perversion of mind, and no perversion of view?
Subhūti said:

"Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva brings those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, together with their assemblies of disciples to mind, he does not form the notion of 'Buddha' nor the notion of 'disciple' therein."
He does not form a perception of roots of virtue. Even with the very mind by which he dedicates, he does not form a perception of that mind.
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates in this way, there is no perversion of perception and no perversion of mind.
There is no perversion of view. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having brought to mind those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and those roots of virtue,
makes them into signs and, having made them into signs, dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— while dedicating in this manner...
There occurs a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view. However, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, those roots of merit,
and that very mind with which he attends to them as being "exhausted, exhausted," and understands that which is exhausted...
That cannot be transformed. The very same *dharmatā* applies to the mind by which one transforms, and the same *dharmatā* applies to that into which one transforms.
If one transforms in this way, one transforms with equanimity, not with partiality.
And he does not dedicate falsely;
in this manner should a bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicate.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva [dedicates] that which belongs to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, up to...

From the first production of the thought of awakening until his final nirvana, and until the disappearance of the true Dharma— including whatever roots of merit were planted there by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as by those ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana), and whatever teaching of the Dharma was heard, and having heard it, whatever roots of merit were planted there by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas— [all these are included].

Whatever true Dharma was heard, whatever roots of merit were planted, and whatever resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment was generated by those of the great *śāla* clans of Kṣatriyas, or the great *śāla* clans of Brāhmaṇas, or the great *śāla* clans of householders, or by the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm— all that, having been condensed and gathered together.
Having weighed it with the foremost rejoicing, he rejoices with the highest, best, excellent, most eminent,
sublime, supreme, unsurpassed, incomparable, and unequaled rejoicing; having rejoiced, he dedicates all that toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If, moreover, one perceives thus: "Those dharmas have been exhausted, ceased, departed, and transformed; even that dharma by which one dedicates is empty of intrinsic nature"—if one dedicates in this way, it becomes dedicated to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
If, however, one perceives thus: "Dharmas do not dedicate other dharmas," for what reason is that?
For all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature.

If one dedicates in this way, it becomes dedicated to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Thus, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom, and thus practicing in the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity, there is no perversion of perception, no perversion of mind, and no perversion of view.
It is so. For what reason?
Because the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not become attached to that dedication;
he does not perceive those roots of virtue, nor that thought of awakening, wherein he might become attached.
This is the unsurpassed dedication of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Thus is the dedication characterized by non-perversion.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that formation of the basis of meritorious action as secluded from the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, and perceives it as secluded by means of the perfection of wisdom; and likewise by means of the perfection of meditation, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of ethical discipline—[this is the dedication].

He perceives it as secluded by means of the perfection of generosity. He perceives it as secluded by means of internal emptiness, up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
