"May the Blessed One explain this; it will serve as a light for future generations, so that those persons who corrupt the Dharma—having performed and accumulated such karma conducive to the ruin of the Dharma—may see that [the results] are like this."
"They will take up an individual existence.
The Blessed One said:
"In this very way, Śāriputra, light will be provided for future generations by means of this [teaching], even though it leads to the ruin of the Dharma."

By means of the karma performed and accumulated, he will experience suffering in the great hells. As for the immeasurability of this very suffering and how much longer he will experience such sufferings—
this is precisely [the fault] of that son of good family or daughter of good family who possesses a portion of virtue, regarding those actions conducive to the ruin of the Dharma.
"Arising will come from actions. They will not reject the Dharma even for the sake of their lives, thinking, 'May we not encounter such sufferings as these.
Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:"
"Blessed One, a son of noble family or a daughter of noble family should be well-restrained in their actions of body, speech, and mind, thinking: 'May I not experience such sufferings;
may it not come to pass that we shall not see the Tathāgata, or shall not hear the Dharma, or shall not see the Saṅgha.'"

"Thinking, 'May we be reborn in Buddha-fields where no Buddhas have appeared,' or 'May we be born among human beings who are poor, or may our words be unheeded'— by performing and accumulating such verbal karma of rejecting the Dharma, O Blessed One, one performs and accumulates karma that leads to calamity."
The Blessed One said:

"Subhūti, by performing and accumulating this verbal action of rejecting all dharmas, one has performed and accumulated karma that leads to the ruin of the Dharma. Subhūti, right here in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, those deluded persons [act in such a way]."

They will become renunciants. Those who think that this perfection of wisdom should be reviled and those who think it should be opposed— Subhūti, by reviling and opposing the perfection of wisdom, they revile and oppose the enlightenment of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

By corrupting and rejecting the enlightenment of the Blessed Buddhas, one corrupts and rejects the omniscience of the Blessed Buddhas of the past, future, and present. By corrupting and rejecting omniscience, the Dharma is rejected. By the rejection of the Dharma, the Saṅgha is rejected.

When the Saṅgha is rejected, mundane right view and supramundane right view are rejected. Likewise, the six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments are rejected.
The gateways to liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—the eight liberations, and the nine successive meditative attainments are also rejected.

The six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are rejected. Inner emptiness (*adhyātmaśūnyatā*), up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāvaśūnyatā*), all meditative concentrations (*sarvasamādhi*), all doors of dhāraṇī (*sarvadhāraṇīmukha*), and the ten bodhisattva stages (*daśabodhisattvabhūmi*) are rejected. The ten powers of a Tathāgata (*daśatathāgatabala*), the four grounds of self-confidence (*catvāri vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*aṣṭādaśāveṇikā buddhadharma*) are rejected.

...they come to be. Up to the point that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is rejected. When omniscience is rejected, an immeasurable, incalculable, and limitless mass of demerit (*apuṇyaskandha*) is acquired. And by the acquisition of that mass of demerit, immeasurable, incalculable, and limitless suffering and mental distress are acquired.
Thus Subhūti spoke regarding the karma that leads to the ruin of the Dharma:
"Blessed One, as for those deluded persons who will reject this profound perfection of wisdom..."
"In what ways will they reject this perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, those deluded persons will reject this profound perfection of wisdom in four ways. What are the four?"

Namely, Subhūti, those deluded persons will be possessed by Māra; they will be uncommitted to the profound dharmas and will not attain serene confidence. They will be attached to the five aggregates and fall into the hands of evil friends.
Those deluded persons will be characterized by malice, exalting themselves and disparaging others. By these [qualities], Subhūti...
"Endowed with four characteristics, those deluded persons will reject the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti said:
'O Blessed One, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is difficult to resolve with faith by one who is not devoted to it, who is devoid of roots of merit, and who has fallen into the hands of evil friends.'"

The Blessed One said: "It is so, Subhūti. This profound perfection of wisdom is difficult to resolve with faith by those who are not devoted to it, who are devoid of roots of merit, and who have fallen into the hands of evil friends.
Subhūti said:
"How deep, Blessed One, is this perfection of wisdom that it is so difficult to resolve upon?
The Blessed One said:
"Form, Subhūti, is neither bound nor liberated. For what reason?"
For form, Subhūti, has the nature of form;
feeling has the nature of feeling; perception has the nature of perception.
For conditioned phenomena have no intrinsic nature;
Subhūti, consciousness is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?
Because consciousness has no intrinsic nature. Subhūti, the perfection of generosity is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?

For the perfection of giving has the perfection of giving as its intrinsic nature. In the same way, Subhūti, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is that? Because the perfection of wisdom has the perfection of wisdom as its intrinsic nature. Subhūti, internal emptiness is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?

For internal emptiness has internal emptiness as its intrinsic nature; and so on, up to: non-existence-intrinsic-nature emptiness, Subhūti, is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Because non-existence-intrinsic-nature emptiness has non-existence-intrinsic-nature emptiness as its intrinsic nature. The applications of mindfulness, Subhūti, are neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?

For the applications of mindfulness have the nature of non-self-existence as their very essence. Likewise, Subhūti, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the factors of enlightenment, and the paths are neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Because the paths have the nature of non-self-existence as their very essence. Likewise, Subhūti, the ten powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the knowledge of all aspects are neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the knowledge of all aspects has the nature of non-self-existence as its very essence. Subhūti, the prior limit of form is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?

For, Subhūti, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have the nature of the non-existence of a prior limit. Subhūti, the prior limit of consciousness is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, consciousness has the nature of the non-existence of a prior limit;
and so on, up to the knowledge of all aspects, Subhūti, the prior limit is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?

Subhūti, the past limit (*pūrvānta*) is indeed the nature of non-existence (*abhāvasvabhāva*), for that is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Subhūti, the future limit (*aparānta*) of form (*rūpa*) is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that?

Because, Subhūti, the future limit is the nature of non-existence; for form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, Subhūti, the future limit is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Because the future limit is the nature of non-existence.
For indeed, Subhūti, consciousness [is thus]. Likewise, Subhūti, up to and including omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), its future limit is unbound and unliberated. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the nature of omniscience is the non-existence of a future limit. Form, Subhūti, in the present is unbound and unliberated. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, the nature of form, feeling, perception, and mental formations is the non-existence of the present.
Consciousness, Subhūti, is neither bound nor liberated in the present. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, consciousness has the nature of non-existence in the present. This extends up to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is neither bound nor liberated in the present. Why is that?
Because, Subhūti, all-knowledge has the nature of non-existence in the present.
Subhūti said:

"O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to resolve with faith by those who are not devoted to it, who have not planted roots of merit, who have fallen into the hands of evil friends, who are under the sway of Māra, who are indolent, lacking in vigor, and whose mindfulness is lost.
The Blessed One said:

"So it is, Subhūti. This perfection of wisdom, Subhūti, is difficult to resolve with faith by those who are not devoted to it, who have not planted roots of merit, who have fallen into the hands of evil friends, who are under the sway of Māra, who are indolent, lacking in vigor, deprived of mindfulness, and lacking clear comprehension.
These are the four causes of the obscuration of karma."
Subhūti, that which is the purity of form is itself the purity of the fruit;

that which is the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is itself the purity of the fruit. That which is the purity of the perfection of generosity is itself the purity of the fruit. Likewise for the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of vigor.

The purity of the perfection of wisdom is itself the purity of the fruit. The purity of internal emptiness is itself the purity of the fruit; likewise, up to the purity of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, that is itself the purity of the fruit.
In this way, the purity of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is itself the purity of the fruit.

In this way, the purity of the noble truths, the immeasurables, and the meditative absorptions and formless attainments is itself the purity of the fruit. The purity of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is itself the purity of the fruit. The purity of the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments is itself the purity of the fruit. [The purity] of the six higher knowledges...

Purity is indeed the purity of the fruit. Likewise, whatever is the purity of all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and all gateways of dhāraṇīs, that is indeed the purity of the fruit. Whatever is the purity of the ten bodhisattva stages (*bhūmi*), that is indeed the purity of the fruit. Whatever is the purity of the ten powers (*bala*) of a Tathāgata, of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); [that too is the purity of the fruit].
Up to the purification of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, that is indeed the purification of the fruit. That which is the purification of awakening is indeed the purification of the fruit.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that which is the purification of form is indeed the purification of the fruit.
That which is the purity of the fruit is the purity of the perfection of wisdom;
that which is the purity of the perfection of wisdom is the purity of form. For indeed, this purity of form, this purity of the fruit, and this purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual.

It is non-dual, undivided, and uninterrupted. Thus, up to the point that the purity of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the purity of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), and the purity of the perfection of wisdom is the purity of the knowledge of all aspects. For this purity of the knowledge of all aspects and the purity of the perfection of wisdom are non-dual, undivided, and uninterrupted. This is the commonality of purity.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that which is the purity of the self is the purity of form;

that which is the purity of form is the purity of the self. For this purity of the self and this purity of form are non-dual, not divided, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted. Likewise, that which is the purity of a being, a soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer is the purity of form.

That which is the purity of form, up to and including the purity of the seer—this purity of the seer and this purity of form are non-dual; they are not divided, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted. Likewise, up to the point that the purity of the seer is the purity of omniscience, and the purity of omniscience is the purity of the seer—this purity of the seer and this purity of omniscience are non-dual; they are not divided, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted.
Furthermore, Subhūti, through the purity of the self there is the purity of form, and through the purity of form there is the purity of the self;
for this purity of the self and this purity of form are non-dual, undivided, indivisible, and inseparable.
It is the same with the purity of a sentient being, a living soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, and a seer.

The purity of form is, through the complete purity of form, up to the complete purity of the seer; for this complete purity of the seer and the complete purity of form are non-dual, undivided, indivisible, and uninterrupted. Likewise, up to the complete purity of the seer through the complete purity of omniscience, and the complete purity of the seer through the complete purity of omniscience; for indeed, the purity of the seer...
And omniscience-purification—these two are non-dual, not divided, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted.
Furthermore, Subhūti, through the purification of passion there is the purification of form, up to the purification of omniscience;
for indeed, the purification of passion and the purification of omniscience are non-dual, not divided, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted.
It is uninterrupted. Thus, through the purification of hatred and delusion, there is the purification of form, up to the purification of omniscience.
For indeed, the purification of hatred and delusion and the purification of omniscience are non-dual; they are not divided, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted.
Furthermore, Subhūti, through the purification of passion, hatred, and delusion, there is the purification of form, and so on, up to the purification of omniscience.
For thus, the purification of passion, hatred, and delusion and the purification of omniscience are non-dual; they are not two, undivided, and uninterrupted.
Such is the purification of the Śrāvaka’s obscuration of afflictions.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that which is the purification of form is itself the purification of the fruit.

In the same way, feeling, perception, and mental formations [are purified]; that which is the purification of consciousness is itself the purification of the fruit. Thus, up to: through the purification of ignorance comes the purification of formations; through the purification of formations comes the purification of consciousness; through the purification of consciousness comes the purification of name-and-form;

through the purification of name-and-form comes the purification of the six sense bases; through the purification of the six sense bases comes the purification of contact; through the purification of contact...

The purification of feeling; through the purification of feeling comes the purification of craving; through the purification of craving comes the purification of grasping; through the purification of grasping comes the purification of becoming; through the purification of becoming comes the purification of birth; through the purification of birth comes the purification of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; and through the purification of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair comes the purification of omniscience—thus it is.
The purification of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair, and the purification of omniscience— these two are non-dual, undivided, indivisible, and uninterrupted.
Thus is the Pratyekabuddha’s purification of one portion of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, Subhūti, there is the purity of the perfection of generosity; through the purity of the perfection of generosity comes the purity of the perfection of ethical discipline;

through the purity of the perfection of ethical discipline comes the purity of the perfection of patience; through the purity of the perfection of patience comes the purity of the perfection of vigor;

through the purity of the perfection of vigor comes the purity of the perfection of meditative concentration; and through the purity of the perfection of meditative concentration comes the purity of the perfection of wisdom.
Through the purity of the perfection of wisdom, there is the purity of internal emptiness; through the purity of internal emptiness, there is the purity of external emptiness;

through the purity of external emptiness, there is the purity of internal-and-external emptiness; through the purity of internal-and-external emptiness, and so on, up to the purity of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence; through the purity of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, there is the purity of the applications of mindfulness.

Through the purification of the foundations of mindfulness comes the purification of the right efforts; through the purification of the right efforts, the purification of the bases of psychic power; through the purification of the bases of psychic power, the purification of the faculties; through the purification of the faculties, the purification of the powers; through the purification of the powers, the purification of the factors of enlightenment; through the purification of the factors of enlightenment, the purification of the path; and through the purification of the path, the purification of the noble truths.

Through the purity of the noble truths comes the purity of the immeasurables; through the purity of the immeasurables, the purity of the meditative concentrations; through the purity of the meditative concentrations, the purity of the formless attainments; through the purity of the formless attainments, the purity of the superknowledges; through the purity of the superknowledges, the purity of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

through the purity of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the purity of the eight liberations; and through the purity of the eight liberations, the purity of the nine successive meditative attainments.

Through the purification of the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), there is the purification of all meditative concentrations (*sarvasamādhi*); through the purification of all meditative concentrations, there is the purification of all gateways of mnemonic formulas (*sarvadhāraṇīmukha*); through the purification of all gateways of mnemonic formulas, there is the purification of the ten powers and the grounds of self-confidence (*daśabalavaiśāradya*); through the purification of the ten powers and the grounds of self-confidence, there is the purification of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); through the purification of the analytical knowledges, there is the purification of the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*); and through the purification of the unique qualities of a Buddha...
"Purity of omniscience" means that the purity of omniscience and the purity of the unique qualities of a Buddha are non-dual; they are not divided, undifferentiated, and indivisible.
This is the bodhisattva’s purity of the paths of the three vehicles.
Furthermore, Subhūti, that which is the purity of the perfection of wisdom is the purity of form;
that which is the purity of form is, up to and including, the purity of the knowledge of all aspects.
For indeed, the purity of the perfection of wisdom, the purity of form, and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, not divided, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted.
The purity of feeling, perception, and mental formations is the purity of consciousness; the purity of consciousness is the purity of the knowledge of all aspects.

For indeed, the purity of the perfection of wisdom, the purity of consciousness, and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, not divided, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted. Thus is the purity of the perfection of meditative concentration.

The purity of the perfection of vigor, the purity of the perfection of patience, and the purity of the perfection of ethical discipline—the purity of the perfection of generosity is the purity of form;

and the purity of form is the purity of the knowledge of all aspects. For indeed, the purity of the perfection of generosity, the purity of form, and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, not divided, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted.
The purity of feeling, perception, and mental formations is the purity of consciousness; the purity of consciousness is the purity of the knowledge of all aspects.
For indeed, the purity of the perfection of generosity, the purity of consciousness, and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects are non-dual, undivided, indivisible, and uninterrupted.
Thus is the weak-weak path.
Furthermore, through the purity of internal emptiness up to the purity of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence, there is the purity of the knowledge of all aspects;
for indeed, the purity of internal emptiness up to the purity of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence is identical to the purity of the knowledge of all aspects.

And this is non-dual, without division, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted. Through the purity of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination, up to the purity of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, there is the purity of the knowledge of all aspects.
For indeed, the purity of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and dependent origination is itself the perfection.

The purity of the factors conducive to enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, all samādhis, and all doors of dhāraṇī; and the purity of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique buddha-qualities, and the purity of the knowledge of all aspects— this is non-dual, not divided, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the purity of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the purity of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) are non-dual; they are not divided, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted. This is the path of weak-middling intensity. Furthermore, Subhūti, through the purity of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), there is the purity of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); through the purity of the unconditioned, there is the purity of the conditioned. For indeed, the purity of the conditioned and the purity of the unconditioned are non-dual; they are not divided, undifferentiated, and uninterrupted.
Furthermore, Subhūti, through the purity of the past there is the purity of the future; through the purity of the future there is the purity of the past;

through the purity of the past and the future there is the purity of the present; and through the purity of the present there is the purity of the past and the future. For indeed, the purity of the past and the future and the purity of the present are non-dual, being without division.
"Undivided and uncut. Thus is the path of weak and intense [cultivation]. Then, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, this purity is profound."
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
"Through the purity of what?
The Blessed One said:
"O son of Śāna, through the purity of form, there is profound purity; [so too] of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."

It is profound because of its purity. Likewise, it is profound because of the purity of the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element. Likewise, it is profound because of the purity of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. It is profound because of the purity of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena. It is profound because of the purity of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom. It is profound through the purity of internal emptiness.

It is profound by virtue of the purity of the emptiness of non-existence as intrinsic nature; it is profound by virtue of the purity of the foundations of mindfulness; it is profound by virtue of the purity of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path; it is profound by virtue of the purity of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; it is profound by virtue of the purity of the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments; [it is profound] by virtue of the purity of the superknowledges.

It is profound. It is profound through the purification of all samādhis and all dhāraṇī-doors. It is profound through the purification of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. It is profound through the purification of the bodhisattva’s knowledge of all aspects. Thus is the middling-mild path. Śāriputra said:
“Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is a light.
The Blessed One said: “Śāriputra, because it is absolutely pure, there is the absolute purity of light.”
Śāriputra asked: "Through the purification of what?
The Blessed One replied:

Śāriputra, because of the purity of the perfection of wisdom, there is the absolute purity of light. Likewise, because of the purity of the perfection of meditation, the purity of the perfection of vigor, the purity of the perfection of patience, the purity of the perfection of ethical discipline, and the purity of the perfection of generosity, there is the absolute purity of light. Through the purity of internal emptiness, there is the absolute purity of light.

Up to the purification through the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence, there is the ultimate purity of light. Through the purification of the foundations of mindfulness, there is the ultimate purity of light. Through the purification of the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path, there is the ultimate purity of light.

Through the purification of the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments, there is the ultimate purity of light. Through the purification of the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments...
It is the ultimate purity of light. Through the purity of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges, there is the ultimate purity of light.
Through the purity of all meditative concentrations and all doors of dhāraṇī, there is the ultimate purity of light.
Through the purity of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, there is the ultimate purity of light.
Up to the ultimate purity of light through the purity of the knowledge of all aspects.
Thus is the middle-of-the-middle path.
Śāriputra said:
“Non-reconnection, Blessed One, is purity.
The Blessed One said: “Because of its absolute purity, Śāriputra.”
Śāriputra asked: "Through the non-transmigration of what is there purity?
The Blessed One replied:
The non-transmigration, non-relinking, and purification of form;

the non-transmigration, non-relinking, and purification of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Thus, up to the non-transmigration, non-relinking, and purification of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This is the medium-superior path.
Śāriputra said:
“O Blessed One, purity is unafflicted.
The Blessed One said:
"Because it is absolutely unafflicted, Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
"Of what, Blessed One, is there purity through non-affliction?"
The Blessed One said: "Purity arises because form (*rūpa*) is by nature undefiled;

purity arises because feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are by nature undefiled. In this way, up to and including all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), purity arises because it is by nature undefiled. Thus [it was said].
Śāriputra said:
“Non-attainment and non-realization, Blessed One, are purity.
The Blessed One said:
“Because of the absolute non-attainment and non-realization [of it], Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
“Of what, Blessed One, is there purity through non-attainment and non-realization?”
The Blessed One said:
"Purity comes through the non-attainment and non-realization of form;

purity comes through the non-attainment and non-realization of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. In this way, up to the point of the non-attainment and non-realization of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā), there is purity. Thus [he spoke].
Śāriputra said:
"Non-origination, Blessed One, is purity.
The Blessed One said:
“Because it is absolutely non-arisen, Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
“Of what, Blessed One, is there purity through non-arising?”
The Blessed One said:
"Śāriputra, purity comes from the non-attachment to form;

purity comes from the non-attachment to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. In this way, up to the non-attachment to the knowledge of all aspects, there is purity. This is the path of the highest-of-the-high degree."
Śāriputra said:
"O Blessed One, the purity of the desire realm is non-arising.
The Blessed One said:
“Because of its absolute purity, Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
“How, Blessed One, is non-arising in the realm of desire purity?”
The Blessed One said:
"Śāriputra, through the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of the desire realm, non-arising is purity.
Śāriputra said:
“Blessed One, the purity of the realm of form is non-arising.
The Blessed One said: “Because it is absolutely pure, Śāriputra.”
Śāriputra said:
"Blessed One, how is it that the non-arising of the realm of form is purity?
The Blessed One replied:
“Śāriputra, because the intrinsic nature of the form realm is non-arising, non-arising is purity.
Śāriputra said: “Blessed One, the non-arising of the formless realm is purity.”
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
"Blessed One, how is it that non-arising in the formless realm is purity?
The Blessed One said:
"Śāriputra, through the non-arising of the intrinsic nature of the formless realm, non-arising is purity. Thus is the state of being the antidote to the three realms for the path of cultivation.
Śāriputra said:
"Blessed One, purity does not know.
The Blessed One said:
"Because it is absolutely pure, Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
"How is it, Blessed One, that purity does not know?"
The Blessed One said:
"Śāriputra, because of the dullness of phenomena, purity is not perceived.
Śāriputra said:
“Form does not know, Blessed One, because of purity.
The Blessed One said: “Because of its absolute purity, Śāriputra.”
Śāriputra said:
"How, Blessed One, does purity not know form?
The Blessed One said:
"Based on the emptiness of specific characteristics, Śāriputra, form does not know purity.
Śāriputra said:
"O Blessed One, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not know purity."
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
“Blessed One, how is it that purity does not know feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness?
The Blessed One said:
“Śāriputra, by way of the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics, purity does not know feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.”
Śāriputra said:
"Blessed One, purity does not know all phenomena.
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
"How, Blessed One, is there purity such that one does not know any phenomena?"
The Blessed One said:

"Śāriputra, through the non-apprehension of all dharmas, one does not know any dharmas. Thus, Śāriputra spoke regarding the path of the equality of the non-duality of the object of knowledge and the knowledge itself.
"Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom neither benefits nor harms omniscience.
The Blessed One said: "Because it is absolutely pure, Śāriputra."
Śāriputra asked:
"How, Blessed One, does the perfection of wisdom neither harm nor benefit omniscience?
The Blessed One replied:
"Based on the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthititā*), Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) neither harms nor benefits omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Śāriputra said:
"Lord, does the purity of the perfection of wisdom not grasp at any phenomenon whatsoever?"
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said:
“Blessed One, how is it that the purity of the perfection of wisdom does not grasp any dharma?
The Blessed One replied:
“By virtue of its being embraced by the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).”
Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, from the purity of the self comes the purity of form.
The Blessed One said:
"By virtue of ultimate purity.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is there purity of form through the purity of the self?"
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, because the self is non-existent and form is non-existent, there is ultimate purity.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, through the purity of the self, there is the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The Blessed One said:
“By virtue of their ultimate purity.”
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is it that through the purity of the self, there is the purity of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, because the self is non-existent, and because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-existent, there is ultimate purity.
Subhūti said:

"Blessed One, through the purity of the self, there is the purity of the perfection of generosity. Likewise for the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, and the perfection of vigor."

“Blessed One, through the purity of the self, there is the purity of the perfection of meditation. Blessed One, through the purity of the self, there is the purity of the foundations of mindfulness. Likewise for the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment;

Blessed One, through the purity of the self, there is the purity of the path. Through the purity of the self, there is the purity of the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditations, and the formless attainments.”

Through the purity of the self, there is the purity of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Through the purity of the self, there is the purity of the eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments.

Through the purity of the self, there is the purity of internal emptiness, up to the purity of the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature. Through the purity of the self, there is the purity of the gateways of meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs.

Through the purity of the self, there is the purity of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the analytical knowledges. Through the purity of the self, O Blessed One, there is the purity of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Subhūti."
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, through the purity of the self, there is the purity of all phenomena.
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is there the purity of all phenomena through the purity of the self?"
The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, because the self is non-existent, and because all phenomena are non-existent, there is purity.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, through the purity of the self, there is the purity of the fruit of stream-entry;
likewise, there is the purity of the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, and pratyekabuddhahood.
The Blessed One said:
"By way of the emptiness of specific characteristics.
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, through the purity of the self, there is the purity of awakening."
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is the purity of awakening through the purity of the self?
The Blessed One replied:
"By way of the emptiness of intrinsic characteristics."
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, through the purity of the self, there is the purity of omniscience.
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Subhūti.
Subhūti asked:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is there the purity of omniscience through the purity of the self?"
The Blessed One said:
"By way of the emptiness of specific characteristics.
Subhūti said:
“O Blessed One, the purity of duality is neither attainment nor realization.
The Blessed One said: “Because it is absolutely pure, Subhūti.”
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is the purification of duality neither attainment nor realization?
The Blessed One replied:
"Based on the equality of phenomena that are neither afflicted nor purified.
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, because the self is limitless, form is limitless."
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is the purity of the boundlessness of form due to the boundlessness of the self?
The Blessed One replied:
"By way of absolute emptiness and the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end."
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, because the self is limitless, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are limitless.
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is there the purity of the boundlessness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness through the boundlessness of the self?"
The Blessed One said:
"By way of absolute emptiness and the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end.
Subhūti said:
“Thus, Blessed One, is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Blessed One said: “Because of its absolute purity, Subhūti.”
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is this the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Blessed One replied:
Subhūti, it is by means of the knowledge of the aspects of the path that this perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva exists.

Thus, through the refutation of objections regarding the path and the cultivation of the purity of the two extremes of thought, the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*) has been explained. This concludes the second chapter, "The Purity of the Two Extremes," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-five Thousand Lines, as refined according to the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* III.
Subhūti said:
"Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, is not apprehended on this shore, nor on the other shore, nor in between the two."
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"For what reason, Blessed One, is the *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas not found on this shore, nor on the other shore, nor in between the two?
The Blessed One said:
"Because of its absolute purity, Subhūti, by virtue of the equality of all phenomena throughout the three times. Thus was stated the non-abiding in *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*.
Subhūti said:

"Furthermore, Blessed One, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family belonging to the Mahāyāna, being unskilled in means, should understand this perfection of wisdom in such a way by way of apprehension, they will abandon it and distance themselves from it.
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is so, Subhūti. Even by way of a name, Subhūti, there is attachment; even by way of a sign, Subhūti, there is attachment. For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, all dharmas are signless and nameless.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, how is it that there is attachment even to a name, and attachment even to a sign?
The Blessed One replied:
“In this regard, Subhūti, sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the Mahāyāna will grasp the Perfection of Wisdom even by its name.”
They will grasp [the perfection of wisdom] by way of signs; and having grasped it both by way of signs and by way of names, they will neglect and distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom.
Thinking they possess the perfection of wisdom, they will neglect and distance themselves from the perfection of wisdom.
Thus it is said that there is remoteness through lack of skillful means.
Subhūti said:

"It is wonderful, Blessed One, how far this perfection of wisdom has been well-expounded and perfectly established for the sake of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas—both these attachments and these non-attachments. Thus, even by means of this teaching, it is difficult to master."
Then the Venerable Śāriputra said this to the Venerable Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti, what is attachment for bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom, and what is non-attachment?
Subhūti replied:
In this regard, venerable Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, a son of good family or a daughter of good family, who is unskilled in means, perceives that "form is empty," that is an attachment;

if they perceive that "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty," that is an attachment. Likewise, if they perceive that the aggregates, elements, sense bases—whether individually or collectively—and the factors of dependent origination are empty, that is an attachment. [The same applies to] the perfection of generosity...
To perceive that "emptiness" is a conceptual attachment; to perceive that "the perfection of ethical discipline is empty" is a conceptual attachment;
to perceive that "the perfection of patience is empty" is a conceptual attachment.
To perceive that the perfection of vigor is empty is attachment;
to perceive that the perfection of meditation is empty is attachment;
to perceive that the perfection of wisdom is empty is attachment. Likewise, to perceive that the applications of mindfulness are empty is attachment.

Attachment is the perception that the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are empty. Attachment is the perception that the noble truths are empty. Attachment is the perception that the immeasurables, the dhyānas, and the formless attainments are empty. [Attachment is the perception that] the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness [are empty].

To perceive that "the [superknowledges] are empty" is attachment. Likewise, to perceive that "the superknowledges, all the emptinesses, all the samādhis, and all the doors of dhāraṇī are empty" is attachment. To perceive that "the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four fearlessnesses are empty" is attachment.
To perceive that "the four analytical knowledges and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are empty" is attachment.

To perceive that "omniscience is empty" is attachment. Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is unskilled in means perceives past phenomena as "past phenomena," that is attachment; when he perceives future phenomena as "future phenomena," that is attachment.

Attachment. To perceive present phenomena as "present phenomena" is attachment. Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to practice the perfection of generosity from the first production of the thought of awakening (prathamacittotpāda) by way of apprehension (*upalambha*) is attachment; to practice the perfection of ethical discipline is attachment.
To think, "I am practicing the perfection of patience," is attachment;
to think, "I am practicing the perfection of vigor," is attachment; to think, "I am practicing the perfection of meditative concentration," is attachment.

To think "one practices in the perfection of wisdom" is attachment. To think "one practices in the applications of mindfulness" is attachment; to think "one practices in the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path" is attachment. Likewise, to think "one practices in the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, and the formless attainments" is attachment. [The same applies to] the noble truths, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the eight liberations.

To practice in the nine successive meditative attainments, the superknowledges, all the emptinesses, all the samādhis, and all the doors of dhāraṇī is attachment. To practice in the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha is attachment; even to practice in omniscience is attachment. Thus is the adverse side.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, as to what you asked:

"What is the non-attachment of bodhisattva mahāsattvas practicing the perfection of wisdom? Indeed, Śāriputra, it does not occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom who is skilled in means [to think] thus:
Form does not perceive form;

likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not perceive consciousness. Past phenomena do not perceive past phenomena; future phenomena do not perceive future phenomena; present phenomena do not perceive present phenomena.
He perceives phenomena. Furthermore, Śāriputra, it does not occur to a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom who is skilled in means that "I am giving a gift."
"I give this gift to him;
I give this gift;
I maintain moral discipline."
"I maintain this morality; I maintain morality for these [beings]; I cultivate patience."
I cultivate this patience;
I cultivate patience toward these [objects];
I exert vigor.
I shall exert this vigor;
for their sake, I shall exert vigor;
I shall enter into meditative absorption.
"I shall enter this meditative absorption; I shall enter such a meditative absorption; I am cultivating wisdom."
"I cultivate this wisdom; for this purpose I cultivate wisdom; I produce merit."
In this way I produce merit; I shall enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva; I shall purify a buddha-field.
"I shall bring sentient beings to maturity;

I shall attain omniscience"—all such conceptualizations, O Venerable Śāriputra, do not exist for those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who course in the perfection of wisdom and are skilled in means. Why is that?
Based on internal emptiness, based on external emptiness, based on internal-external emptiness, and so on, up to based on the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence—
these, Venerable Śāriputra, are the attachments-free skillful means of a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom. This is the counteractive measure.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the elder Subhūti:
"In what sense, venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become attached?
Subhūti replied:

In this regard, Kauśika, a bodhisattva perceives the mind; he perceives generosity; likewise, he perceives ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom. He perceives internal emptiness, he perceives external emptiness, and he perceives internal-external emptiness.

...up to the point that he perceives the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence. In this way, [he perceives] the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the superknowledges, the concentrations, the doors of dhāraṇī, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the four [fearlessnesses]. (PSP_2-3:168)
He perceives the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*). He perceives the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

He perceives the roots of virtue planted by those Buddhas; having condensed all of these, gathered them together, and weighed them, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. This, Kauśika, is the attachment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Because of this, one is unable to course in the unattached perfection of wisdom. For what reason?
Because, Kauśika, the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of form cannot be transformed;
nor can the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness be transformed, Kauśika.

In this way, the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields— whether taken individually or collectively— and of dependent origination cannot be transformed. Likewise, [the intrinsic nature] of the perfections, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening,

the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the eight liberations, and the nine successive meditative attainments cannot be transformed.

The nature of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the concentrations (*samādhi*), the doors of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇīmukha*), all the modes of emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatā*), the ten powers of a Tathāgata (*tathāgatabala*), the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*) cannot be transformed. For indeed, Kauśika, the nature of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) cannot be transformed. Thus, this is the counter-position (*vipakṣa*).

Furthermore, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to instruct others, to encourage them, to inspire them, and to gladden them regarding unexcelled perfect enlightenment, should instruct, encourage, inspire, and gladden others with a mind that follows reality as it is.
Furthermore, he should be encouraged in such a way that the bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom,
does not fall into conceptualization, thinking, "I am giving a gift."
"I maintain ethical discipline; I cultivate patience; I exert vigor."
"I enter into meditative absorption;
I cultivate wisdom;
I course in internal emptiness."
I practice in external emptiness; I practice in internal-external emptiness; I practice in all [the remaining types of emptiness] up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence.
I cultivate the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening; I cultivate the noble truths;
I enter into the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments.
"I cultivate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; I cultivate the eight liberations; I enter the nine successive meditative attainments."
"I enter into meditative absorption; I enter into the gateways of dhāraṇī; I cultivate the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha."
"I am practicing for the sake of awakening. In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva demonstrates, encourages, inspires, and gladdens others;
he does not harm himself, and he gladdens others in the manner of practice authorized by the Buddhas.

For in this way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be shown, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening. For in this way, a son of good family or a daughter of good family will have avoided all forms of attachment. Thus, furthermore, is the counteragent.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is well that you point out these points of attachment for the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, I shall explain to you other, more subtle points of attachment; listen to them and attend to them well and thoroughly."
"I shall speak to you. "So be it, Blessed One," the venerable Subhūti replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
"In this regard, Subhūti, a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment..."

Subhūti, as long as one attends to the Tathāgatas by way of signs, for that long there is attachment. Furthermore, regarding those Tathāgatas— from the first production of the thought of awakening until they have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and from then until their final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder, and as long as the true dharma remains— in this interval, [to attend to them by way of signs is attachment].
Whatever root of merit there may be, he attends to it all by way of signs; having so attended to it, he dedicates it toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Subhūti, as long as one attends to things by way of signs, for that long there is attachment. This includes even those roots of merit belonging to those Tathāgatas who have departed from all attachment—roots of merit that are themselves free from all attachment.
Then he also attends to the roots of merit of other beings by way of signs; having attended to them, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Subhūti, as long as one attends to things by way of signs, for that long there is attachment. Why is that?
Because those Tathāgatas are not to be attended to by way of signs.
Nor should one attend to the roots of virtue of those or others by way of signs. This is subtle attachment. Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is profound."
The Blessed One said:
"Subhūti, it is because all phenomena are by nature secluded.
Subhūti said:
"I pay homage, Blessed One, to the perfection of wisdom.
The Blessed One said:
"For indeed, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is uncreated and unconditioned; it cannot be fully awakened to by anyone. Thus is the profundity of the Dharma."
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, all dharmas are difficult to fully awaken to.
The Blessed One said:
For it is thus, Subhūti: there are not two natures of phenomena; there is, Subhūti, only one nature of phenomena, which is the nature of the Buddha-phenomena. That is no-nature.

That which is intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) is non-intrinsic nature; that which is intrinsic nature is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*). For in this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva knows and sees that single intrinsic nature as being without intrinsic nature and unconditioned, all millions of attachments are abandoned. Thus ends the abandonment of all attachments.
Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to fully awaken to.
The Blessed One said:

For in this way, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom has not been seen by anyone, nor heard, nor thought, nor cognized, nor fully awakened to. Thus, regarding its difficulty to be understood, Subhūti said:
"O Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is inconceivable."
The Blessed One said:
"For indeed, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom has not been cognized by anyone;
it is not cognized by form, nor by feeling, nor by perception, nor by mental formations, nor by consciousness, nor even by them individually or collectively."

It is not by means of the aggregates, elements, or sense-fields; nor by the factors of dependent origination; nor by the perfections; nor by the factors conducive to enlightenment; nor by the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, or the formless attainments; nor by the eight liberations; nor by the nine successive meditative attainments;
nor by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; nor by the superknowledges; nor by all the modes of emptiness; nor by all the samādhis.

It is not known by means of all the gateways of dhāraṇīs, nor by the powers of a Tathāgata, nor by the grounds of self-confidence, nor by the analytical knowledges, nor by the unique qualities of a Buddha.
Subhūti said:
“Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to perform.
The Blessed One said:

“Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is difficult to perform because all phenomena are non-apprehendable. Thus, in this statement regarding inconceivability, both the adverse factors and their remedies have been explained.
Subhūti said:
"How, O Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva course in the perfection of wisdom?
The Blessed One said:
In this regard, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom,
if he does not course in form, he courses in the perfection of wisdom; if he does not course in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, he courses in the perfection of wisdom.

Thus, when one does not course in the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and dependent origination— whether considered individually or collectively— one courses in the perfection of wisdom. Likewise, when one does not course in all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the meditative concentrations, all the doors of dhāraṇī, the foundations of mindfulness,
the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path, one courses in the perfection of wisdom.

One does not course in the noble truths, yet one courses in the perfection of wisdom. One does not course in the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, or in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet one courses in the perfection of wisdom. One does not course in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the specific analytical knowledges, or the unique qualities of a Buddha, yet one courses in the perfection of wisdom.
One does not course even in omniscience; one courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Thus is the application regarding form and so forth:
if one courses with the thought that "form is neither permanent nor impermanent," one courses in the perfection of wisdom.

If one practices with the thought that "form is neither pleasure nor pain," one practices in the perfection of wisdom; if one practices with the thought that "form is neither self nor non-self," one practices in the perfection of wisdom;
if one practices with the thought that "form is neither beautiful nor ugly," one practices in the perfection of wisdom.
If one practices with the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither permanent nor impermanent, one practices in the perfection of wisdom;

if one practices with the thought that consciousness is neither pleasant nor painful, one practices in the perfection of wisdom; if one practices with the thought that consciousness is neither self nor non-self, one practices in the perfection of wisdom; if one practices with the thought that consciousness is neither pure nor impure, one practices in the perfection of wisdom.
He courses in the perfection of wisdom. In this way, he courses in the individual and collective aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; the factors of dependent origination;

the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, limbs of awakening, and the path; the noble truths; the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments;
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the superknowledges, all the emptinesses, all the concentrations, and all the doors of dhāraṇī.

If one practices with the thought that the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, the unique buddha-qualities, and even omniscience itself are neither permanent nor impermanent, one is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
if one practices with the thought that omniscience is neither pleasant nor painful, one is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

One who practices that "all-knowledge is neither self nor non-self" is practicing the perfection of wisdom; one who practices that "all-knowledge is neither pure nor impure" is practicing the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
Because that form does not exist in such a way as to be either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, or pure or impure.

Feeling, perception, and mental formations do not exist as that consciousness which is either permanent or impermanent, pleasant or painful, self or non-self, pure or impure. In the same way, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields— whether taken individually or collectively— as well as dependent origination, the perfections, the factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, the formless attainments, the eight liberations, and the nine successive meditative dwellings, do not exist [in such a manner].
The superknowledges of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; all the emptinesses; all the concentrations; all the gateways of dhāraṇī;

the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the analytical knowledges, and the unique qualities of a Buddha—even up to omniscience itself—do not exist in such a way that it could be characterized as permanent or impermanent, as pleasure or suffering, as self or non-self, or as beautiful or ugly.
Or: thus is the application [of the syllogism] regarding the impermanence of form and so forth.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if he does not practice with the thought that "form is incomplete" or "form is complete," he practices the perfection of wisdom; if he does not practice with the thought that "feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are incomplete" or "they are complete," he practices the perfection of wisdom.

Thus, when one does not course in the thought that the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and the factors of dependent origination are incomplete or complete, one courses in the perfection of wisdom. Likewise, when one does not course in the thought that all the perfections, all the emptinesses, all the samādhis, and all the doors of dhāraṇī are incomplete or complete, one courses in the perfection of wisdom. Thus [one courses] with regard to the applications of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.

If one does not practice with the thought that "the [perfections] are incomplete" or "they are complete," one practices in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Likewise, regarding the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative concentrations, the formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges—if one does not practice with the thought that these are incomplete or complete, one practices in the perfection of wisdom. Likewise, regarding the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four...

If one does not course with the thought that the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are incomplete or complete, one courses in the perfection of wisdom; likewise, as long as one does not course with the thought that omniscience is incomplete or complete, one courses in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
If one does not course even in the idea that the non-perfection or perfection of form is itself form, then one courses in the perfection of wisdom;

if one does not course even in the idea that the non-perfection or perfection of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is itself consciousness, then one courses in the perfection of wisdom. This applies likewise up to the non-perfection of omniscience.
"Or, that which is fullness is not omniscience; even so, when one does not course [in such a way], one courses in the perfection of wisdom.
This is the application regarding the non-fullness of form and so forth.
When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“It is wonderful, Blessed One, how this attachment and non-attachment of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, has been explained!
The Blessed One said:

“So it is, Subhūti; it has been well-explained. Subhūti, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, has indeed explained both the attachment and the non-attachment of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.”

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not practice with the thought that form is "attached" or "unattached"; thus he practices the perfection of wisdom.

He does not practice with the thought that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are "attached" or "unattached"; thus he practices the perfection of wisdom. He does not practice with the thought that the eye is "attached" or "unattached"; thus he practices the perfection of wisdom.

In this way, when one does not course in the idea that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are with attachment or without attachment, one courses in the perfection of wisdom. Likewise, when one does not course in the idea that the perfection of generosity— within all the sense bases and elements— is with attachment or without attachment,
one courses in the perfection of wisdom.

In this way, if one does not practice with the thought that the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom are "with attachment" or "without attachment," one practices in the perfection of wisdom. Likewise, if one does not practice with the thought that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the noble truths, the immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments are "with attachment" or "without attachment," one practices in the perfection of wisdom.

If one does not course in the thought that emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the superknowledges, and all the emptinesses are "with attachment" or "without attachment," then one courses in the perfection of wisdom. Likewise, if one does not course in the thought that the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges,

the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all meditative concentrations, all doors of dhāraṇī, and omniscience are "with attachment" or "without attachment," then one courses in the perfection of wisdom.
He does not course, yet he courses in the perfection of wisdom.
Coursing in this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive form as being with attachment or without attachment;
nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being with attachment or without attachment. Thus...
One perceives that the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, perfections, emptinesses, factors of enlightenment, noble truths, immeasurables, meditative absorptions,

formless attainments, superknowledges, the concentrations on emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the doors of dhāraṇī, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the specific understandings, and the unique buddha-qualities are neither with attachment nor without attachment. While practicing the perfection of wisdom, one does not perceive omniscience as being either with attachment or without attachment.

He perceives: neither the fruit of stream-entry, nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the fruit of non-returning, nor arhatship, nor pratyekabuddhahood, nor unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. He perceives them as "with attachment" or "without attachment. This is the application of non-attachment regarding form and the other aggregates. Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:
It is marvelous, O Blessed One, that this profound perfection of wisdom neither diminishes when it is being taught, nor does it diminish when it is not being taught;
and it does not increase even when it is being taught.
Even when not being taught, it does not increase.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Subhūti:
"It is so, Subhūti; even when the perfection of wisdom is being taught, it does not diminish."
Even when not being taught, it does not diminish;
even when being taught, it does not increase;

even when not being taught, it does not increase. Subhūti, it is just as if a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to remain for the duration of his life speaking either the praises or the dispraises of space.
Furthermore, when praise is spoken of space, there is no increase; when dispraise is spoken, there is no decrease.
Space does not increase through praise nor does it diminish through dispraise.
This is the application of the governing principle (*adhikāra*).
Subhūti, it is just as if, for example, an illusory person does not increase when praise is spoken,
nor does he diminish when blame is spoken; and when praise is spoken, he is not led into attachment.

When disparagement is being spoken, one is struck down. In the same way, Subhūti, that which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena remains exactly the same whether it is taught or not taught. Thus [is] the application of non-agency.
Subhūti said:

O Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is a doer of what is difficult, who, while practicing the perfection of wisdom and when the perfection of wisdom is being taught, does not sink down, does not turn his mind away,
and applies himself to yoga in this very perfection of wisdom.
And he does not turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Why is that?
Blessed One, this cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is a cultivation of space;
yet the perfection of wisdom is not perceived within space.

The perfection of meditation is not discerned; the perfection of vigor, the perfection of patience, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of generosity are not discerned. Form is not discerned in space;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not discerned in space. Internal emptiness is not discerned in space.
External emptiness is not discerned;
internal-external emptiness is not discerned;
and so on, up to the emptiness of the essential nature of non-existence is not discerned. The applications of mindfulness are not discerned in space. In space...

The right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path are discerned; the noble truths are not discerned in space. The immeasurables, the meditative absorptions, and the formless attainments are not discerned in space. The eight liberations and the nine successive meditative attainments are not discerned in space. Emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the superknowledges are not discerned in space. The gateways of concentration and dhāraṇī are not discerned in space.

They are not perceived. The gateways of meditative concentration and mnemonic formulas (*samādhi-dhāraṇī-mukha*) are not perceived in space. Calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) are not perceived in space.

The ten powers of a Tathāgata are not perceived in space. The four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are not perceived in space. The fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpatti-phala*) is not perceived in space.
It is discerned. The fruit of the once-returner is not discerned in space. The fruit of the non-returner is not discerned in space.
Arhatship is not discerned in space. Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment is not discerned in space. Unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is not discerned in space.
Subhūti said:
I pay homage, Blessed One, to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, by whom this armor has been donned.

O Blessed One, they who don the armor for the sake of sentient beings are desirous of acting, desirous of striving, and desirous of meditating for the sake of space. O Blessed One, they who don the armor for the sake of sentient beings are desirous of liberating space.

They arm themselves. Blessed One, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, for the sake of phenomena that are like space, arm themselves with armor, are armed with the great armor. This is the application regarding the difficulty of the objective.

Blessed One, those who, for the sake of sentient beings, arm themselves with armor, are like those who wish to lift up the sky, the atmosphere. This is the application regarding the difficulty of the practice.

"Blessed One, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, for the sake of sentient beings, desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, have attained the perfection of great vigor. Why is that?
Blessed One, if this trichiliocosm were filled with Tathāgatas, just as a thicket of reeds, or a bamboo grove, or a sugarcane field, or a field of *śara* grass, or a field of rice,"
Those Tathāgatas might teach the Dharma for an eon or for the remainder of an eon, and each individual Tathāgata might lead immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings to final nirvāṇa;
yet, Blessed One, no decrease or increase in the realm of sentient beings is perceived. Why is that?

Based on the non-existence of sentient beings and based on the solitude of sentient beings. In this way, in each single direction, and so on up to the ten directions, all world-systems might be filled with Tathāgatas,
just as, for example, a thicket of reeds, or a bamboo grove, or a field of sugarcane, or a thicket of *śara* grass, or a field of rice.

And suppose those Tathāgatas were to remain for an eon or the remainder of an eon and teach the Dharma, and each individual Tathāgata were to lead immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite sentient beings to final nirvāṇa;
yet, Blessed One, no decrease or increase in the realm of sentient beings is perceived. Why is that?
"Based on the non-existence of sentient beings and based on the solitude of sentient beings, O Blessed One, it is by this very method that I say:

those who, for the sake of sentient beings, desire to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, O Blessed One, they are desirous of liberating space. Thus is the application of the difficulty of the task.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to a certain monk:
"I pay homage, Blessed One, to the Blessed Mother Prajñāpāramitā, wherein no dharma whatsoever is apprehended nor does it cease,
yet the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha) is made known."
The aggregate of concentration is discerned, the aggregate of wisdom is discerned, and the aggregate of liberation is discerned.
The aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation is discerned;
the fruit of stream-entry is discerned;
the fruit of once-returning is discerned.
the fruit of non-returning is discerned,
arhatship is discerned,
and the state of a pratyekabuddha is discerned;
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is known; the Three Jewels are known; the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha are known.
The turning of the wheel of Dharma is made known; thus is the unfailing application. Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the venerable Subhūti:
"Venerable Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva applies himself to yoga in this profound perfection of wisdom, where does he apply that yoga?"
Subhūti said:
"Kauśika, he who thinks that one should train in this profound perfection of wisdom will be practicing yoga in space.
Then Śakra, lord of the gods, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"O Blessed One, whichever son of good family or daughter of good family shall take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, master it, and attend to it with wise reflection— I, O Blessed One, will certainly provide for their protection, defense, and guardianship. Subhūti said:
“Kauśika, do you perceive that dharma for which you wish to provide protection, defense, and guardianship?
Śakra replied: “Venerable Subhūti, I do not perceive that dharma for which I shall provide protection, defense, and guardianship.
Subhūti said:

If, Kauśika, sons of good family or daughters of good family abide in the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, that itself will be their protection, defense, and guard. But if they are separated from the perfection of wisdom as it has been taught, humans and non-humans alike will find an opportunity to harm them. Kauśika, one would be seeking to provide protection, defense, and guard for space!

"Whoever thinks that he should provide protection, defense, and guardianship for the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who course in the perfection of wisdom—what do you think, Kauśika, are you capable of providing protection, defense, and guardianship for illusions, mirages, dreams, echoes, optical illusions, reflections, and cities of the Gandharvas?
Śakra replied: "No, Venerable Subhūti."
Subhūti said:

"In just this way, Kauśika, whoever thinks that he should provide protection, defense, and guardianship for Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, who are coursing in the perfection of wisdom, would only share in frustration and exhaustion. What do you think?"
"Kauśika, are you capable of providing protection, shelter, and defense for a Tathāgata or for a magical emanation of a Tathāgata?
Śakra replied, "No, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said:

"It is so, Kauśika. Whoever thinks that they should provide protection, defense, and guardianship for those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas who course in the perfection of wisdom, would only share in weariness and exhaustion. What do you think, Kauśika? Are you able to provide protection, defense, and guardianship for the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), suchness (tathatā), or the inconceivable realm?"
Śakra said: "No, venerable Subhūti.
Subhūti said:
"In just this way, Kauśika, regarding the protection, defense, and guardianship of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who course in the perfection of wisdom..."
He would consider that he ought to provide for them; however, he would only be a partaker of weariness and exhaustion. Thus ends the application of not relying on others.

Śakra said: "To what extent, Venerable Subhūti, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom [realize] that all phenomena are like a dream, like an illusion, like a mirage, like an echo, like a reflection, and like a city of the Gandharvas?"
